OF 
NAPOLEON FIRST. 
YEAR 1811. 


18245. - TO M. MARET, DUC DE BASSANO, 
MINISTER OF EXTERNAL RELATIONS, PARIS. 
Saint Cloud. November 12, 1811. 


Monsieur le Duke de Bassano, it appears that Russian couriers passed to Meiz yesterday; we will 
have news today. I wish you to prepare for General Lauriston a dispatch which you will submit to me, 
and in which you will inform him of my arrival at Paris, the continuation of my pacific dispositions, and 
my desire to see the conclusion, this winter, of our differences with Russia. You will tell him that a 
division of cuirassiers has gone to Erfurt; that the uncertainty of all that was done in Prussia seemed to 
necessitate the increase of our forces in cavalry; that we know nothing of the manner of acting of this 
power; you will tell him what has happened with regard to armament, disarmament, the announcement 
that it was disarming and the continuation of armaments, so that I do not know what that means; that it 
must make it clear how the question is embarrassed, how it might lead to it, and how much it is 
necessary to appoint commissioners on both sides to tranquillize on all points and put an end to this state 
of affairs. 

You will be careful to make known that all this must be said without affectation and of course. 

Count Lauriston may even slightly insinuate that it is very unfortunate that Prussia interferes in 
arming; that it is in the interest of this power that it does not interfere with the question and does not 
allow itself for movements which may immediately lead to others. 

The same courier will carry a letter to M. de Saint-Marsan on the movements of Prussia and the 
necessity where it has put us’ 





Page 2 


to operate cavalry. He will again press Prussia to remain calm. 
NAPOLEON. 
From the original. Foreign Affairs Archives. 


18246. - TO THE COUNT OF MONTALIVET, 
MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR, IN PARIS. 
Saint-Cloud, November 8, 1811. 


Order the Prefect of La Roer to go to Wesel and terminate the affairs of that city: 1 to settle in 
receipts and to spend the budget for 1811; 2™ submit without delay the budget of 1812, so that it be 
submitted to my signature before the 1st of December; 3™ to create income, and therefore to establish a 
French-style grant for 1812. 

For the budget, the first question that comes up is debt. The debt has not been recognized; my 
intention is to regulate it as in Belgium; to constitute it in its entirety would absorb too much revenue; 
but a draft decree will be presented to me to form part of it on the principle of what has been done for 
Antwerp. 

The prefect will present a plan to set up a sub-prefecture, a court of first instance, at Wesel, and 
to form a district in the departments of Lippe and Roer, so that there are at least 50,000 souls. We will 
not take anything in the Grand Duchy of Berg. There is, I believe, a tribunal at Reuss; from then on, it 
will simply be to transfer it to Wesel. The decree will also designate the dwelling where the court and 
the sub - prefecture will be established. 

We will take care to repair the pavement perfectly; this is necessary for military 
communications. The prefect will also establish a lighting system such that the city is perfectly lit. The 
houses to be slaughtered will be evaluated, and the decree will order the demolition of the houses near 
the great church, which obstruct the communications from the Miinster gate to that of the Rhine. The 
prefect, the mayor and the commander of the engineering will meet, and the prefect will present a plan 
of alignment of the city, so as to destroy all the existing excavations, to regulate the traffic and to create 
a new place between the door of ....... (1) (and the current government house.) There could be a large 
square fort, one side of which would support the door, and one side of which would be used to build a 
hotel for the governor. hostel, a theater and 





1) The name 1s left blank on the minute.” 





Page 3 


the other necessary dwellings in a city of great garrison and which will be a considerable center of 
passage. 

The prefect will also present me a project to make known the place where one could establish a 
civil hospital, intended to contain ordinarily 100 beds and able to contain 300; what is needed in a war 
place. 

This commission will also present a project, with the estimate of the appropriate indemnities, to 
bring down all the houses which hinder the defense of the city; some were built on the very ground of 
the fortifications. 

The prefect will also present a draft decree and the measures to be taken to establish a French 
secondary school at Wesel and primary schools where French is shown, and finally to establish a 
bourgeois artillery company like the one in exists in Lille, and a fire department. 

The prefect will remain at Wesel until all these projects and estimates are perfectly written.

18247. - TO GENERAL CLARKE, DUKE OF FELTRE, 
MINSTRE OF WAR, IN PARIS. 
Saint-Cloud, November 12, 1811. 


I see with pleasure, by your letter of the 9th, that the two battalions of the 1st and 2nd regiments 
of Banat are in good condition. Have them rest in Dijon two or three days, and order them to be directed 
to Paris, where I wish to see them. You will have them stay in a barracks two leagues from Paris, where 
you will pass the review, and when you have ascertained their correct condition, I will see them on the 
parade. 

The demand for French officers is right. You have to give them German speaking. 

As for the other regiment at Trieste, I do not know whether it would be proper to withdraw so 
many Croats; I do not think I asked. I would take them with pleasure, since that would make Germany a 
new brigade, but I would like to know if it is political. Give me a report on that. 

It is good that you write to these two regiments, before they arrive at Dijon, that their destination 
is for Paris, because I want to see them. This could be a good effect and may prevent some desertions.

18248. - TO GENERAL CLARKE, DUKE OF FELTRE, 
MINSTRE OF WAR, IN PARIS. 
Saint Cloud. November 12, 1811. 


I answer your letter from the 6 on the armament of cuirassiers and lancers; it is an extremely 
important question. 

It is recognized that the armored cavalry can hardly use its carbine; but it is also very absurd that 
3 or 4,000 men of such good people are surprised in their quartering or arrested in their march by two 
companies of voltigeurs. It is therefore essential to arm them. The regiments of cuirassiers of the old 
regime had carabiners, which they wore, not like light cavalry, slung over their shoulders, but which 
they wore to use as rifles. 

I want you to form a council of cavalry officers and determine something about this object. I can 
not get used to seeing 3,000 elite men who, in an insurrection or surprise of light troops, would be 
kidnapped by a partisan, or in a march stopped by some bad skirmishers behind a brook or a house: this 
is absurd. My intention is that every man has a rifle; that it is a very short carabiner, worn in the most 
suitable manner to the cuirassiers, I do not care. I have already given the big cavalry carabiners. At 
peace they sent them away; in the last campaign they did not have one. 

Present me a project on this, so that these 3,000 men do not need infantry to keep in their 
cantonments, and, dismounting, can emerge when there is an infantry force a great disproportion with 
them. The war is composed of unforeseen events; it is not to have any idea of it that supposing that 
15,000 men of heavy cavalry can always be held in order to be covered. 

As for lancers, see if it is possible to give them a rifle with their spear; if it is not possible, it 
would be necessary to have at least one-third of the company armed with rifles, that is to say, all the first 
rank and half of the second rank, all the marshals of the houses and the third of the company (about 40 
men, supposing them complete), armed with carbines. The Cossacks have the spear, but they have rifles 
and even large guns with which they fire very far." 


Page 5 


You will also bring this into the object of the work of the commission of general officers. 
According to the minute. Archives of the Empire. 


18249. - TO GENERAL CLARKE, DUKE OF FELTRE, 
MINSTRE OF WAR, IN PARIS. 
Saint-Cloud, November 12, 1811. 


I see in your letter of the 6th of November, that the three Swiss regiments which are in France 
will be able to offer me only six battalions, and the Ist, which arrives at Placentia, only two. It would be 
only eight battalions instead of twelve. But I expect a recruitment of 3,000 men during the winter; This 
will allow each regiment to supply one more battalion. To have these 3,000 men, it is urgent to attend 
diligently. See the Duke of Bassano and M. Maillardoz. Switzerland costs me immense money and does 
me no service; until this hour I am very duped, since I have a cohort of officers without soldiers. It is 
necessary that the cantons undertake to recruit; 2" reduce battalions from nine to six companies, which 
will reduce officers by one-third. I will then have four regiments, each regiment of four battalions, each 
battalion of six companies, each company of 140 men, and 3,200 men per regiment or 12,000 men. To 
recruit these 12,000 men, it is necessary that the cantons undertake to keep them in full. I approve, 
however, that they are not obliged to furnish more than 3,000 men a year. 

3,000 men in eight years equal 24,000 men; in taking away the dead, the deserters, etc., it is to be 
hoped that this will be maintained at 12,000 men. 

It would be necessary, however, that in the case of a war with Russia or Austria, a war which 
interests the Swiss, since in case of unsuccessful they would be compromised, they supply 4,000 men 
instead of 3,000. Here are the basics on which to work without delay. 

However, they must provide 16,000 men; there will therefore be for them economy. 

According to the minute. Archives of the Empire.”

18250. - TO GENERAL CLARKE, DUKE OF FELTRE, 
MINSTRE OF WAR, IN PARIS. 
Saint-Cloud, November 12, 1811. 


During my stay in Givet, a detachment of British prisoners worked to restore a flying bridge. 
Among these I noticed the zeal and activity of eight or ten of those especially who threw themselves into 
a batelet to help maneuver the bridge. Order that the state of the ten men who are most distinguished in 
this circumstance be trained; that the men should be dressed to nine, and that each one should be given 
five napoleons with an order of the road to Morlaix, where they will be handed over to the Transport 
Office, making known the reason for their deliverance. You will inform the Minister of the Navy, whom 
this correspondence looks upon. It is necessary that there be no injustice, and that the men who have 
behaved best be chosen preferably. There is an English minister there who has asked for permission to 
spend three months in England; give it to him. He could be responsible for driving others. Finally, I send 
you a petition which has been handed to me in the same circumstances by an Englishwoman; give me a 
report on what she is asking for. 

According to the minute. Archives of the Empire. 


18251. - TO GENERAL CLARKE, DUKE OF FELTRE, 
MINSTRE OF WAR, IN PARIS, 
Saint-Cloud, November 12, 1811. 


The captain of the artillery company of the 3rd regiment on horseback, which is at Bonn, is 
missing; the lieutenant is a young madman, having three or four years of service: it is very important to 
send a good captain to this company. I even wish it to be sent to an infantry division in Germany, since 
it is composed of conscripts, and to be replaced by another company of the 2nd regiment of mounted 
artillery. By this means, the division of cuirassiers would be served by the companies of the same 
regiment. 

I would like the same thing for all the divisions of cuirassiers. Instead of two companies from 
two different regiments, each would have two companies of the same regiment. 

Likewise for the battalions of the train, there are at Cologne two companies of the same battalion 
of the train which serve in two different divisions; there are similarly in Bonn two other companies of 
the same 





Page 7 


battalion divided between two divisions; it would be much more convenient to unite them. It is 
necessary that the two companies of the train which appear necessary for the service of the same 
division of cuirassiers are of the same battalion. 

An important observation, too, is to give the command of the light artillery of cuirassiers to men 
who have made previous campaigns with the divisions of cuirassiers. I saw in Bonn a chef who has not 
yet done this service and who is going to do his apprenticeship. 

These divisions of cuirassiers serve differently. It is therefore necessary to have men who have 
experienced the campaigns of Austria, Iena or Friedland. 

These mounted artillery companies have no workmen, so that the twenty-four pieces of cannon I 
saw in Cologne and Bonn did not have a single workman. Why do horse-drawn artillery companies have 
no workers? 

Do not attach to the service of the cuirassiers any artillery company which has been ruined in 
Spain, and which has been recruited with the conscription of this year; but put on horse-drawn artillery 
companies that have not suffered and rested since 1809. 

It is necessary to appoint a general of artillery brigade to take the command of the artillery of the 
cavalry of reserve. He will have forty-eight pieces under his orders, will review it, put everything in 
order, and may hold himself at Wesel. 

It would also be necessary to have a brigadier general who had served the cavalry, either as 
colonel or general, in past campaigns. 

According to the minute. Archives of the Empire. 


18252. - TO GENERAL CLARKE, DUKE OF FELTRE, 
MINSTRE OF WAR, IN PARIS. 
Saint-Cloud, November 12, 1811. 


I answer your letter of the 9th on the artillery crews of the observation corps of the Elbe. 

I do not know why the 7th Division is carried to twenty-eight pieces of cannon; it seems to me 
that he must only have fourteen, like the others. This division is also at Danzig. 

Have state n°1 redone. 

The artillery of the 1st, 5th and 6th divisions will be placed in the 32nd military division, as well 
as sixteen pieces of the reserve division. Their’ 





Page 8 


park must be organized so that they have their dual supply. 

The 7th division will be placed at Danzig; To this end, we will take all the equipment, staff and 
teams on what exists today in Danzig. 

The artillery of the 8th and the 9th Division, as well as the two batteries of the reserve, will meet 
at Wesel: to know, their supply and a half by division, and the remainder forming a portion of the part of 
the reserve park which will remain at Wesel. 

Lastly, the artillery of the four cavalry reserve divisions, forming a state apart, having the 
artillery of two divisions at Wesel, and that of a division at Hanover, with a supply of one and a half; 
one to Erfurt with a supply and a half, and the other half-supply with half-supply of the divisions which 
are on the Rhine, to Wesel, where they will form the reserve. 

Depending on your condition, it takes 7,000 horsepower to do this service. I think that the four 
battalions which are in Germany should be completed in men and horses, and destined for the service of 
the nine infantry divisions and the four batteries of the reserve and the park, and employ another 
battalion of those who are in France, which one would also complete, for the service of the four 
divisions of the cavalry reserve. By this means the big park would be divided into two fractions: one in 
Minden and one in Wesel. The whole organization of the cuirassiers would be attached to an artillery 
general and a director of the cavalry reserve park, who would reside at Wesel and report to the director 
general of the park. It would then remain to send workers to Wesel to mount a strong repair workshop. It 
would also take all the churches of Wesel, except for one for the Catholics and one for the Protestants, to 
be able to deposit all this material and shelter it during the bad season, without however unloading it: the 
horses will be in Wesel and in the surroundings; so that, twenty-four hours after the reception of your 
order, the whole column may set out to march on the campaign. 

It seems to me that there is a need for a colonel at Minden, an artillery general and a director of 
the park at Wesel. The equipment becoming very considerable, it would be necessary to have a general 
of division to command the artillery, and three brigadier generals, each of them charged with the 
command and supervision of the artillery of three divisions, and who would be employed according to 
the circumstances and modifications that events would necessitate. As for companies 


Page 9 


in the artillery, it is necessary to seek the companies of the regiments on foot or on horseback, which are 
already in Germany, since there is so great an advantage in keeping the regiments together as much as 
possible. 

It is necessary that this does not affect the organization of the corps of Italy or that of the corps of 
observation of the Rhine, so that these corps can organize an artillery as it was set on paper, without the 
need for new calculations; for the observation corps of the Elbe must be independent of the organization 
of the other two corps. 

Independently of the reserve of the Guard, you will make me a state of recapitulation which 
makes known the state of all the artillery: 1st, that of the corps of the Elbe, as has been said above, 2nd 
of the reserve of the cavalry, 3rd that of Italy, and 4th that of the Rhine, as they were previously 
regulated.

18253. - TO GENERAL CLARKE, DUKE OF FELTRE, 
MINSTRE OF WAR, IN PARIS. 
Saint Cloud. November 12, 1811. 


The 127th, 128th and 129th regiments give serious concern; all the tests that have been made by 
placing them on the islands have not succeeded. This justifies the rumors that had reached me for several 
months by England about these regiments. It is time to take a party. We must first separate them. Order 
the Prince d'Eckmiihl, by the evening dispatch, to send out the one of the three regiments, which is the 
worst, and direct him to Maestricht. Order a good brigadier general, speaking German, to take command 
of this regiment and to pass a severe inspection. The two other regiments will be placed under orders, 
one of General Latour, the other of a brigadier-general, speaking German, whom the Prince of Eckmuhl 
will designate. The Prince of Eckmiihl, where he will review it himself, or pass a rigorous review by his 
staff officers. He will direct by detachments of 100 men, on the regiments of the Tour d'Auvergne and 
Isembourg, the Prussians, Mecklenburgers, Russians and Danes who are in these regiments. It will send 
to the colonial pioneers the bad subjects that there would be. Finally he will proceed to the cleaning of 
the cadres in the following way: he will see the colonels, majors, chiefs of battalion and adjutants- 
majors, will make sure that they are French speaking German, having made the war with us and having 
the qualities” 





Page 10 


required. He will be authorized to send to Maestricht or Wesel, where they will be at your disposal, the 
officers who do not possess the necessary qualifications, with notes, so that you may offer me 
employment for them; the captains, lieutenants and second lieutenants who leave the Austrian service; 
he will also send notes on them. Those who will be suspected will also be sent back to Wesel. As for 
those coming out of the old service, from the cities of Bremen, Hamburg, Oldenburg, he will distinguish 
those who are native to the cities, who are domiciled there, and of their parents, of those who are 
foreigners, and who have been admitted to service of these cities. 

Foreigners will be sent to Wesel, with notes, so that you can propose to give them employment 
or to place them in foreign regiments. Those who are of the country, the prince of Eckmiihl will make 
two classes: some, which we will try to keep in the regiments until further order, and the others, that we 
can send to Italy and Spain in the corps. He will have the vacant officers and non-commissioned officers 
replaced, so as to complete only three battalions in each regiment. The result of this operation will be 
that there will be in these regiments other superior officers only French officers, and other captains, 
lieutenants and sub-lieutenants than Frenchmen or officers who have made war with us, or officers 
leaving the Austrian service, and provisionally officers of the country, good subjects, domiciled and 
known. The same operation will be done for non-commissioned officers. No foreign NCO will be 
suffered in these regiments; only NCOs born in the 32nd Military Division, but domiciled and known, 
will be kept there; still this number will be noted, in order to insensibly make them pass elsewhere. 
Finally the same operation will be done for the soldiers. All that will be Prussian, Danish, Swedish, 
Mecklenburger, Russian, will be directed, by detachments of 100 men, to the regiments of Strasburg and 
Tour d'Auvergne, so that only men born in the 32nd military division will remain in the regiment; and 
those who would be considered bad subjects, either foreigners or the natives of the country, will be 
governed by detachments of 25 men from the settlements of colonial pioneers. You will authorize Prince 
Eckmiithl to replace the officers and non-commissioned officers by men drawn from his army corps, but 
speaking German; he will send you the report, and you will present to me draft decrees to be signed. 
You will give the same instructions for the regiment when it reaches Maestricht. We will see, when the 
regiments are thus purified, if they present a more satisfactory aspect. '

Tell the Prince of Eckmiihl that it would be important for him to be able to see these regiments himself, 
at least that he should have this operation done by a man of a more sure and finer tact than General 
Latour.

18254. - TO GENERAL LACUEE, COUNTY OF CESSAC, 
MINISTER DIRECTOR OF THE ADMINISTRATION OF THE WAR, IN PARIS. 
Saint-Cloud, November 12, 1811. 


In the visit I made to different corps of the army, I found that the troops were better dressed than 
in the revolution, where the supplies were made by the suppliers of the time; but I was far from satisfied, 
considering the immense sums which they cost me and the regularity which is carried in the 
administration in the present times. It is impossible to provide anything to the troops who are good; 
because how can they want to fight against the interest of suppliers? In general, knits are bad, shakos are 
of poor quality, or they are often of good quality, but poorly made. It is the same of the gibbets. No 
reproach can be done to the corps, because they answer all that the administration of the war sent them 
to them ". As for the sheets, most of the one I saw is much worse than the one I saw at the regiments that 
bought them themselves. 

The light infantry regiments, which used to buy sheets, find, in general, that the sheets [woolen 
fabric] they bought were much better than the ones they are sent. 

I therefore wish to know in what manner dress will be made in 1812. It is my intention that the 
administration of war supplies nothing, at most cloth; and again I think that this is a question: for it is the 
fact that the regiments of light infantry, during the time they have dressed, have been better than they are 
today. A major who is pressed by a large number of conscripts whom he has to clothe receives all that is 
sent to him, although of bad quality. There are also people who do not want to do business and establish 
a litigation. It is therefore necessary that effective measures are taken to ensure that the sheet that will be 
provided is provided good, especially as it is not reasonable to send sheets to the bottom of Illyria so 
they come back then. It is late for everything, is detrimental to my service and ruins the suppliers. We 
must give the regiments the latitude not to receive the sheet that would be bad, but first and foremost!’ 


alls 


Page 12 


take steps to ensure that the sheets we send are of good quality. The present offices of clothing are 
organized only for accounting; they do nothing to ensure the accuracy of shipments, what is in store and 
the kindness of supplies; so that, instead of welcoming and encouraging the complaints of corps, they 
are badly received in general. 

In the Grand Duchy of Berg, I give all the money to the corps; the masses are a little less strong 
than in France; I have not seen troops so well dressed and in such good condition; that can not make any 
comparison with ours. 

In your rides, I found a lot of bad horses. Market conditions are generally to be redone. 

According to the minute. Archives of the Empire. 


18255. - TO COUNT LACEPEDE,

Saint-Cloud, November 12, 1811. 


I am assured that Chief of Battalion Everts, of the 4th of line, has been appointed officer of the 
Legion of Honor not yet legionnaire. You had to verify the fact, and if it was true, send me back my 
decree. You are not excusable. 

You know that I always have the principle of never being an officer in the Legion of Honor if 
one is not already legionary, as well as for all ranks. 

When an error occurs, it is up to you to represent the decree.

18257.-VICE-AMIRAL COUNT DECRES, 
MINISTER OF THE NAVY, IN PARIS. 
Saint-Cloud, November 14, 1811. 


There is a decree for La Spezia. However, construction continued to take place in Genoa. What 
had led me to place the establishments at La Spezia was less the beauty of the harbor than the bad 
establishment of Genoa. The constructions took place outside the fortifications, in an isolated place, 
which was not reasonable; but since you have made known to me that we can build in the dock, I think 
that we must stick to Genoa, for all sorts of reasons, first because it is the center of a large population, 
and that offers all ease. Give me a report on that; because, if you can build in the dock, you will have a 
superb arsenal. I would not be far from prolonging the dikes and spending 2 millions for that; which, 
moreover, has the political advantage of being very agreeable to this great population. That supposed, it 
would be necessary that the marine kept the establishment of the quarantine station of Spezia. This year, 
I made work for the fortifications, since in maneuvering in the Mediterranean there is no doubt that this 
gulf will be necessary to us, and that it will be useful even to repair our ships. 

According to the minute. Archives of the Empire. 


18258. - TO THE VICE-AMIRAL COUNT DECRES, 
MINISTER OF THE NAVY, IN PARIS. 
Saint Cloud. November 14, 1811. 


The Gulf of Villefranche can be useful to our squadrons, as well as the Gulf Juan. Draw on a 
map the batteries that exist, as well as the armament and their current state. It is to be expected that our 
ships of Toulon, continuing to leave, will be obliged to seek their refuge in the harbor of Marseilles. Let 
me know where they are going and the current situation of the batteries, so that I can determine what 
needs to be done.

18239. - TO MARSHAL DAVOUT, PRINCE OF ECKMUHL, 
COMMANDING THE CORPS OF OBSERVATION OF THE ELBE IN HAMBURG. 
Saint-Cloud, November 14, 1811. 


Cousin, it would be proper for you to submit to me a plan for a movement, on the following 
bases, to be executed in the event of Prussia being in bad faith. Prince Poniatowski, with the Army of 
the Grand Duchy and the 7th Division, would meet in a combined movement, in a few days, and before 
the news reached Berlin, to intercept the road from Berlin to Graudenz and Dirschau; so that all the 
existing Prussian soldiers would be disarmed and taken prisoner, the convoys taken, Graudenz first 
blocked, Marienburg occupied and immediately entrenched, and the entrenchments the enemy made on 
the from Pillau, in the isthmus which communicates with Danzig, surprised, at the time that all the 
Saxons would march by Glogau, and you by Stettin and Magdeburg on Berlin and on Kolberg. This 
project aims, if Prussia continues to be in bad faith, to take the initiative; it must be well calculated to 
make it profitable. Mark me on a map the current position of the Army of the Grand Duchy, that of your 
divisions, the troops of Saxony and Westphalia, and let me know how you would hear these movements, 
and finally what are the forces Prussia would have to oppose Berlin and Kolberg. It will be necessary, 
when I have approved this plan, that you communicate it to Prince Poniatowski and General Rapp, so 
that they know him well, and that, informed of my intentions, they have an eye on the gatherings of the 
Prussians and know where it hits as soon as you give them the order. 

I do not need to tell you that this is all very hypothetical. Count Saint-Marsan is at present 
negotiating with Prussia; but I see so much bad faith and uncertainty in this cabinet, that I believe it will 
be impossible to prevent its ruin. I believe that on the Oder the Prussians have only one bridge; it will 
therefore be easy to seize and destroy it, and to envelop all their garrisons between the Oder and the 
Vistula before they perceive it. The forces of the Prussians are divided, I believe, between Saxony and 
Silesia, between the Elbe and the Vistula, between the Vistula and the Niemen. How many troops are 
there in each of these parts? how much can they bring together? For this operation I do not need to tell 
you that Modlin and Zamosc will be well supplied and armed; that part of the army of the Grand Duchy 
will be under observation on the side of Russia, and that all'* 


14 


Page 15 


your corps d'armee and the Saxons will be on the Vistula before the Russians, since you would be in 
Berlin that one would not know it yet in Petersburg. Share the situation in Marienburg. Have the 
fortifications I had been established destroyed, or could this post be promptly restored? If the 
entrenchments on the side of the .... (1) could not be removed with a hand, we must have a good number 
of howitzers and small mortars, to overwhelm them with shells and bombs and the to destroy in a few 
days, in order to close the passage of Pillau at once. Let me know how far the boundary of Danzig's 
territory is on this side. It might be convenient to have a good redoubt established at the edge of the 
Danzig territory. By this means we could mask the movement, and instead of leaving Danzig, we would 
leave the redoubt. Besides, since the Prussians work so much at Pillau, the occupation of a point on this 
side is very cautious. 

Do not write anything about it to General Rapp or Prince Poniatowski. Start by taking 
information before responding to me; it does not hurry. It is better to wait a fortnight for you to let me 
know the state of the chessboard. When I have your plan, I will ratify it, and then I will only allow you 
to communicate this possible project to Prince Poniatowski and General Rapp. 

NAPOLEON.

peace so far as to conclude, I am assured of Austria.

18264. - TO THE VICE-AMIRAL COUNT DECRES, 
MINISTER OF THE NAVY, IN PARIS. 
St. Cloud, November 16, 1811. 


Count Decres, I send you notes on the flotilla of Boulogne, which will make you perfectly know 
in what spirit I consider it. The flotilla of Boulogne will be one of the most powerful means of 
influencing England; and whenever our squadrons begin to stir and the fleet is doubled or tripled, the 
fishermen and sailors of the coast will be required to embark on the flotilla of artillery and materiel. 
England will expect a combination which will bring squadrons to Boulogne, and from then on she will 
be obliged to keep a large part of her ships in the Thames and the Dunes, and a body of troops large 
enough to cover London and its yards. I therefore think that four or five hundred vessels of the flotilla 
will always be necessary to have at Boulogne, in order to be able to transport forty thousand men and 
several thousand horses on the other bank; that artillery and equipment can be reduced at will, in order 
to relieve the buildings and to give more space for transport; lastly, that we can use indifferently all the 
buildings we have; that the expense will consist in the maintenance of the 500 buildings. Let me know 
the situation of the flotilla as I ordered it, which has since been subtracted, what remains in material and 
personnel, in order to definitively settle the organization of all that is necessary for the flotilla. 

NAPOLEON. 

According to the original comm. by Madame la Duchesse Decres.

Saint-Cloud, November 18, 1811. 


You will find letters from the King of Naples; you will answer it. As soon as we know the 
quantity of mortars which is necessary for it, we will keep it at Toulon; it will be necessary for him to

fired, so that he may be sent to them who have the requisite qualities. Having ordered the establishment 
of a camp at Scilla, my intention was that this camp should be permanent like those of Boulogne, of the

Sicily without the enemy being able to prejudge the determined period; but the King having judged it 
expedient, although commanding my army, to raise the camp and return to Naples, he thereby made my 
projects miss, and made the position of the English in Sicily beautiful, bad that it would become. It is of 
the first importance to have a stronghold at the end of the boot, where a garrison of 2 or 3,000 men can 
hold six weeks open trench and give time to come to their rescue. In this place, supplies of countryside, 
siege and strong batteries to intercept the strait, will have to exist. This place was to be built for three

Consequently, what is of the first necessity is to have a strong point on the continent, towards Sicily, 
which ensures the communications of the army in Sicily; it's the first thing to do. I want to have a map 
of the place where we work, and to know when it can be finished. As for an expedition to Sicily, it 
should not be considered as an expedition of a month or two; it must be considered a permanent war and 
must be firmly established. Meanwhile, a camp of 10 or 12,000 men must be placed near Sicily; it will 
also serve to accelerate the work of the fortress. A flotilla of war must be reunited. When these 
preliminary operations are done, the movement of the squadrons of Toulon, Texel, and the Scheldt, with 
troops that I send from France, will do the rest, But the Sicilian expedition to the English line, which is 
the mistress of the sea can be combined and followed to be put to an end only with secrecy and activity; 
the role to be played by the King of Naples is to gather 10 or 12,000 men and a flotilla on the side of the 
strait, and to establish a place which can support two months of open trench, with formidable batteries at 
the point opposite the strait. 

If English frigates have approached the coast, it is because the batteries are badly armed or badly 
arranged; they must be armed with cannon of a higher caliber. 

Indeed, it seems that a sharp dissension takes place in Sicily. The action taken by the King, to 
have closed the camp of Sicily without my order, having disturbed my dispositions and missed the 
opportunity to take advantage of them, steps must be taken to remedy them as soon as possible, starting 
an operation plan that can have these results.

18271.-TO THE COUNT MOLLIEN, 
MINISTER OF THE PUBLIC TREASURY, IN PARIS. 
St. Cloud, November 20, 1811. 


I beg you to secretly take some information, and to see if you could not suggest to me some ideas 
to give the administration of the games a fixed rule. 

The administration of the Paris Games, it seems, employs a fund of bankers from 11 to 1200,000 
francs. Independently of 3 or 4 million which it pays in the police fund and expenses of any kind, that 
administration makes a profit which one estimates from 100 to 150 per cent, so that this house reread 2 
to 3 million the placing of a capital of 1,200,000 francs. It is calculated, I believe, that games make 
bankers 7 to 8 million gross. It seems to me extremely absurd to leave a house which has made a huge 
fortune an annual bonus of 1,800,000 francs. There was a time when the sum of 1,200,000 francs it takes 
every day could be an object. 

It would be necessary to learn the mechanism of this machine, and see if it could not be exploited 
by a company, either for the benefit of hospitals, or that of the supply of wheat reserves of the city from 
Paris. 

One named Davelouis was very much occupied with these matters; he is good at listening, 
without believing in all his assertions. He can indicate men versed in this part. This must be done with 
secrecy and some kind of skill, because the police are very much on the lookout, viewing the games as a 
farm that many of the minister's agents want to exploit for their benefit.

18274. - TO GENERAL CLARKE, DUKE OF FELTRE, 
MINISTER OF WAR, IN PARIS. 
St. Cloud, November 20, 1811. 


I am deeply satisfied with the results of the tests at La Fere. I see that the 9-inch Villantroys 
mortars, with 30 pounds of powder, were at 2,650 toises, and that the 11-inch mortar, with 45 pounds of 
powder, was at 2,980 toises, that is, to say nearly 3000 fathoms: it is a prodigious result. We must 
continue these tests with the greatest activity. I do not know what time has in common with events of 
such importance. The purpose of the tests must be to load the bombs, to determine the length of the 
rocket, and finally to push the discovered one to the end. 

So I want you to give orders to the era to continue” 





25 


Page 26 


experiment, and appoint a commission of artillery officers to preside over it. I do not object to you doing 
models of 10 inches and 12 inches to compare them with them; but I do not think that one must, without 
trials, compromise the great significance that has been obtained. 

I think we have to test big, to find the possibility to reach 3,500 toises. The English had the plan 
to spend this winter in the harbor of Hyeres; the shells thrown at the angle of 40 degrees, with pieces of 
36 and plate mortars, made them abandon this project. I wish to have these mortars at the Villantrors 
from 11 inches to ten, to place them at the different batteries of the lees of Hyeres and on the continent. I 
also think that it must be poured iron, the foundries of Isere; but I think we have to wait two or three 
months, until new experiences have learned what can be learned from this important discovery. 

I would need to place these mortars on the battery of La Perrotine, in the harbor of the 
Saumonards. I would need it at the battery of the Isle Madame, so that all the points of the harbor of the 
Kits, where enemy vessels can anchor, were beaten by these mortars. I would need it in the harbor of 
Morbihan, which, considering this new invention, I plan to occupy, and of which I wish to forbid the 
anchorage to the enemy. These three points are the most important. It will be necessary for the navy to 
put some on, which will be placed on bombardments, to prevent the enemy from anchoring in the harbor 
of the Basques, and even for the harbor of Hyeres. You will show my satisfaction to Colonel 
Villantroys, and you will propose a reward for this officer. As I look at every hundred fathoms as a very 
great advantage, take care that the trials are covered with the greatest mystery, so that the enemy will not 
know them; that the trials are done in secret, and that this is surrounded by a little quackery. 

I therefore desire that the tests be continued; let me be aware of all the sowing; that this be done 
exactly, so that we know what is the powder that we will have used and that we will test beforehand 
with the test-tube. As for the mortars of 10 and 12 inches, on the account that you will give me within 
two months, it can be done in Liege, Indret, on the Isere, and bronze in Douai.

and Strasbourg. 

You demand a return of 600 artillery horses; this is suitable. Present me a state of the companies 
to go up and the horses that you need; as it is, I believe, the minister of the administration of war who 
furnishes you the horses, I will understand them in the first order of return which will be ordered. To

18285. - TO MARSHAL DAVOUT, PRINCE OF ECKMUHL, 
COMMANDING THE CORPS OF OBSERVATION OF THE ELBE, HAMBURG. 
St. Cloud, November 24, 1811. 


My Cousin, I receive your letter of the 18th. The state of situation that you send me can not be 
what I want, since all the conscripts of the Wesel and Strasbourg depots had not yet arrived at the date of 
this state. Send me a part of the situation of the corps to November 15th. 

I think it is advantageous that you keep General Compans to order a good reserve. I will take 
care of the generals to send to the 6th, 8th and 9th divisions of your army. 

When I told you to operate alone, it was not that I did not intend to go to the army, if the war was 
going on; but war can have several acts. It is possible that I resolve to send your army on the Vistula to 
join the Poles and Saxons, putting your headquarters in Danzig, and that without beginning the 
hostilities, in the time that the corps of observation of the Rhine, the observation corps of Italy and my 
Guard would march on forced marches to meet on the Elbe. You feel that you need to be organized in 
artillery and engineering to be able to cope. I am perfectly of your opinion that, during the time I leave 
you with the nine divisions, you have two lieutenants general, who may be divisional generals. 
Moreover, these hypotheses are still** 





34 


Page 35 


distant, and I will decide at the last moment. You would thus have a vanguard of 150,000 infantry, more 
than 30,000 cavalry and four to five hundred pieces of cannon; which would make you an army of 
nearly 200,000 men. I will be within reach of you with 200,000 others. 

I asked you to put some artillery companies and staff officers in the squares. Send a good 
regiment of French infantry to Glogau; which will allow you to push on Magdeburg the battalions of the 
46th, the 19th and others which are sent to you. It seems to me that these broom lions would be good in 
the citadel of Magdeburg. The cadres being good, these battalions would form quickly by doing little 
service; you would put them under the orders of a general who would take special care of them.

18289. - TO MARSHAL DAVOUT, PRINCE OF ECKMUHL, 
COMMANDING THE CORPS OF OBSERVATION OF THE ELBE, HAMBURG. 
St. Cloud, November 25, 1811. 


Cousin, I can see from the state of the Polish army on the 1st of November, that the 5th, 10th, 
and 11th infantry regiments, which should be 3,500 men, are only 2,500 or 2,600 men. I suppose, 
however, the 4th battalions are formed; therefore, I do not see what precludes these regiments from 
being complete. I see that the 9th cavalry regiment is only 400 horses; what prevents him from being 
1,000 horses? Make sure that the bodies are promptly completed. Men must not fail, since the Duchy 
has four million inhabitants, and that Duchy should be able to offer 70,000 men. I see with difficulty the 
complaints of the Poles about the misery of their army. Poles do not pay 42,000 men; it is not 10,000 
men per million inhabitants. You will confess to me that there must be some disorder so that such a 
populous country can not pay so few troops, since the division in Spain and the one in Danzig do not 
count. Write to Prince Poniatowski to make him feel how ridiculous it is. 

NAPOLEON.

18290. - NOTES 
DICTATES IN TRADE AND MANUFACTURING BOARD, 
St. Cloud, November 25, 1811. 


His Majesty deals with the proposal made by the English to receive*® 


36 


Page 37 


wine, obtaining the exportation of sugar in the proportion of a barrel of wine for twelve quintals of 
sugar. 

The Minister of the Interior will give a report on the proposal made by the English; he will 
examine whether we can deceive the exportation of wine. 

Licenses would be given to bring to Bordeaux only 120,000 quintals, weight of marc, raw sugar, 
and not ground or refined sugar, as opposed to 10,000 tons of wine. The building would be French, the 
crew too, the Prussian flag or whatever. 

The building and the merchant will be named in the license. He will have to export such quantity 
of wine (up to 10,000 barrels), and the quantity he will have to import will be stated in the license. The 
trading house will be subject to prosecution in the customs courts if the wine is thrown away, if it is 
deceived in the load or if more sugar is imported. 

An operation of 120,000 quintals of sugar, being too considerable, will be divided by tenths. At 
the same time, licenses will be given to import 12,000 quintals of sugar against 1,000 tons of wine; it 
will be the subject of five or six licenses. 

Traders will be able to export anything that is allowed, such as millstones, clover seeds, etc. 
Then it would be an export of | million francs, a movement of four or five buildings, and a sugar import 
of a mediocre value. One-third of the silks would be exported. 

It is proposed to bring in wool, leathers, potash, medicines, cinchona, raw copper. It is necessary 
to determine the quantities which will be made of them; then these quantities would be divided by 
licenses and in tenths, in order to be able at each moment to see where one would be. 

The objects of exportation would be wine, brandy, all manufactures, so that half or one-third of 
the export would consist of objects which England does not care to receive, and the rest in objects she 
needs, like cheese, clover seed, etc. The licenses should be distributed between Amsterdam, Rotterdam, 
Ostend and Le Havre; it would be necessary to make this distribution, and fix the report of the various 
objects which will have to compose the loadings. 

In the report that the minister will make on this subject, he will indicate the rights that these 
operations will provide to customs. 

The Minister will present at the same time a draft license for the export of wine, and one for the 
introduction of leather, potash, etc.?” 





37 


Page 38 


The Emperor will grant entry by cotons-Motril Coins coming from Malaga and Valencia, when 
one will be master of these two cities, with permissions of the consuls and commanders. By land as well 
as by sea, everything will be taken to Bayonne and put in warehouse. The total of the transaction will be 
inserted in the minutes of the council of commerce to form part of the Customs budget of 1812, and 
licenses will be given in tenths. It will be necessary to export manufactured silks for an equal amount. 
The quota of fees to be charged for the introduction of these cottons, either by land or by sea, will be 
proposed. 

The regulations of Holland seem to contain very good things; it should be adopted for the whole 
of France. 

It would be necessary to propose the total suppression of the supervisors; allow fishing for two, 
three, four days without returning; to oblige to return to such a port, to put the boats on the ground, and 
to arrive there only, unless necessary; to organize on these points a gendarmerie brigade, a 
reinforcement of the customs and a surveillance of the police. 

This system would not interfere with fishing, and it is more advantageous than the present 
system, since it will not be open to a fisherman from Dieppe to keep his boat ashore a quarter of a 
league from the port. 

There is nothing to be feared from the fishermen except smuggling and the passage of spies and 
malevolent ones; but the greatest security is to watch for their arrival, their departure, and to keep them 
in one place. Spies coming out of Dieppe left their boat in a nearby cove; and threw it to the sea without 
being seen. 

If any fisherman were to leave a given point, the question would have been cleared up; add to 
this that there must be established on these sworn labor court points, obliged to declare all that comes to 
their knowledge; they would be real supervisors who would not cost anything. 

It is necessary to designate, and this is an important thing, the points from which the boats would 
go; they would always be designated far from points where there are wheel; never to Texel, to Flushing, 
to Brest, & c. And indeed, unless they are fishermen for the harbor of Toulon, for example, what does it 
matter to them to be in Saint-Nazaire? They will have no knowledge of what is being done in the harbor. 
Those who leave Toulon, on the contrary, would know that food, men, etc. are loaded. 

To make this system complete, it is necessary to foresee the extraordinary cases and to authorize 
the admiral, the captain commander to the divisions, the general commanding a department, to prevent 
the departure and fo” 





38 


Page 39 


put the embargo on fishermen; order them to give an account of it without delay, so that in a week the 
ministers will be informed of it. 

This power can be limited to officers of such rank in the navy and to land commanders, and then 
the fishermen would be freed from the vexations of subordinate commanders. 

According to the copy. Archives of agriculture, commerce and public works. 


18291. - TO GENERAL CLARKE, DUKE OF FELTRE, 
MINISTER OF WAR, IN PARIS. 
Saint-Cloud, November 27, 1811. 


Have an artillery manual containing shooting tables showing the range of the guns and that of the 
gun from all angles. We will make special tables for ricochet shooting; we will join tables for firing the 
rifle. The second part will contain details on the construction of the batteries, the location of each thing, 
the care to be taken to make the most of the batteries, finally a meeting of old and modern maxims on 
the shooting which can serve as an instruction to officers. This manual should not be, as you see, the 
manual of the smelter, the forger, the chemist, or the manufacturer; it must contain what is necessary to 
know, not to make arms, but to use them. However, I do not accept bullet and bullet cartridges, infantry 
cartridges, bolts, rockets for any kind of bomb, on whose manufacture the manual must give instruction. 
This manual should not be more than one volume. It must be done with care and clarity. It is a work that 
every officer and sergeant of artillery must be able to carry in his pocket. The exercise of the 
maneuvering of the pieces, found everywhere, will complete all that knowledge is indispensable to the 
true and principal officer of artillery. It is necessary to make known, in the tables of fire, the ratio of the 
lines, inches and feet of rise, with the angles under which one draws. 

I can hardly see what is called a howitzer at the Villantroys what must be called a mortar. The 
idea of shells is attached to the ricochet, but we can not ricochet with this huge machine; we must name 
this piece mortar Villantroys. 

Napoleon.

18296. - TO THE PRINCE OF NEUCHATEL AND WAGRAM, 
MAJOR GENERAL, OF THE ARMY OF SPAIN, IN PARIS. 
Saint Cloud. November 30, 1811. 


I sent you several models for the flags; you did not report to me about it; Come talk to 
me tomorrow. Bring me the state of all the regiments of the army, with the name of the battles in 
which everyone has been. The Minister of War has not understood my idea, and moreover he is 
not in a position to do this work; he put all the battles in the 26th, although this regiment was not 
there. Each regiment must speak on its flag only the names of battles in which it has been found; 
regiments that have not been at any battle must not be named on their flag. Only you can do this 
job, and do it carefully; present it to me without delay. 

I have charged you with the details of the flags. I give only one per regiment of infantry; 
one per cavalry regiment; one per regiment of artillery, and one per regiment of gendarmerie; 
point to departmental companies or guards of honor or others. No one must have an eagle unless 
he has received it from the hands of the Emperor. All other bodies must wear pennants. Any 
infantry corps of less than 1,000 men and any body of cavalry that does not have 500 men can 
not have an eagle. 

All the regiments of infantry having had one eagle per battalion, and the regiments of 
cavalry one by squadron, these eagles will be sent, except one, to Paris, and deposited with the 
Invalides, until they can be put in the Temple of Glory. Each infantry battalion will have a 
pennant where there will be nothing written. The"! 





41 





Page 42 


four battalions of the regiment will have the pennant of different color. 

The eagle of each regiment will have its two armed bearers, independently of a pair of pistols on 
the chest, a sponge, whose dimensions must be determined, so that it is a good weapon. This snake will 
have a banner to frighten the horses and that can be seen from afar. 

The eagle will have a sort of pennant like the one they have today, but of a very solid double silk, 
and where will be embroidered, on one side, the names of the battles where the regiment will have been, 
and on the other, these words: the Emperor Napoleon at such a regiment. These pennants will be made 
without delay and sent to all the corps of the army which must receive them. This can be renewed every 
two or three years, without renewing the eagle. One regiment will be allowed to ask another when its 
will be destroyed, which will be sent to me on my approval. 

I had ordered that the city of Paris made gold laurel wreaths for the regiments which were at the 
battle of Austerlitz; inform the prefect where they are, in order to use them. Be sure to take care of all 
this and that it will be finished by next Thursday. You will bring me the decree with the state of the 
regiments; because the part of the flags of the regiments is today in a great chaos.

concerned. This relation would be made without maps or plans; it would be a staff diary from which one

Cousin, I receive your letter of November 25th. I am totally opposed to the idea that you are 
demonstrating in the staffs five officers who would have served in Austria. I do not understand that: 
leave them in the regiments where I have placed them. I want in the staffs only men who, since 1789, 
have not left the French flags. If you had caught them, send them back right away. Far from it, | have a 
review done to ascertain the number of these men in our ranks, my intention being to keep them in 
special regiments. I do not want to worry about the loyalty of my army. Nor do I approve of putting 
officers coming out of Austrian service into French regiments. 

NAPOLEON.

18300. - TO MARSHAL DAVOUT, PRINCE OF ECKMUHL, 
COMMANDING THE CORPS OF OBSERVATION OF THE ELBE, HAMBURG. 
Paris, December 2, 1811. 


Cousin, I answer one of your questions of November 26th. If the Grand Duchy of Warsaw, 
which has more than 4 million inhabitants, can not feed its troops, in spite of all the advantages that I 
make him by favoring his loan, which has already given him several millions, by feeding, paying and, 
dressing up the division which he has in Spain, which is a quarter of his infantry, I can not understand 
how this country can pretend to become a nation. 

I'm responding to one of your last letters, November 28th. The Germans complain that all these 
noises of insurrection of Germany are fomented by the French, who, by dint of talking about it and 
warming themselves up on this object, will eventually make you believe it. They complain that you told 
Rostock that you would be able to prevent Germany from becoming a Spain; that as long as you 
command there, you would not dare to undertake anything. These words are a real pain. There is nothing 
in common between Spain and the provinces of Germany. Spain would have been reduced for a long 
time without her 60,000 English, without her 1,000 leagues of coast, which makes our armies 
everywhere on the frontiers, and finally without the 100 millions provided by America, for England is 
not in a position to provide him with money. But, as in Germany there is no America, neither the sea, 
nor an immense quantity of fortresses and 60,000 English, there are™* 


44 


Page 45 


nothing to fear, the German was even as idle, as lazy, as murderer, as superstitious, as much delivered to 
the monks as the people of Spain, where there were 300,000 monks. Judge, then, what there is to fear 
from a people so wise, so reasonable, so cold, so tolerant, so far removed from all excesses that there is 
no example that a man has been murdered in Germany during the war. Austria was much more likely to 
be revolutionized. The effects proved the lack of foundation of the fears that one wanted to conceive. It 
is, therefore, very unfortunate that the generals of these chimeras are maintained, and that comparisons 
are allowed to circulate in the country, which can only do harm, without producing any good. If there 
was a movement in Germany, it would end up being for us and against the little princes. 

As for Westphalia, the people of Hesse, who is the principal, are far from regretting the elector, 
the army is attached to the King. It will be advantageous for you to be more amenable towards the 
Westphalian Government and the King; it is better to conciliate than to be angry. 

I do not know why Rapp interferes with what does not concern him; there are only two facts in 
his report: 1‘ that Kotzebue made a pamphlet; 2™ that the English have made another, which is entitled 
Campaign of Portugal. He had to give you an account of these two facts and not talk about anything 
else. What will he talk about what is happening in Hungary, the spirit that drives the Confederation and 
these countries, he who is so far away! Let him confine himself to his government, let him meddle with 
his own interests, and confine himself to realizing to me Danzig and the surrounding countries. Please 
do not give me such rhapsodies in front of me. My time is too precious for me to lose in dealing with 
such nonsense. You probably do not pretend that I am acquainted with what is happening in Hungary 
and Austria by reports from Danzig, especially transmitted by such a weak man, of which I do not care 
much, except for a day's business. only Rapp, all this serves only to waste my time and dirty my 
imagination with absurd pictures and suppositions. You had to send me the extract from Rapp's report 
and say in two words: General Rapp tells me that a pamphlet, entitled Country of Portugal, is spread by 
the English (libel of which we have 1,000 copies), and that Kotzebue did another one. 

What you should recommend to General Rapp is that generals are not interested in privateers, 
and that these pirates

Page 46 


do not abuse this to ravage coasts and commit unjust things which then engage me in years of quarrels. 
An officer must not appear in such undertakings, especially a general whose provisional decisions have 
influence over the matter. 
NAPOLEON.

18308. - TO MARSHAL DAVUT, PRINCE OF ECKMUHL, 
COMMANDING THE CORPS OF OBSERVATION OF THE ELBE, HAMBURG. 
Paris. December 5, 1811. 


Cousin, I'm getting your letter on Modlin's work. Since the crown A can not be completed this 
year, we must finish the telescope No. 19 and put it in a state of defense; it is only 300 fathoms from 
arrow No. 27 and 100 fathoms from the river, and the enemy can only seize it by opening the trench.” 





52 





Page 53 


will be able to do it only after its siege crew has arrived and put in measure for this operation, It is very 
interesting to be master of this point n° 19 as long as it is possible, since by this position one is master 
also from the Vistula bridge. So give orders so that the book No. 19, with a good blockhouse at the 
throat, able to hold 100 men, be made without delay and armed. Then, as soon as possible, we must 
finish crown A, because we must, above all, make sure the bridge, since this is the main goal of all the 
place of Modlin. It is seen from the general profile that the gorge of the square dominates more than 60 
feet Kazun's work, so it is not likely that the enemy is housed in this work, under the fire of the entire 
gorge of the square. Moreover, nothing will prevent the establishment of a front ditch, wide and full of 
water, which offers an obstacle to the assault that one would like to give to this bridgehead. 

I see with pleasure that the place is supplied; it must be for six months. 3 to 4,000 garrison men 
seem sufficient to me, to wit: an entire regiment, two companies of sappers, four companies of artillery, 
a squadron of cavalry, and finally a company of deposit of each regiment, which will make 1,500 men 
of deposit; in all 4,000 men. The service must not be done by guards who get up, but by battalions or 
companies which remain stationary in bastions, half-moons and counter-guards; it is the Turkish 
method; it is the best for defense and the most economical in men. Thus, for example, a half-battalion of 
the defense of the crown C would be charged; he would settle there, would always have there half or a 
third of his world of service, during the day, all these men would work to fortify the post which they 
would have to defend and would put it with eagerness in the best possible state; at night, everyone 
would still be there. The infantry would furnish the number of men necessary to serve the artillery of 
this part of the place. You understand the advantages that this service must have over the ordinary 
method, where positions are relieved every 24 hours; which makes the soldier settle badly and has no 
interest in fortifying the post where he is. You must therefore give instructions that, if the siege were to 
take place, an officer and a portion of the garrison should be charged to the defense of each front; the 
soldiers would stay there forever. As there is a great quantity of wood at Modlin, the master soldiers 
would be allowed to arm themselves, by pressing the wood against the slope of the rampart; which will 
make barracks easy to build, perfectly safe from the bomb, and in which” 


53 


Page 54 


the soldiers will be able to sleep in case of bombing. The barracks will remain available for hospitals 
and the reserve; by this means, instead of 300 workers a day for genius, a number which we see in the 
memoir, there would be 3,000 a day; for, apart from the sentinels and some grand guards, everybody 
would work; in the same way, instead of 200 servants for the artillery, there would be 3,000; everyone 
would practice serving the parts that must defend the portion of the place that will be entrusted to them. 
Give instruction accordingly and correct all these ideas. 

As the book of the artillery was not attached to the state, I can not judge of its situation; but give 
orders that the coins of 24 which are useless in Warsaw be sent to Modlin; that only the smallest number

It is necessary to provide constantly for the defense of the borders of the 10th military division, 
that is to say, the departments of the Pyrenees-Orientales, Ariége, Haute-Garonne and Hautes-Pyrénées, 
It must be provided by three means: 

1“ The formation of the National Guard in these four departments, according to the laws. Give

You will organize the bodies by sub-prefectures. This national guard thus organized in these four

6,000 rifles will be distributed to all National Guards who are in the adjoining sub-prefectures 
and one march from the border.**

Page 55 


They will be exercised on Sundays, so that each event may have 6,000 men in arms. Municipalities of 
the communes will be responsible for rifles. There will be depots of cartridges, and at the alarm signal 
the National Guards will march to the aid under the command of the Commanding General. 

2™ Each of these four bordering departments will furnish two elite battalions to six companies of 
150 men; in total, 900 men per battalion; which will make, for the four departments, a manpower of 
7,200 men. They will be under the orders of the senator, and paid, dressed, organized as they have been 
in the North. 

The departments of Aude, Tarn, Tarn-et-Garonne and Gers, will each provide an elite battalion,

who will always have 9,000 men under arms, the departments to be charged with keeping them in full. 

The two elite battalions of the Pyrénées-Orientales will be placed at Mont-Louis and in front of 
Perpignan; the two of Ariége, two of the Haute-Garonne, four of the four departments of the second line, 
total eight, will be under the direct orders of the senator, in Foix, and will be responsible for the defense 
of Ariége and valley of Aran; the two battalions of the Hautes-Pyrenees will be placed at Venasque, in 
the valley of Aran, and on all other neighboring points. There will be on this frontier 6,000 men, 
national guards, armed, 10,000 elite, in all 16,000, only in charge of the defense of the borders. 

The third way is to preserve mountain hunter battalions, made up of refractory conscripts, and so 
on. You must have state of training and know if they are recruited by the National Guard or conscripts. 

These measures will protect these borders from devastation; we will not have to groan over the 
consequences of the irruptions of the Spanish bands. 

You can tell Senator Rampon that I chose him; and even if Councilor Pelet is still in these 
countries, he could remain there until the end of the final organization, in which he would help Senator 
Rampon.

18311. - TO THE VICE-AMIRAL COUNTY, 
MINISTER OF THE NAVY, IN PARIS. 
Paris, December 6, 1811 


Count Decres, it follows from my various information that I have in France sixteen million trees 
having 5 feet of turn, or 480 million cubic feet, or enough to make four thousand eight hundred vessels. 

Thus, with a single order, I can, by the month of February, cut off throughout my empire a 
quantity of wood sufficient to make four thousand eight hundred vessels, and that without detriment to 
my forests; for only trees of one hundred and fifty to two hundred years would be cut, and from that 
moment on, this cut would do no harm to ordinary hammering. If we wanted to take trees 3 feet in 
circumference, as the navy employs today, I could make 2400 more ships, so that I would have enough 
to build seven thousand two hundred ships. And finally, if one wanted to use the woods which the Dutch 
use in constructions, having less than 3 feet of circumference, I would have an infinite quantity. 

The countries located on the Saone, on the Doubs, on the Rhone, on the Canal du Languedoc, on 
the Isére, the Mediterranean coast, which”° 





Page 57 


can feed the port of Toulon, are included, in the calculation that I have just established, for a third. In a 
year, then, I could have enough wood in Toulon to make two thousand ships. 

In deducting from these calculations what we wish for the forests too far from the rivers, and 
where we could however hammer curves and some precious woods, if we did not take ordinary woods, 
it always results that there is in France an immense quantity of wood, and that it must arrive at Toulon a 
quantity such that one can build there as many vessels as one can desire it. 

The forests that can provide the Antwerp yards are those of the Rhine, Moselle, Meurthe, Meuse, 
Scheldt, etc., to which we can join those of the Aisne, part of forest conservation from the Seine and the 
Aube, since, by the channel of Saint-Quentin, all this can go to Antwerp. 

I have a precise job on the Compiégne forest; it follows that, if I wanted to cut down all the trees 
proper to the constructions, having 5 feet in circumference, I would have enough to make twenty ships, 
or more than two million cubic feet of wood; that by cutting the trees of 3 feet in circumference, I would 
have enough to make forty ships. This is positive: all trees are counted and calculations done. This work 
is done in the greatest detail; there is nothing to fall back on. These two million cubic feet of wood 
would be delivered to the navy on the banks of the Aisne and Oise. Now the forest of Compiegne, which 
can supply wood for the construction of forty vessels, is nothing, since it has only 30,000 acres, I expect 
the same work on the forest of Fontainebleau and other forests of the Crown, where I am guaranteed 
such a satisfactory result. 

These glimpses are the results of observations made for several years in the forests of the 
Domaine and those of the communes. 

It is another simple and equally satisfying overview. The navy pounds about two million cubic 
feet of wood a year; there is no difficulty in hammering in the reserved wood of the cuts sold in the 
years 1810, 1809, 1808, 1807 and 1806, which is five years. That would give her ten million cubic feet 
of wood that could be hammered in the year and in the same places where she made her hammering. 
Now these ten million cubic feet would provide for the construction of a hundred ships of war, with 
precautions the cutting of the woods of the reserve can be done in all copses; but in the copses of four 
years it can be done without inconvenience. 

Result. - It follows from what has just been established that make extraordinary cut line of two 
million cubic feet of wood’

Page 58 


in the basin of Toulon and the Mediterranean, and that it is necessary to make a line of three millions for 
the shipyards of the Scheldt and Holland; that these cuts will cost the navy nothing more than to 
transport them to its ports; that this extraordinary cut can be made within the limits nearest the rivers and 
ports, and where the farms are cheaper; that, consequently, the markets made in Holland with wood 
merchants may be reduced, and that this quantity of wood may be at 40 or 50 sols per cubic foot; that 
the yard of Antwerp, that of Amsterdam, and that of Rotterdam, may be supplied with power, and that 
that of Toulon may be considerably increased, so that we shall immediately have an extraordinary 
means of producing wood which It is possible to cut this year and have, in the ports of Toulon and 
Antwerp, in sufficient quantity to build fifty vessels; that some of what was directed to Le Havre may be 
sent back to Antwerp by means of the Saint-Quentin canal; that, far from asking for timber from 
Germany, Prussia, and other countries, we have more than enough in France. 

As for Brest, I have no sufficient information, given the circumstances of the transport. I will 
only have this information in a few days. But, by reasoning in the same way, we will have enough to 
build five or six warships, which will give a little activity to these yards. 

The wood being almost useless in Nantes, we can reduce the cuts and let the forests rest, which

It is all the more necessary that measures be taken, that the cuts of the administration will be

18317. - DECREE. 
Tuileries Palace. December 9, 1811. 


THE ABOLITION OF THE FEDERAL REGIME. 


ARTICLE 1. The feudal regime is abolished in the departments of Ems-Superior, Bouches-du- 
Weser and Bouches-de-l'Elbe. 


GENERAL EFFECTS OF THE ABOLITION OF THE FEDERAL REGIME. 


ART. 2. All honorary distinctions, superiority or power, resulting from the feudal system, are 
abolished, without prejudice to the provisions of the decree of 26th August, 1811. 

ART. 3. The seigniorial courts are likewise abolished. Consequently, all the external signs of 
seigneurial justice will be slaughtered within two months of the publication of this decree. Failure of the 
lords to have done so within this period, the destruction will be at the diligence of the prosecutor at the 
court of first instance and the mayor, at the expense of the municipality, which will benefit from the 
materials. 

ART. 4. The law recognizes only allodial property. As a consequence, all the fiefs situated in the 
extent of the three departments, whatever their nature and denomination, or that they were formerly 
foreign sovereigns, or that the direct domain (Lehenherrschaft, Lehenherrlichkeits belongs to private 
individuals ( Lehenherrn), whether they are immediate fiefdoms or fiefs, are converted into free-wills 
and freed from all duty and subjection resulting from the feudal bond, so that the possessors may freely 
alienate or mortgage them. 

ART. 5. Similarly, the rights of feudal inheritance, of whatever nature, are abolished. 
Nevertheless the feudal succession will take place one last time in favor of the successors existing at the 
time of the publication of the Westphalian law of March 28, 1809 for the countries formerly 
Westphalian, and for the other countries forming part of the three departments at the time of the 
publication of our present decree. 

ART. 6. In the case where, at the opening of the succession, the person who was called upon to 
collect it feudal at the time of the publication of the law of March 28, 1809 - or at that of the publication 
of the present Decree, according to the distinction made in the preceding article, would have been no 
longer called upon, the feudal system subsisting, or would have been so only for a certain portion, the 
succession will be regulated allodially,” 


62 


Page 63 


either for the whole) or for the portion in relation to which his vocation has ceased. 
ART. 7. The seigneurial and feudal rights are suppressed without indemnity or preserved until 
the repurchase, according to the distinctions established hereafter. 


SEIGNURAL AND FEDERAL RIGHTS ABOLISHED. 


ART. 8. All serfdom is abolished without compensation. 

ART. 9. Are deemed acts of serfdom: 

1“ The right to compel the settler and his children to serve the master as servants (Gesinde- 
Zwangrechts); 

2"! The rights of the master over the education of the children of the settler, the obligation to 
remain attached to such profession or soil; 

3 The obligation to ask the lord's consent to marry) and the rights he could demand regarding 
the marriage (Bedingung, Broutkauf, Klauenthaler, etc.); 

4" The rights which were paid to the seignior in order to be able to build factories, to exercise 
professions, or to perform acts which must be free to everybody; 

5" The oath of fidelity or submission to lend to the master; 

6"" The incapacity to acquire in all property, to dispose of, to dispose of between life or by an act 
of last will, to act and defend in judgment; 

7" The right to a portion of the movable inheritance of the colonist or his wife, called mortuary 
right (Sterbfall, Betthaupt); 

8" The usufruct of the property of the vassals, tenants or censuses during their minority. 

ART. 10. The right of lords to appropriate the inheritance of aliens, bastards, dead persons 
without heirs, vacant property, movable and immovable property, vacant and vacant land, heathland, the 
shipwrecked effects, without prejudice to the rights acquired by the lords who have already made an act 
of property, as well as the property and customary rights which the lords, the communes or the private 
individuals may have, by virtue of titles independent of the seigniorial justice . 

ART. 11. The feudal withdrawal, and generally all right under which a lord was subrogated to 
the purchaser, is abolished without indemnity. 

ART. 12. Are also removed without compensation: 

The rights levied on the persons, by reason of the residence, the number of the cattle or to any 
other liter which would hold only at the®

protection and not to a grant of funds owned or in use; 

Rights in furniture sales; 

Weighing, measuring, inspection, display, warehouse, transportation of goods and merchandise.

Tolls, tolls and the like, except discharge for the lords of the obligations to which they were

Are excepted, as for now, those rights that have been granted to the lords, either for the cost of

ART. 20. The employee, employed for a public service, on the day he must work for the former

ART. 21. If chores exist only for the needs of the owner's property, they can not be leased or sold 
without such property; but, if it is permitted to use it otherwise than for the cultivation and exploitation 
of the said goods, they may be leased and sold, provided that the condition of the commodities does not 
become harsher. 

ART. 22. The existing chores can not be increased. It is forbidden to establish new ones, even for 
the grant of funds. 

ART. 23. The above-mentioned abolition also includes the right to compel settlers by corporal or 
pecuniary punishment, without recourse to justice, to fulfill non-suppressed obligations (Dienstzwang), 
and all such rights. 

ART. 24. The persons liable for the canceled rights may not claim those they have already paid. 

It will be the same for lords with regard to the rights that would still be due. 

ART. 25. When the owners of the rights preserved by the articles 10, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16 and 17 
above will not be able to represent the primitive title, they will be able to supplement it by two

the forty-year period, from the Westphalian law of March 28, 1809, for the Westphalian countries, and, 
in the other parts of the three departments, to run of the publication of this decree, and that they recall 
either the conventions or the concessions described in the aforementioned articles. 

ART. 26. When there is a reason for the same inheritance of several titles or recognitions, the

ART. 27. Those who have acquired private rights abolished without compensation may not 
demand any restitution of prices or damages; those who would have acquired the domain of the State 
will have the right only to the restitution either of the finances by them advanced, or of the other objects

ART. 28. It shall be free to farmers who have leased none of the same rights, without a mixture

18322. -NOTE 
ON A REPORT OF THE MINISTRY OF THE MARINE, RELATING TO TRIESTE. 
Paris, lst December, 1811. 


There is no question of fortifying Trieste; Trieste is so far from England, that an expedition, 
having disembarkation troops on board, can not be made of London to torch a vessel; a cruise of two or 
three ships, carrying 5 or 600 men, can not be strong enough to repel the garrison of Trieste; it would be 
only in case of war with Austria, where the army of Italy would be defeated, and the Austrians masters 
of this place; but the Austrians would not be interested in burning a ship. This hypothesis, moreover, is 
very remote; but that is enough not to make a great work in Trieste, and it is not enough so as not to risk 
the construction of a ship and a frigate. For a frigate, there is no big expense beforehand; the minister 
will order that a frigate be placed on the site. It will be decided, at the formation of the budget of 1812, 
whether it is advisable to build vessels. 

I had the desire to have ships everywhere, because I thought I lacked wood in France; but today 
that I have other ideas and I am convinced that we can build in Toulon, Cherbourg, Rochefort, Antwerp, 
Genoa, as much as we want, it seems to me that it becomes less urgent to take advantage of the woods of 
remote localities to disseminate our workshops.
