circumstance of the canal of Saint-Quentin makes me wish that a portion of the woods of the basin of 
the Oise, the Aisne and the Seine be directed on Antwerp. Toulon my needs are such that the 
constituency of its basin is such that the Canal du Center, the Saone and the Languedoc Canal can 
conduct wood there. In handing me over this work, I want you to show me the state of hammering by 
department, as it has been done for the last three years. 

I suppose that hammering annually gives the navy 1,500,000 cubic feet of wood, namely: one 
million from the forests of the Estate, and the rest from individuals. I believe that supplies by purchases 
that do not come from hammering amount to 5 or 600,000 cubic feet, which depends on the 
circumstances and years: These purchases, which are very expensive, can now no longer instead, since I 
will have my own woods. So I only count on the hammering of 1,500,000 cubic feet per year. It may 
even be reduced for points where large supplies of wood are not needed. For example, why pile up so 
much wood in Le Havre, especially in Bayonne and Nantes? It will be more appropriate to only make 
cuts proportionate to the constructions that one wants to undertake, and to leave the woods on foot to 
exploit them at the time of the peace, where their transport to Brest will be easier. This is only an idea to 
be deepened. 1,500,000 cubic feet per year is about what”!

Monsieur le Comte de Cessac, I reply to your contribution of the 27th November concerning the 
supply of Danzig. From January 1, 1812, the service will be entirely taken in my account, disgrace 
housing and barracks, military beds, woods and lights, and any rent of ovens and shops. This expense 
must be regulated so that it does not exceed 500,000 francs a month. Prussian regulations are also 
required, which tax commodities for exact payment. The bread must be very cheap, since wheat has no 
value in Gdansk. It is necessary to put as much order as possible in these provisions: the day of hospitals 
must not exceed 20 sous. As for the supply of siege, I have issued a decree which you will receive and 
which regulates everything. Of the 2 million francs which you ask, the sum of one million has already 
been granted to you under the budget of the Danzig Special Fund for 1811; the other million you will be 
similarly granted on the special fund from Danzig for 1812. I have adopted many of your bases; but I 
added the obligation to have flours. I changed”

Page 74

immense supplies. 

You will see in my decree that I brought under the title of reserve stores 50,000 quintals metric

Guard must have a pontoon company with a small deck crew. 

What does the Guard have in military crews, bringing back all that is in Spain? Make me a report 
on that organization. 

The Ist Division needs 4 ambulance caissons, 28 military transport caissons, which, with the 
forges, caissons for papers, etc., will make about forty wagons. The other divisions need the same 
number of wagons; which will make 160 wagons for the Guard. But these 160 wagons would only carry 
bread for four days; Assuming 40,000 rations per day, it would be necessary to have means to carry 
400,000 rations, or 100 more wagons. So it would be about 300 caisson, it would take the Guard. 
Organize this in detail. 

Make also the organization of the administration: commissioners of the wars, surgeons, 
foodstuffs, etc., finally all that it is necessary to complete it. 

As for the cavalry, it must be considered as composed of two divisions, since I will not have 
nearly 6,000 horses, including the 600 horses of the Italian guard, and because it is possible that the six 
regiments of lancers and part of the Italians are often detached.

The first division of the observation corps of Italy will meet in Trento and Bolzano. It will be

The 3rd division, which will be the 15th, will be composed of sixteen Italian and Dalmatian 
battalions.

18341. - TO JEROME NAPOLEON, KING OF WESTPHALIA, 
A CASSEL. 
Paris. December 17, 1811. 


Brother, I receive your letter of December 13th. I I do not see in the states that accompany it the 
organization of the artillery, the engineers, the crews and caissons of every kind of your army. I do not 
see the ambulance caissons, the military transport caissons for food. Your army needs to have a quantity 
of wagons needed to carry ten days of food. I do not see either the organization of the corps that you 
want to leave in Kassel to guard the country, suppress the insurrections and go where it would be 
necessary. 

General Morio is quite incapable of commanding your army corps. You must keep him near you 
as grand marshal or aide-de-camp, or charge him to command the genius of your army. These sixteen 
thousand men, commanded by this general, would be of no value. I do not see either a man capable of 
commanding the cavalry and knowing how to get out of a charge. 

Finally your corps needs, to enter the campaign, to be provided with all the necessary equipment 
for this purpose. It is necessary that he has sappers and tools to be able to entrench himself. As it appears 
that Prussia will be with me in case of war, your army corps, if it is to be employed beyond the Vistula, 
must be completely organized and equipped with everything. To make the great war, you can not have 
less than forty pieces of cannon and 250 wagons, that is to say 1,200 artillery horses. 

If you must be away from Westphalia, who will govern the country during your absence? What 
forces would you leave him to contain him? 

NAPOLEON

18343. -NOTE 
DICTATED IN COUNCIL OF MINISTERS. 
Tuileries Palace. December 18, 1811. 


The conscription was established on the coasts: it resulted that the maritime inscription has 
removed some men. It is concluded that any individual who was enrolled in the registration numbers 
owed nothing to the conscription because he was supposed to be already in an army and on a ship. 

But today the system is changed; the coastal cantons are no longer subject to the conscription of 
land, but to that of sea. It follows that every individual, even forming part of the inscription”! 


91 


Page 92 


maritime, is subject to conscription, unless, by the effect of registration, he is on board a vessel, in which 
case he is in the same position as the conscript voluntarily one year before conscription. A sailor who 
has begun by being a moss and who finds himself, either voluntarily or by the effect of the inscription, 
on a vessel, is not liable to conscription. But no individual can escape by saying that he is required by 
the trustees and that he will go on board. 

This matter is therefore likely to be decided for the organization of the army by the same 
principles as for the army. A man on board is like a voluntary conscript. 

Will it follow from the fact that an individual fired at the conscription and did not fall for the fact 
that he has fulfilled all he owes to the navy? No. This individual of sixteen to twenty years, if he is 
appointed by lot, will become a sailor; if he is not, if he wants to be a man of the land, a wigmaker, a 
carpenter, we will have nothing to say to him, and he will not be worn on the inscription. But if he 
continues to engage in navigation, he is registered, because fishing is allowed, cabotage only for the 
enrollees; and, by the result of the inscription, it is at the disposal of the navy, which takes among the 
enrolled a third, a quarter, according to its needs. It is therefore necessary that the Minister of the Navy 
present a decree which orders, for the past, that all conscripts who did not appear in the draw because 
they were registered have to join the ports, under penalty of being treated as refractory. This operation 
will be a great pleasure to the whole coast, and if the states of these individuals were drawn, there would 
be enormous abuse and evidence that the trustees have tampered with their signature to remove many 
individuals. 

As for Holland, there is no doubt that the inscription must be established as in France. The 
subscription that has been made is only one way of arriving at another order of things. Holland can 
supply 20,000 sailors, who, if they are not ours, will be to the enemy. 

It would be very carefree, if we had a squadron ready from the Texel, to be wanting the sailors 
who are on board the vessels of the Dutch trade. But for this year it is not the question. 

Conscription is due by a man, not because he is a sailor, but because he is French and when he is 
twenty; the inscription is due, not because he is French, but because he practices the sea,

18355. - TO MARSHAL BESSIERE, DUKE OF ISTRIA, 
COMMANDING THE IMPERIAL GUARD, IN PARIS. 
Paris. December 21, 1811. 


Cousin, I answer your work on the administration of the Guard. I'm sticking to the organization 
of August 24th. 1 authorizing officer, 6 commissioners of wars and 3 deputies, in all 10, appear to me 
sufficient. A war commissioner or deputy will be attached to each division. The cavalry will count for 
two divisions, 48 health officers seem to me sufficient. 302 employees and administrative workers also 
seem to me sufficient. But it is necessary to maintain the number in full, and to this end you must order 
that as soon as the Guard is gone we have to form again a company of 100 workers, composed mainly of 
bakers, to recruit the companies active. They will then be joined by detachments of 50 men. The 
battalion of the military crews has six companies, 17 officers, 771 men and 1,200 horses; it serves 30 
vans and 12 corps forges, 28 ambulances, 52 food vans; 120 new model wagons, 6 forges, 4 extensions, 
total 252 wagons; which seems to me enough. The distribution will be made, for the vans of 
administration, at the rate of 5 vans by division and 10 in reserve for the cavalry; for ambulance vans, 5 
per division and 8 for cavalry, for the old model food cases, 14 for the first two divisions, and 12 for the 
last two, and without understanding the vans of the Italian guard. I see that all that is missing is 229

18363. - TO MARSHAL DAVOUT, PRINCE OF ECKMUHL, 
COMMANDING THE CORPS OF OBSERVATION OF THE ELBE IN HAMBURG. 
Paris, December 24, 1811. 


Cousin, I read carefully your letter of December 19th. Here's how I want things to be settled. 
Your authorizing officer will give you a report, which will show that for so many days, so many 
thousand men and horses, beyond the number fixed by the conventions, have been borne by Westphalia; 
that this number of men and horses must have cost so much to Westphalia, and you will diminish on 
every object 25 per cent of the price where things are in the 32nd military division, to equal the money 
that comes out of my house; thus the ration of fodder will be less than 20 sous, the hospital day less than 
20 sous. We can also count the supply of sheets. The food of the Westphalian troops in Danzig will be 
compensated for. The conclusion of this report will be that such a quantity of troops has occasioned so 
much expense at Westphalia, not to mention the pay. You will communicate this result to my minister, 
and you will write to him that, in view of the report of the intendant of the army, the intention of his 
majesty being to do something advantageous to Westphalia, you order that the balance of the surplus 
troops who were in the charge of the King are paid up to the same price, and you beg the King to pay the 
rest. The King will acquit or not, since the note of my minister to the Westphalian Minister will be 
confidential, and will not make known the reason, but will be limited to saying that a sum of so much 
has been sent to pay the balance of 12,500 men and that it remains due so much to align the balance. By 
this means, this will not be the rule for the other princes of the Confederation or for Westphalia, which, 
when it receives a greater amount of

18370. - TO PRINCE CAMBACERE, 
ARCHICHANCELIER OF THE EMPIRE, PARIS. 
Paris. December 26, 1811. 


My cousin, Count Auguste Talleyrand, at his wedding, declared to his wife's family that he had a 
sum of 200,000 francs, as given to him by his cousin the Prince of Benevento, then Minister of Foreign 
Relations. The Prince of Benevento, however, demanded promissory notes for the said sum. These bills, 
which have since been placed in circulation, are in the hands of the agents of exchange; so that, if they 
were not to be paid in a short time, Count Auguste Talleyrand would be dishonored. I can not approve of 
this double procedure. The matrimonial clauses are sacred, and since it was said that the Prince of 
Benevento gave 200,000 francs, he ought not to demand notes; but, since he had demanded them, 
delicacy did not allow him to put them into circulation. Having made the sacrifice of 2,200,000 francs to 
purchase the Prince of Benevento's Hotel, in order to facilitate the arrangement of his affairs, I desire 
that this sum should serve also to settle the affair of Count Auguste Talleyrand.'” 





Page 110 


I accordingly ordered the intendant general of my extraordinary domain to retain this sum. My intention 
is that you speak to the Prince of Benevento, to Count Auguste Talleyrand, and that you constitute their 
arbitrator. If the 200,000 francs are to be paid by Count Auguste Talleyrand, you will determine the 
times at which it will be reasonable to fix the payments, and you will finish this affair by giving it the 
form of a family arrangement and not a commitment of commerce, which must not take place between 
people of honor. 

NAPOLEON. 

According to the copy comm. by the Duke de Cambaceres.

18374. - TO THE GENERAL LACUEE, COUNTY OF CESSAC, 
MINISTER DIRECTOR OF THE ADMINISTRATION OF THE WAR, IN PARIS. 
Paris, December 26, 1811. 


Count de Cessac, we should take a serious look at the supply of Barcelona. We can not hide from 
ourselves that the expedition which will leave Toulon is very hazardous. It is therefore necessary, 
independently of what one does by sea, to take surer means by taking them on the ground. I have three 
companies of the 3rd battalion of the military crews at Pau, each of which harnesses 40 new model 
wagons; which makes 120 wagons. Each wagons can carry 40 quintals of flour or wheat; that would be 
4,800 quintals that these companies would transport in one trip. Assuming that the daily consumption of 
Barcelona is 9,000 rations, it would only be 100 quintals of flour a day. This transport of 4,800 quintals 
would increase the supply of Barcelona by forty-eight days or two months. The place is supplied until 
March; a single trip would bring this supply until May. 

The 5th Battalion of the year of Catalonia must have 3 or 400 mules; which would increase the 
transport of a thousand quintals. Finally I do not see what would oppose the fact that we make a market 
for a hundred wagons, taking only wagons that carry 40 quintals at least. If it were possible to organize a 
convoy of 3 to 400 wagons, General Decaen would escort him by force; it would be sent out in January, 
which is, in this country, the season of the best season; and Burcelone supplies for April, May, June,

18877. - TO JEROME NAPOLEON, KING OF WESTPHALIA, 
A CASSEL. 
Paris, December 26, 1811. 


Brother, I receive your letter of the 22nd; I answer them without wasting time. I think that 
General Morio, who has your confidence, is very well placed in your house. It is even a distinguished 
official, who would be useful in your general staff or in your genius, these services being analogous; but 
he never led a company of voltigeurs to the fire. Could a perfect honest man and a man of honor desire 
to be grand marshal of a prince who has dethroned his family? He may wish to be colonel or general, 
having recognized you; he may be with honor the grand marshal of your son, but not yours. Suppose a 
defeat, the march of Elector on Cassel: in this case, could you defend yourself from a feeling of dread of 
finding at your side a man who would have so many links by which one can seize him? As for the 
regency you want to leave at home in case of absence, I see that Simeon deserves all confidence for the 
administration; I suppose that the chief, or even the gendarmerie, Bongars, would remain in Westphalia; 
but there would still be a general of some distinction who would be inclined to lead the troops wherever 
it was necessary. 

You have eighteen battalions and eight squadrons online. You would need sixty pieces of 
cannon. The least possible would be forty-eight pieces, namely: twelve regimental pieces; two batteries 
on foot, each of six pieces of six and two howitzers, sixteen pieces; two horse batteries of four pieces of 
six and two howitzers, twelve pieces; a reserve battery of six pieces of 12 and two howitzers, eight 
pieces; total, forty-eight pieces. 

For the service of your thirty-six spare parts, you need 200 wagons, because you have to have 
400 shots per piece. These 200 wagons would require 1,000 horses: you only have 600, that is to say that 
you can only harness 120 wagons with your train. It would therefore be necessary that the other 80 
wagons were harnessed, at the time of the war, by a lifting of horses of requisition. Your thirty-six 
pieces of reserve would naturally march, that is, sixteen with the infantry, which will make twenty-eight 
with the twelve regimental pieces; the eight pieces of the spare battery with the guard; the twelve of two 
batteries on horseback, one with the guard, the other with the brigade of cuirassiers. 

This is the least organization you can have, and again'' 


15 


Page 116 


will you only have half the current organization of my troops, and less than the foreign troops. 

Your artillery companies on foot to serve eight pieces must be 120 men. The two companies on 
horseback and the six companies you see seem sufficient: three of them will serve the artillery divisions 
and three will be at the park. 

Eighteen battalions, representing 12,000 bayonets, must have sixty men's cartridges in the 
caissons, in addition to those of the cartridges. You would need 48 cartridge cases; you have 18 with the 
regiments, so there would be 30 left with the reserve. These 30 caissons would walk, namely: 18 with 
the infantry and 12 with the park or the Sardinian. But the infantry caissons enter the evaluation of the 
200 wagons. 

I go to the genie. It is not having an army that can not be entrenched. You have a company of 
sappers; it should be increased to at least 120 men. It would be necessary to have half a company of 
organized engineers as they are in France. This half-company would serve 25 cars carrying 3,000 
pioneer tools, ropes and other items needed to repair bridges and help pass a small river. 

FOOD. - To make war in the country where your army corps will serve, you need to have bread 
for fifteen days, carrying biscuit and flour. I suppose that your corps will rise to 18,000 mouths, for a 
fortnight it is the employment of 270,000 rations of flour or grain. By having big wagons each carrying 
four thousand, you would need 40 or 50 carriages. 

SHOES. - It is necessary that each man leaving Cassel has a pair of shoes on his feet, two pairs 
in the bag and a pair carried in wagons, so that a summer campaign can be done without the soldier 
comes to be barefoot. 

All preparations are made here as if the war were certain. I have in my crews 2,000 large model 
wagons carrying 4,000, and 4,000 artillery wagons hitched by 20,000 horses. My Guard alone has two 
hundred pieces of cannon harnessed, with 600 boxes of transport, etc. The French army has only eight 
hundred pieces of cannon. 

You will always be notified fifteen days in advance. Try to have your army equipped with 
everything, especially artillery and means of transport for food. 

NAPOLEON.

TO THE VICE-AMIRAL COUNT DECRES, 
MINISTER OF THE NAVY, IN PARIS. 
Paris, December 27, 1811. 


Count Decres, you told me that the transport of wood from the forest of Compiegne to Antwerp 
would cost 3 francs. I send you a report from the forest captain of Compiegne, who estimates it only at 
the end of the year. It has already returned to me from many quarters that the prices agreed by the navy 
with the transport contractors are exaggerated, that these prices were made at a time when they were 
paying badly, and that the naval council can turn them down half by paying well: it would be a saving of 
2 millions. It is obvious that anything that is being paid today at the same price as it was paid six years 
ago must have a moderation of more than 30 to 40 per cent. 

NAPOLEON.

18382. - TO EUGENE NAPOLEON, VICE-KING OF ITALY, AT MILAN. 
Paris, December 27, 1811. 


My Son, I refer you your draft decree of September 9, on the currencies, of all the questions, if 
that of the wheat is the most important, that of the currencies holds the second rank. Nothing is more 
likely to stir the spirits and to give substance to slander and popular riots, I do not believe that the 
current moment is that of touching these questions, which interest especially the poorest classes of the 
population; wheat is too expensive for that. It is necessary to postpone this and, in the meanwhile, to 
study the matter. No doubt that reductions are soon ordered and soon made, but the people, whose 
operations diminish their fortune, retain a long agitation: even in France, what I made last year stirred a 
lot for several months. We must continue to walk as we did until this time, waiting for other 
circumstances. 

NAPOLEON.

18386. - TO THE GENERAL LAKE, COUNT OF CESSAC, 
MINISTER DIRECTOR OF THE ADMINISTRATION OF THE WAR, IN PARIS. 
Paris, December 29, 1811. 


I wrote to you yesterday for Barcelona; I had the idea of sending in the 120 wagons I have, 
although they are very necessary for the army of Portugal. I do not give up on this idea, but it must be 
admitted that these cars will soon be lost, and that, moreover, without any restraint, it becomes a very 
expensive operation. On the other hand, sending wine, rice and dried vegetables, meat, by cabotage suits 
me perfectly; but the sending of corn and flours by this means is extremely harmful to me: the harvest 
being bad in France, every building I lose can no longer be evaluated by money, but by the real loss of 
grain, which supply the enemy, who has the greatest need for Cadiz and Lisbon. That being the case, I 
have 18,000 metric quintals of wheat already bought to pass to Barcelona: this would be the supply of 
this important place for a year. In the present situation of our crops, this employment would be 
imprudent; I will therefore content myself with sending 10,000 quintals of pomace, if it were more 
advantageous, in flours:!*° 





125 


Page 126 


it would be a supply of two hundred days or seven months. Supply being assured until April, these seven 
months would lead me until the end of October: that would remove us from all anguish for this 
important object, These same quintals, I do not want to transport them by sea: would lose half of it; I 
want them to be carried on the ground in five convoys, each of 100 wagons: Ist, January 15th; the 2nd, 
February 20th; 3rd, March 20th; the 4th, April 20th; the 5th, May 20th. I suppose eight days to go, eight 
days to return, six to stay; there would be another eight days to repair the wagons and prepare for the 
second convoy. 

I would like this transport not to be done at my expense; but that a house of commerce, like the 
house Durand or any other of this kind, undertook to provide 100 wagons with 6 horses with 2 or 3 men 
to Perpignan. You will supply by convoy 4,000 quintals of flour, which he would be required to carry to 
Barcelona and under the escort of the army. It would charge back sugar, coffee, indigo, colon and wool, 
etc. These commodities would be brought to Perpignan; it should be noted: 1‘ the number of the cart; 
2™ the weight equal to wheat worn; a customs employee would accompany from Barcelona to 
Perpignan. Thus, 100 wagons would bring 400,000 francs of sugar, coffee, or cotton, the house would 
have the privilege of introducing these commodities without a certificate of origin, and would pay 
customs customarily. You will calculate what would be his gain: this calculation will be easy to do. 
Comparing the price of sugar in Barcelona with that of France, I estimate it at | million per trip or 
10,000 francs per wagons; for five trips, it would be 5 million gain for this house. 

Assuming the wagon worth the 6 horses of the maintenance for five months to a total of 12,000 
francs per wagon, I will always have the result, for every 100 wagons, of 1,200,000 francs; but 
nevertheless the gain would remain of 3,800,000 francs. It is true that I have brought into France 2 
millions of pounds of cotton, of sugar, 1 coffee, but also I will have obtained a great advantage; for I 
observe that, by the tariff of August 5th, the pound of colonist of Brazil pays 4 francs of rights: a wagon 
which would carry 4,000 pounds will therefore pay on its return to Perpignan only 16,000 francs. 

If it's sugar, the pound pays 30 cents; the 4,000 pounds would therefore pay me 6,000 francs. If 
it's coffee, the pound pays 40 cents; the 4,000 pounds would thus pay me 8,000 francs. If it's indigo, the 
pound pays 4 francs 10 cents. If it's cocoa, the pound pays 5 francs, etc, !7°

You see, therefore, that with this privilege, I have enough to do all that is right, without spending 
anything, and granting one-third and one-quarter of the freeing of duties and assuming the loading of the 
100 wagons, that is, to say 4,000 quintals: 1,000 in sugar, 1,000 in cotton, 1,000 in coffee, 1,000 in 
indigo or other commodities. 

Sugar will make 150,000 francs, cotton 800,000, coffee 200,000, indigo 1 million; total, 
2,150,000 francs: five journeys will make 10,750,000 francs. 

I think that traders will earn enough when they have the advantage of not being required to have 
certificates of origin, and they will submit to pay all my rights net. The hides of Buenos Ayres, etc., the 
cottons Motril will be part of the returns. 

See tomorrow morning the people who can give you positive information on this matter; you will 
give me an account after mass. 

I do not know of any effective and simpler means of supplying Barcelona. I count on your 
wisdom to make the company the greatest benefits, however, losing as little as possible. Of course if the 
link of 100 wagons the company wanted to provide 2 or 300, it would be accepted, so instead of five 
trips, we would only do two or three. 

Once the above principles have been laid down for Barcelona, I have no problem in establishing 
them for all the rest of Spain. For this purpose, all the transport of clothing and artillery effects from 
Bayonne to Madrid, from Bayonne to Seville, from Bayonne to Zaragoza and Valencia, would be 
established on the same principle. A convoy would leave every month, escorted by 500 men; it would be 
100 or 200 wagons and would go to Burgos, part of Valladolid, part of Madrid, part of Seville. It would 
be granted the privilege for the convoy of Burgos; this is more considerable for that of Seville; the same 
principle for that of Valencia; by this means, clothing, the very effects and ammunition of artillery 
would be transported in quantity without cost. 

It is necessary to calculate the needs of clothing per year for Burgos, Valladolid and Seville. For 
Seville, it takes two months of road and so much return; the convoy of Seville can only make three trips 
a year. Assuming 100 cars, that would be 300 wagon goods returning to France; 300 garment wagons 
are not needed, but we would transport war ammunition, we would reduce the convoys to 50 wagons, or 
we would only'”’

two trips to 100 wagons a year. The convoys of Madrid, four a year to 25 wagons, 100 wagons; the

Valencia, to two a year to 50 wagons, 100 wagons. That would be about 500 wagons that would carry

however, a proportion could be established for colonial commodities, if necessary. 

Having thus applied these ideas to my needs in Spain, I wish to use them for my needs on the 
Vistula. 

The transports from Magdeburg to the Vistula are by water; it is therefore a question of dealing 
only with those of Magdeburg in France. I want to have 28 million bottles of wine, 2 million bottles of 
brandy; a total of 30 millions of liquid, forming 60,000 rations of wine for 300,000 men for two hundred 
days, and 32,000 rations of brandy for 300,000 men for a hundred and thirty days; which would water 
an entire army for a year. I wish it only cost me redemption at Bordeaux; 28 million bottles of wine 
make up about 12,000 barrels of wine, which, at 60 francs, cost 720,000 francs in Bordeaux, 12,000 
barrels would represent 6 million pounds and would require 1,300 wagons; from Bordeaux to 
Magdeburg this should cost a sum to be calculated. I will grant the right to bring back from Magdeburg 
cottons, sugar, and coffee, by paying to the custom-house, and establishing a rule which should be 
sought. I wanted to sink the idea, but the important thing now is to take care of Barcelona. 


P.S. When I realized the operation on Barcelona, I made the following calculations: a roll-on 
wagon carrying 5,000 pounds must be worth 2,000 francs; 6 horses must be worth 6,000 francs; total, 
8,000 francs. So I estimate the first bet of a wagon at 8,000 francs; I believe this assessment 
exaggerated, the minister will put the real price. Three men are needed; for the engagement of the three 
men, for their equipment and for their clothing, I put 600 francs at 200 francs one; total approximately 
9,000 francs; I believe this price exaggerated. I suppose the maintenance of the horses, per day, at 2 
francs per horse, 12 francs, and at 3 francs per man, 9 francs; !78

that's 21 francs a day; 21 francs multiplied by 365 days are 7,665 francs. I put for the value of the car,

suppose that the carriage and the horses will last three years, the first year must be taken into account 
only 3,000 francs for the first time and for food 7,665 francs; total, 10,665 francs. 

By neglecting the 665 francs, I will have 10,000 francs carrying 40 quintals; assuming twelve 
trips, they will carry 480 quintals; thus 10,000 francs divided by 480 quintals will make about 21 francs 
the quintal in expenses; it would be enough, then, to obtain a profit of 4 to 5 sous per pound, or 25 francs 
per quintal, or 1,000 francs per car, so that the individual who would have the certainty of a year's 
journey would be out of business. The privilege of importing sugar, coffee and cotton, without paying to 
the Customs, without a certificate of origin, can not be valued at less than 10 sous per pound; if it was 
cotton, probably it would go to 40 cents. Thus, without losing any of the customs duty, this simple 
privilege can be assessed at that. 

It seems that the cost of transport from Bordeaux to Magdeburg must be estimated at 60 francs, 
which is 12 cents a pound. Thus, by giving a privilege of customs which assures the return a profit of 10 
or 12 under the pound, the individuals must be found. The privilege of receiving sugar, coffee, cotton 
taken at Magdeburg and transported to France, paying the duties and without a certificate of origin, is 
equivalent to more than that.

18396. - NOTE 
DICTATED TO THE TRADE AND MANUFACTURING COUNCIL. 
Palace of St. Cloud, December 30, 1811. 


The Minister of the Interior, up to this hour, has always maintained that establishments would 
not fail; the opinion was that they would be wanting, and that one could only make beets. It was 
therefore of the greatest importance that there were many establishments, otherwise the farmers would 
be disgusted, since, in the absence of these establishments, it was to take a step backward and to expose 
itself to the fact that the farmer who did not find the flow of the sugar beet no longer sowing it next year. 

It is extraordinary that in this report we talk about budgets. The fund made available to the 
minister has not been spent; if it had been, and the minister had made another request, his Majesty 
would not have refused ten millions. 

The Minister of the Interior will make a new report, to which he will attach the account of the 
funds employed, and explain why he has not made a new request. 

The Minister concludes that there are no measures to be taken: however, if new establishments 
are not formed, the culture will be downgraded, or at least will be established only over the years. The 
question must be taken in the opposite direction, and as many manufactures as are necessary to make 
beet harvested this year, and in such numbers everywhere that the formation of these establishments 
encourages the farmer to sow. Nor can it be known from the report how much France loses by the 
insufficiency of these establishments. !*° 





133 


Page 134 


To be printed in the Moniteur, this report must only say what has actually been sown, make 
known in note the reasons which prevented the sowing, make known in another column what one has 
manufactured. The general report and the report for Moniteur will be presented next Monday. 

1,200 acres planted with sugar beet would each make 300 quintals of sugar beet and 600 pounds 
of sugar, which would have been 7,200,000 pounds; instead we had only 2,790,000 pounds. Thus the 
lack of means of manufacture has caused the farmers to lose 4,410,000 pounds of sugar, and must 
necessarily have caused them a loss for having indulged in this crop; they have been fooled by their 
confidence in the government. 

Count Chaptal will carry on Monday a detailed brief on manufacturing. This memoir should be 
accompanied by plans, and make known what is a beet factory, how much it would take to make all the 
beets harvested in 1811, how much would be needed for what will be harvested in 1812. Conclusion will 
be a distribution project to order the formation of institutions in 1812; and wherever there is a crop, a 
quantity of factories proportionate to the sowing will be placed at the expense of the Government. 

The 7,200,000 pounds of sugar that one could have had this year would have required 200 
factories like that of the Sieur Fay in the department of Doubs. After all, they would have cost, at the 
rate of 12,000 francs one, only 2,400,000 francs. With the sum of a million which his Majesty has 
granted, it would have been possible to establish a hundred, and it appears that only two or three have 
been established. 

The Minister of the Interior will examine, as well as M. Chaptal for his part, if it would not be 
advisable to set up beet factories as an exclusive privilege. Government alone can safely engage in an 
operation of this nature. How would an individual expose considerable funds to speculation that can be 
destroyed by a treaty of commerce or a change in the customs tariff? For it is proved that beet sugar will 
always cost double or triple the original price of cane sugar. 

On the other hand, if beet sugar sells like cane sugar, is it not a great harm to the treasure, which 
loses the right of entry, and yet by this right of entry keep up the price? Thus, on the one hand, the 
people are obliged to pay dear sugar, on the other the profit is not in the treasure; which is always 
contrary 


134 


Page 135 


on the principle that all the sacrifices that the people endure must be for the treasure. 

After considering this measure from the point of view of finance, it must be examined from the 
political point of view. France may one day want to return to cane sugar; and then, will not we have 
given rise to the complaints of those who have raised manufactures on the word of the government? 
Instead that the government, having made the sacrifice of only a few millions, will be repaid in a few 
years, and will be able to calculate the advantage of the return to the system of colonies. It appears that 
until now there are few established factories: they would be bought by the government. It also appears 
that it would take only 5 or 6 millions to establish the manufacture: the government alone can give this 
result; it is not probable that in many years the trade can make these establishments. 

The problem is to arrive in 1813, to prohibit cane sugar, to bear a large price decrease to the 
consumer and yet have a good product for the treasure. 

The Minister of Finance will also make a memorandum on this subject. 

According to the copy. Archives of Agriculture, Commerce and Public Works. 


18397. - TO GENERAL CLARKE, DUKE OF FELTHE, 
MINISTER: OF THE WAR, IN PARIS. 
Paris, December 30, 1811. 


Pontonniers. - The corps of the pontonniers of the Grande Armée will have thirteen companies, 
namely: seven companies of the Ist battalion (this battalion has four companies in Spain) and six 
companies of the 2nd battalion. The 3rd company, which is at the Bayonne reserve, will be ordered to go 
to Metz. What these two battalions have available at the depot will be sent to recruit the thirteen 
companies. 

Thus there will be: a company of pontooners in the corps of the Elbe, a company with the corps 
of the Ocean, a company with the observation corps of Italy, a company with the Guard and nine 
companies with a large park of the bridges ( three per crew, or divided as circumstances would like). 

All the companies of the 2nd battalion which are in Italy will follow the movement of the 
observation corps of Italy; those in Germany will follow the movement of the observation corps of the 
Elbe and the crews of the bridge. 

SAPPERS. - The sappers will be distributed as follows:'*°

Page 136 


the 1st battalion has two companies in Spain and seven in Italy: these seven companies will be 
employed at the Grande Armée. The 3rd Battalion, which is in Alexandria, has eight companies present 
and one in Corfu. The 5th battalion, which is in Metz, has its nine companies present. So there will be to 
the Grande Armée, namely: Ist battalion, seven companies; 3rd battalion, eight companies; 5th 
battalion, nine companies; total, twenty-four companies. 

All that deposits have available will be incorporated into these twenty-four companies. 

The depot of the 4th battalion, which is at Metz, will be used to carry the companies of the 5th 
battalion in full. 

Have a report on the battalion that is on the island of Elbe, to see what this battalion can provide

Of the twenty companies that are in Spain, I should be presented with a project to bring in the

MINERS. - I have twelve companies of miners. The Ist Company of the Ist Battalion is in

I also wish to make an exchange, send back to the Army of Portugal the four regiments of march, 
and bring a division of the army of Portugal to Burgos, so that the number of men will be compensated: 
the Army of the North is would then find strong enough and composed of good troops. 

You will write to the Duke of Dalmatia to send out without delay the three regiments of the 
Vistula, that of the Lancers of the Vistula, and all the officers of the Polish Staff. This weakening in the 
Army of the South is no consequence, and the order will be given to execute this movement within 
twenty-four hours after the receipt of your letter. 

You will hand me a project for the recruitment of cadres to withdraw from various armies, 
executives of artillery companies and train battalions, sappers or miners, to return. 

The three pack mule companies which exist at the 3rd, 4th and 13th battalions at Pan, will be 
destined for the Ebro Corps; consequently, they will go by Pau, under good escort, taking advantage of 
the escort which will lead the prisoners of Valencia to Zaragoza; By this means, General Reille will have 
600 packets, which will be of great use to him. As these three companies belong to three different 
battalions, you will order the general of the army of Portugal to agree with the general Reille for the 
exchange, so that a complete battalion is the army of Portugal and one to the corps of the Ebro. 

Finally, propose me to bring for the Grande Armée the engineering company which was at 
Bayonne, for the observation corps, a company of pontooners, one of miners and, I believe, two 
companies of artillery which were destined for the same corps. There will remain a considerable staff 
and equipment. My intention is to use the carriages, when I will know perfectly the organization of those 
who have the army of Portugal. The armed one, being in the presence of the English, needs a strong 
organization of this kind. If you have no situation, the aide-de-camp of the Duke of Ragusa, who is an 
artillery officer, may give it to you. 

I attach the greatest importance to the fact that the Army of Portugal has at least one hundred 
pieces of cannon harnessed, with the proper provisions, the Souham division must be twenty-two, the 
army of Portugal eighty, the Bonet division four or five; we

Page 140 


it would be one hundred and six. I think he needs it just as much, and that he needs his artillery to be

to the 1,000 horses of the train which I have in Toulouse. 

The reserve corps being thus dissolved, let me know the destination to give to each, either for the 
corps of the Ebro or for any other; do me a very detailed work on all this, with the states in support. The 
result of these measures will be to weaken the armies of Spain of the four regiments of the Vistula, 
forming eight battalions, of three Polish regiments, forming six battalions; total, seven regiments or 
fourteen battalions, which will form a division of a marvelous effect to the Grand Army. 

I ordered that the 40th and 34th return to France; you will repeat these orders. I will also have 
weakened the Spanish armies of the Polish lancers regiment, some Polish generals and officers of the 
Staff, and twenty-two battalions of the Guard; total, thirty-six battalions; but I have recently sent the 
Souham division, which has fourteen battalions, the Reille division, as well as the Caffarelli division, 
idem; total, forty-two battalions. Thus, instead of losing, the armies of Spain will find themselves 
winning. 

It is very necessary that you make known to the Duke of Dalmatia that as soon as the 34th and

government and who belong to his body army, will leave to join him. 

In sending to the Minister of War the state of the troops of Catalonia, I beg you to propose to 
tighten the cadres, and to return those who are fit to receive the conscription.

18400. - TO MARSHAL DAVOUT, PRINCE OF ECKMUHL, 
COMMANDING THE COPRS OF OBSERVATION OF THE ELBE IN HAMBURG. 
Paris. December 30, 1811. 


Cousin, you will receive a decree which I have just taken to place entirely in my pay the three 
regiments of infantry and the Polish cavalry regiment which are at Danzig: that puts an end to 
everything. Order that the 400 horses which I grant by my decree to the 9th Polish be bought without 
delay in the Duchy of Warsaw, so that this regiment has its 1,000 horses. Order also that this regiment 
have, like our lancers regiments, a certain number of carbines. Take steps for the Polish 5th, 10th and 
11th each to have 3,000 men; which will make 9,000 men for the three regiments. 

The French artillery company in Danzig will no longer be part of the 7th Division, since there is 
a Polish light artillery company. I need this company, since the increase of a 5th division in the 
cuirassiers requires the use of twelve more pieces of artillery. I gave the command of the 5th Division to 
General Valenee, senator. The 11th Cuirassier Regiment has been ordered to march; I recommend you 
to complete his horses. You will thus have three divisions of cuirassiers, each division of three 
regiments, each regiment presenting 900 men in battle; which makes 2,700 horses per division. '*! 


141 


Page 142 


Each division must be attached to a light cavalry regiment of three squadrons. The Ist squadron will 

leave on the 15th of January to go to Germany; the 2nd and 3rd squadrons will follow at fifteen days 
distance. Thus each division of cuirassiers will be 3,400 or 3,500 horses. Each division will have two 
artillery batteries on horseback or twelve pieces. 

I have thought fit to divide the whole Grand Army into fifteen divisions of infantry, all about 
equal to yours; the 7th, however, is part of it. The first nine divisions are under your command; the 10th, 
11th and 12th divisions are at the camp of Boulogne; the 13th, 14th and 15th meet in Bolzano, Italy; the 
Guard is composed of four divisions; which makes nineteen French divisions. The light cavalry is 
divided into fourteen brigades; five brigades are under your command, including that of General Castex; 
There are three in Italy, and six on the Rhine. Brigade generals are appointed and run journals to check 
the returns and organize the regiments. Six generals of division will be attached to these fourteen 
brigades. The cavalry reserve is made up of six divisions, five of which are cuirassiers and one of 
dragons. Each division has twelve pieces of light artillery. A siege crew is organized in Danzig and one 
in Magdeburg. Three bridge crews are organized at Danzig; these crews employ 400 cars and 2,000 
horses. 

The Bavarians, the Wurtembergers, the Saxons, the Poles, are not included in this organization. 

All calculations made, I hope to have in the month of March more than 200,000 infantrymen, 
45,000 cavalrymen, eight hundred pieces of cannon harnessed by more than 20,000 horses, and 1,500 
military transport vehicles. The French army will amount to nearly 300,000 men. You see that I have 
never made greater preparations. 

We lack horses of cavalry in France; it must be lifted from your side as much as you can; I am 
assured that there is a large enough quantity in Jutland and Holstein. 

NAPOLEON. 

From the original comm. by the Marechal Princess Eckmiihl.

18402. - TO EUGENE NAPOLEON, VICE-KING OF ITALY, AT MILAN. 
Paris, December 30, 1811. 


My son, Aldini sends you a decree by which I order the formation of a battalion of Italian 
military crews. This battalion will be formed, in all and for all, like the French battalions. I will have in 
my Italian army a battalion of military crews of six companies, each company serving 42 cars, forges 
and extensions; total, 252 wings for the battalion. I only want extensions and trolleys of new model, 
which carry four thousand. Two of these companies will be attached to the guard, the other four will be 
for the infantry. What you have today in military transport will be melted in this battalion. But this is 
independent of the ambulance caisson of each infantry regiment and the ambulance caisson and the field 
forge of each cavalry regiment. 

The war in Poland bears no resemblance to the Austrian war; without means of transport, 
everything is useless. Each battalion of military crews must have 771 men, 1,227 horses and 252 
wagons. Pass your markets without delay. You will take the men in the depots; you will be contracting 
for the purchase of horses in Switzerland. Have caisson made in the arsenal of Venice. That twenty-four 
hours after the receipt of this letter all your orders be dispatched. It takes sixty days of work to make the 
caisson; it takes 200 workers to make 200 caisson in sixty days; but, as all caissons must be made on the 
lst of February, employ 3, 4 or 500 workers. The woods and irons are not to be missed in Venice. This 
will bring a small delay in the work of the navy; but I do this myself in Antwerp to have as many new 
models as possible, which are preferable to others. '*° 





143 


Page 144 


I wish the 9th Military Transport Battalion to have these new caissons; for this purpose, I have it 
made at the arsenal of Turin; but I fear that this arsenal can not supply so many for so close a time: see if 
the arsenal of Pavia could not help to make a quarantine. So I look at this as a finished affair. 

You know the great need of bakers for the army; I suppose you have a good number in your 
divisions. A company of Italian nurses is also necessary. I suppose you have workers to build six kilns 
in twenty-four hours. These objects are of great importance in a Polish war. I told you that every man 
should have four pairs of shoes; it would even be advantageous to have five pairs. 

Independently of regimental ambulances, you need four Italian ambulances for the Italian 
division and for the guard; each ambulance being 4 caisson, it will use 16 caissons. Field forges must be 
supplied by the artillery; you must have many in the kingdom. 

NAPOLEON.

18403. - TOM. MAHET, DUKE OF BASSANO, 
MINISTER OF EXTERNAL RELATIONS, PARIS. 
Paris, December 31, 1811. 


Mr. Duke de Bassano, it would be appropriate to write to Baron Bignon to urge the government 
of the Grand Duchy to arm and supply Modlin, now that this place is in the case of supporting a siege, 
and to to direct the armaments which it would be useless to have at Warsaw. I would wish all Lancers of 
the Grand Duchy to be armed with rifles, as I have ordered for my own. Ask him for details of how 
these men are armed today. I would also like the lancers regiments to be full of 1,100 men and 1,000 
horses; which would make for men a total of 17,600, and for horses 16,000. If it was too 
disproportionate with the means of the Grand Duchy, I would at least want the complete to be 16,000 
men and 14,400 horses, that is to say 1,000 men and 900 horses per regiment, so as to always have at 
least 850 on the battlefield.'** 





144 


Page 145 


As the full is 12,000 men, it would be an increase of 4,000. I would willingly agree to pay for this run, 
but I would like to pay only the excess that would be beyond the current total of 12,000. 

I see with astonishment in the states of the Ist of November that there are more than 1,800 horses 
at deposits: it's way too much; there should not be more than 30 horses in each depot, except at the time 
of the return. 

I would not be far from organizing a military transport battalion organized like those of France. 
Could we get draft horses, harnesses, wagons in Warsaw? In how many months would these wagons be 
built? Would the duchy provide men? How much would it cost? It would have to be done under the 
colors of the Grand Duchy, in order to preserve appearances. 

It would also be necessary for Baron Bignon, with all the proper discretion, to give information 
which would reassure us as to the facility of having corn, oats, and, lastly, the necessary provisions for 
the army. It would also be necessary for him to take care of the means that could be organized, as was 
done about the month of May in the last campaign, to have a transport service from Thorn, Plock, 
Warsaw and of Zamosc on the points where one could go; a service of 4,000 wagons would be 
necessary. 

He must study men, without affecting anything, in order to know who to turn to when the time is 
right. Recommend to him to send memoirs on all these objects, with the appropriate discretion. 

I also want to know how much wine from Hungary could be obtained from the Vistula, and at 
what cost would these shipments return to Warsaw; what are the means of transport from Hungary to the 
Vistula; how much grain brandy could be produced from Moldova, and at what price. 

Apart from the horses necessary for the duchy, could we obtain 3,000 hussar horses? Where 
would we find them? At what price, and when would they be returned to Warsaw? You feel the 
importance of making these demands only by sure occasions, in order to avoid the way of the ordinary 
posts and that your letters are not read by the princes of the intermediate countries. 

NAPOLEON.

18414. - TO EUGENE NAPOLEON, VICE-KING OF ITALY, AT MILAN.

My Son, the Minister of War has sent you my orders for the organization of the 13th, 14th, and 
15th Divisions, for that of the four brigades of light cavalry and the division of dragoons. Hide your 
movement as long as you can, beginning with everything that is insignificant, that is, the farthest. I 
decided that the 13th division would be reunited in Bolzano and to the limits of the Bavarian territory; 
that the part of the division which comes from the Illyrian provinces would go to Linz; except for the 
Croats, who must leave only well dressed and well armed; that the 14th division would meet on the side 
of Trento and Roveredo, and the 15th division on Lodronc, Rocca d'Anfo, Brescia, and Salo; that two 
brigades of light cavalry should meet in the valley of the Brenta, so that the head is only one march from 
Trent, and the other two brigades in the valley of the Chiese, so as to be able to quickly Rocca d'Anfo, 
that the division of dragoons would meet on the Mincio; the great park, the military transports, and the 
engineers at Verona. Of course, each division will have with it its artillery, its detachment of engineers, 
and all that is necessary to it. As it is possible that divisions!”

18417. -NOTE 
DICTATED IN TRADE AND MANUFACTURING COUNCIL. 
Palace of St. Cloud, January 6, 1812. 


The Minister of the Interior should make a report which will make known the quantity of acres 
of sugar beet required from each department, the quantity supplied, the factories established there, by 
making known the causes which prevented the realization of all what we had hoped. 

The Minister of the Interior would then make a new distribution for next year's crops. Beets are 
sown in March; so we have the necessary time. 

The second operation would consist in drafting a decree, which would say that any individual 
who wishes to establish a factory will have to take a license; that all those who have established it up to 
this day will retain them by right, and will make known if they wish to continue to manufacture in 1812. 

All those who will undertake to manufacture such a quantity, the minimum of which would be 
fifty thousand, will apply for the license. The'*® 


158 


Page 159 


refiners will have preference; to this end, the prefect would write to them to ask them if they want to 
take advantage of it. 

It will be given up to four or five hundred patents. 

It will be understood in the report that, already this year, the farmer has suffered, because the 
factories have not been in proportion with the crop. 

Any patented individual (by realizing these conditions, that is to say, being able to manufacture 
in October next year, will obtain the guarantee: 

1“ That no right shall be established for four years on the object of manufacture; 

2° A declaration would be made that if, as a result of these measures, the five hundred factories 
are active in the month of October, cane sugar will be prohibited in the Empire as English merchandise. 

The second condition should be added, that the departments would have carried the whole crop. 

This is a sacrifice of the Government for four years for the benefit of the people, because sugar 
can not sustain itself at six francs when there are five hundred factories. 

Manufacturers will have four years of exemption from contributions and will be sure of the 
continuation of the continental system through prohibition. 

Finally, everything would be prepared for the management at the end of four years, and the 
Government, leaving the price of the time, would have the benefit for its profit. Assuming sugar at 40 
cents, it would be, on a consumption of 30 millions, a profit of 60 millions. It would be advisable to 
establish four beautiful manufactories in the four points of France where there is the most sugar beet, 
and where one might hope to exploit what to make from 1 million to 4 millions sugar, in them placing 
on canals or rivers. We have nine months from now to October to organize these factories. It would be 
an advance that would not go to 2 or 3 aggravates, and that would put the Government well informed of 
this affair. Good chemists would be placed at the head of these establishments, and many pupils would 
be sent there. 

According to the copy. Archives of Agriculture, Commerce and Public Works.

18426. - TO M. COLLIN, COUNT OF SUSSY, 
STATE ADVISER, DIRECTOR GENERAL OF CUSTOMS, IN PARIS. 
Paris, January 10, 1812. 


Count de Sussy, I have decided that there will be in the future a Minister of Manufactures and 
Trade, and I have appointed you to fulfill these high offices. I had to recognize the good services you 
have rendered by organizing customs as they are today. 

The department of manufactures and commerce will have in its attributions: the direction and the 
administration of the trade. its movement in the ports and in the various places of the interior; 
manufactures and police regulations relating thereto; the appointment of stockbrokers and brokers; 
health administrations (with the exception of Toulon); training and administration of indigenous 
products; the examination of the various processes of improvement of the factories, the surveillance of 
the administration of the customs, the personnel of this administration, the proposal of the tariffs and all 
the regulations relative to this object; the supervision of the general supplies of the empire, the 
movement, the entry and the exit of commodities; correspondence with consuls with foreign powers on 
matters relating to commerce; the formation of the General Council of Commerce and the report of all 
cases submitted or to be submitted to the Imperial Council of the catches. In a few days you will take an 
oath.

18429. - TO GENERAL LACUEE, COUNT DE CESSAC, 
MINISTER DIRECTOR OF THE ADMINISTRATION OF THE WAR, IN PARIS. 
Paris, January 13, 1812. 


Monsieur le Comte de Cessac, I have just granted you an additional sum of 2,400,000 francs 
from Danzig's budget of 1811. It is my intention that you purchase without delay 100,000 quintals of 
wheat, 100,000 quintals of rye, and one million bushels of oats. 

I have given you the order, which I repeat, that the rice which is at Passau, at Hamburg and in the 
places of the Oder, in the hands of the French administrations, and at Magdeburg, should be directed 
without delay to Danzig. I charge the director-general of customs to prevent any sale of rice, and to 
place at your disposal, to be directed on Danzig, all the rice which is at Hamburg and other places of 
Germany. 

My intention is not to pay it at the price of the contractor, which is twenty-five percent too 
expensive, but to pay it at the lowest price possible. I do not need to recommend that we have to put an 
address in these purchases. By this means, I shall have on the Ist of March, namely: on the reserve, 
200,000 quintals of wheat and'® 





165 


Page 166 


rye; at the headquarters supply, 70,000; total, 270,000 quintals. Of these 270,000 quintals, 70,000 will 
be converted into flour, well embroidered, and can make thirty days of walking. I shall have at the 
reserve 4,000 quintals of rice; to the supply of siege, 4,000 quintals of rice; from Passau and the places 
of the Oder, 4,000 quintals of rice; total, 12,000 quintals of rice. I shall have 1,100,000 bushels of oats in 
reserve; to the supply of seats, 600,000 bushels of oats, total, 2 million bushels. 

I will then have 20 millions of rations or bread, or for an army of 400,000 men for fifty days; I 
will have 20 million rations of rice an ounce a day, or 400,000 men for fifty days. I'll have 2 million 
bushels of oats, or 50,000 horses for fifty days. I guess I'm not mistaken in these different data. 
Regardless of this, there is a large supply on the Oder. 

As for the biscuit, I wish that the biscuit which is at Danzig be collected and embarked in a few 
days, as well as the 1,800,000 rations which exist in the places of the Oder, so as to be able to move 
quickly; which will make 2,300,000 rations of biscuit. Let me know how long it would take Danzig to 
make 1,700,000 rations, requiring 4 million rations of biscuit. As this time is most favorable to 
purchases, it is necessary that you give orders without delay. 

NAPOLEON. 

From the original. Deposit of the war.

circumstances, would, in the present state of affairs, put Hamburg under the protection of the invasion of 
the English. We could draw from Holland some reinforcements to keep the batteries. It is necessary that 
these batteries be closed to the throat, either by turns, or by country works, so that they are safe from 
landings and fire from the ships. These batteries, with some men in their enclosure, would be defended; 
In case of a great expedition of the English, they would be taken, but they are made for that, Let me 
know their number, their location and their armament. Understand in this detail the batteries of the 
Mecklenburg coast. It seems to me that I have ordered the formation of coast guards, and I will leave 
three French artillery companies on the coast. 

NAPOLEON. 

From the original comm. by the Marshal Princess Eckmihl. 


18431, -NOTE ON THE CONTINENTAL BLOCKADE, 
DICTATED TO THE TRADE AND MANUFACTURING BOARD, 
Palace of St. Cloud. January 13, 1812, 


There is only one big system to take: or stay as we are, which can be supported by good reasons, 
or walk big to a different order. 

Stay as we are? We know how we are. We must begin by establishing what His Majesty means 
by a great system, so that we can compare the two states. 

The sugar has risen to Italy at an exorbitant price, so that there is a considerable gain on the 
sugar which comes from Koenigsberg and which pays a continental right; which proves that prohibitive 
laws are observed in Italy. 

Sugar is cheaper in the countries of Confederation; and it is because these countries are not under 
the control of His Majesty, and because the princes follow the continental system less well. 

The sugar is worth at Leipzig 51 under the pound, weight of marc, at Frankfort 50 sous; that is to 
say, in these two countries, the law being only 30 sous, it is still worth 20 sous above the law. It would 
be much less if the ordinary channels were open. We can therefore say that France also supplies the 
Confederation, oe 





167 


Page 168 


In Naples, sugar is worth 5 francs; it is as expensive as in Paris and Milan; therefore, in France, 
Italy, and Naples, the laws are executed; and these two countries, which are not under the regime of the 
French Customs, know that they would be united if they did not execute the laws of the Empire, 

The Government has to provide for the consumption of France, which has 43 millions of 
population; to that of Italy, which has 6,500,000; to that of Naples, which has 5 millions, and to that of 
Confederation, which is raised to 10 millions; which is about 65 million, that is to say almost triple the 
consumption of ancient France, 

Assuming that the consumption of all these countries is also the same as it was in ancient France, 
it is supposed to be reduced by two-thirds, 

France consumed 45 million pounds of raw sugar or 450,000 quintals. His Majesty will grant 
licenses to bring 450,000 quintals of raw sugar into the Empire; this will produce 70 million francs in 
duties, will require a cash export of 10 millions, and will result in an export of the products of our soil 
and our manufactures, principally in wines and silks, for a value of 30 millions of francs. 

His Majesty will apply the same system to coffee, Buenos-Ayres leathers, indigo, tea, woolen 
cotton, and dyestuff. Sugar is supposed to enter for one-third, which will be clearly established. in the 
minutes. 

This will therefore produce a great activity in the manufactures, an encouragement for 
navigation, the navy, the brokerage, a right of 200 millions collected by the customs during the year, a 
germ of activity and life in all our ports. 

For France, the result will be a dream that could only be achieved through the passage of the 
exclusive system; for how could it be conceived that England, without the absolute enclosure of the 
continent and scarcity, would have been brought to an order of things so contrary to her commercial 
interest? Even the Americans, who traded with us, made their discount in London, and in return took 
from what they brought us English goods. 

The system of colonial goods will have gained much in this new arrangement; Beet sugar and 
pastel will not be lost, since the advantage of these crops is in the right paid by sugar and pastel from 
abroad. 

But if the good that will result from these measures for France is easy to grasp, it is not so much 
to appreciate justly what in'®* 


168 


Page 169 


will be the effect for England. This will do no good to England, neither for her manufactures, nor for 
brokerage, nor for freight; that will do him good only as an outlet for these commodities; some of these 
commodities belong to Holland and France. This will undoubtedly be good for him, but it will bring 
about a revolution in England; and will this good be less or stronger than for France? 

If things are established as we have just said, we think that the good of France would be as 3, and 
that of England as 1; and if it is not so, it is because the measure can not receive its execution. 

If, after the knowledge of this system, England adheres to it, it will find it more difficult by the 
spite and disappointment of seeing the activity of our manufactures, the product of our customs, greater 
than by the effect of the continental system. 

His Majesty considers this not as a change of system, but as his sequel. The system was war, the 
result is victory. 

By the way, did we say that we would no longer receive sugar, coffee, indigo? No, because we 
were content to establish a right. It was up to England to provide us with it and we have never been able 
to think that our navigation and catches could feed us; but we have said that we should receive these 
commodities only against French soil products, with a very considerable right; that we would only let 
them arrive on our buildings and with our licenses. So it was the perfected system that produced this 
result that was only hoped for in a few years. 

One feels that the system as it has been established is a permanent system, which can be 
perpetual: one can always give one's wine, one's silks, against objects that one does not have; to give 
them, not as the disadvantageous treaty of Versailles, as a consequence of the similarities of units of 
commodities, and thus putting in competition a consumption of 30 millions of men with a of 10 
millions, but by a calculation where the value is multiplied by the quantity, and not appreciated by one 
of its elements. 

Any treaty or stipulation under which one receives the sugar against the silk, or tariff against 
tariff, as in the treaty of Versailles, would be a treaty of 1 against 7. 

Thus we do good to England, no doubt; but we do him the good that we can not prevent, and we 

receives the triple: it would be a bad combination to refuse 3 to 1.'° 





169 


Page 170 


At present it would be idle to consider whether this system will take place; you have to try it. As 
we have been consistent, as we use only licenses, when the license has expired everything fits into 
common law; thus, if that does not succeed, the measure will be established only in the minutes of the 
council. Nothing will prove better the real inferiority of England, and how the decrees of Berlin and 
Milan, supported by victories on the continent, have brought a great result. 

We go to the means of execution. 

It would be given more than two kinds of licenses. The licenses of the first kind would be for 
importation of corn, rice, etc., which is due to the circumstances of the year; they would not be subject 
to any kind of condition. The licenses of the second kind would contain permission to import such 
quantity of sugar, coffee, etc., into Nantes and Bordeaux, as against wines and spirits; in the North, 
against silk for a third, the canvases of Cambrai, the linens and other goods of this kind. 

Each license would be for a trip; a trader could take two or three, if he wanted to, because the 
whole of the licenses would include the whole system, that is to say all the sugar recognized as 
necessary, coffee, etc. 

The system, once established on these bases, may be susceptible of modifications and 
developments. 

For France and Italy, as it is money which will enter into our coffers, it is immaterial that the 
right is perceived by the French or Italian customs; 

2. For Naples, it is not the same thing. 

3. The princes of the Confederation have no ports; they must receive the sugar by Hamburg. It 
would be necessary, by a treaty with each of them, that they should receive nothing from Prussia or 
Austria, and they would be given a bonus. Thus, if the duty is 30 cents, ten of them will be given to them 
by the customs channel; the princes would find a considerable profit, without their people noticing it. 
For example, as Grand Duke of Berg, continental law does not render anything to His Majesty; she 
knows that in this capacity it would be nice to receive 600,000 francs, which would be the share 
produced by the consumption of this country. The king of Westphalia draws nothing from his 
continental right, and if he is offered 2 or 3 millions, as well as Saxony and Bavaria, they will regard this 
treaty as advantageous. 

As for the court of Vienna, we would let him transit through Trieste!” 


170 


Page 171 


and it will be supplied by putting a transit fee equal to the continental right: 20 sous for Austria, for 
example, and 10 sous for France; it would always be for the latter a beautiful right perceived on a 
population of 15 million consumers. 

In Naples, we will proceed in the same manner; the colonial commodities will enter only on 
French licenses, France will take on the right 50 per cent; there will be so much for the King; it will be a 
consumption duty of 50 per cent on the kingdom, and, as the good state of the King's finances is of 
importance to his Majesty, she will be glad that he would be 50 per cent, in the licenses for Naples. His 
Majesty could allow the exportation of some manufactures of the country. It will be necessary to subject 
Prussia to the same system. 

These two powers, who can no longer receive colonial goods, will receive them; they will have 
half the right, and their manufactures will have an export, but it will be only on French licenses, which 
will limit them. 

Here is how we could do the series: 

Hamburg, Bremen, Lubeck, would form a first series; Amsterdam, another, second series; 
Ostend, Dunkirk, a third; Le Havre, Caen, a fourth; Granville, St. Malo, Morlaix, Redon, Quimper, a 
fifth; Nantes, La Rochelle, Bordeaux, Bayonne, a sixth; Marseilles, This, Nice, a seventh; Savona and 
Genoa, an eighth; Livorno, Civita-Vecchia, a ninth; Trieste, a tenth; Kingdom of Italy: Venice and 
Ancona, an eleventh; Kingdom of Naples: Naples, a twelfth; Mecklenburg: Rostock and Wismar, a 
thirteenth; Prussia: a series. 

The series of Naples, Prussia, and Mecklenburg, will be formed last; we have to wait for these 
countries to ask for licenses. 

Importation is a simple thing: sugar, coffee, cocoa, are needed in all these countries; tea in 
Holland. It is necessary to know which are the countries where the indigos must be directed, etc. 

As for the export, it must vary: that of Bordeaux and Bayonne would be established mainly on 
the wines and spirits; In addition to this, it will be possible to export everything that is not forbidden. 
Holland will be able to export its cheese, but the surplus in other commodities will not count in the 
export balance. 

In all this system Danzig remains; he supplies the colonial commodities to Poland; it must be 
made a series apart; the export would be in wood construction. Then comes the question of wheat: 
Poland 


171 


Page 172 


he needs this exportation, and the commerce of Danzig requires the exportation of grain for England, 
and it is very important to drive one out of every two cargoes to France; we could see if this is 
practicable. It would be advisable also to see what right could be placed on the wheats exported from 
Danzig. Thus the importation of colonial commodities could supply all Poland; and the right is not 
strong enough to prevent the Poles from stocking it. 

The Minister of the Interior will make a report in which he will draw up the table of goods to be

A division of light cavalry and two divisions of cuirassiers and carabineers, forming the 2nd 
corps; 

A division of light cavalry, a division of cuirassiers and a division of dragoons, forming the 3rd 
corps. 

Each corps will have a common park; each of the three cavalry reserve corps will have a park.

You need a payer by division. Is it advisable to have a payer per corps, or is it better for division 
payers to have their direct accounts with the paymaster-general? This is what experience alone can make 
known,

into the hands of the enemy, it will be seen from their extreme simplicity that it is without consequence.

18438. -NOTE 
DICTATED IN COUNCIL OF MINISTERS. 
Palace of Tuileries, January 15, 1812. 


His Majesty thinks that an extraordinary cut should be made of all the elm, walnut, and other 
woods necessary for guns and other artillery, so as to supply the arsenals for four years, and 
extraordinary cut for palisades. These cuts would be made in such a way that the Minister of Finance 
would receive the amount, and that the artillery henceforth would not spend more money for this object 
and would be supplied. 

His Majesty turns his attention to the wooden cups for the navy. Here is how it is done:'” 





175 


Page 176 


The officer of the navy hammer; the forestry officer puts the acre in adjudication, with the 
condition of giving to the navy, for a fixed price, so many marked trees (in this price is the condition of 
the transport of these trees until Ruelle), and that the successful tenderer must receive there from the 
navy only by cubic feet. As is usually the case, this coin is worth more (and it is a vice in the forest 
administration system, because the same price should be paid to the navy as to an individual, with a 
reduction of 20 or 40 per cent. ), it follows that the naval officer agrees with the contractor who buys his 
tree. The naval officer, if he is not faithful, declares a marked wood not proper to the navy, and receives 
a gratuity for that declaration, It is a loss for the Estate and for the Navy. If, on the contrary, the wood 
was given to the navy for nothing, the purchaser would receive, by his specifications, the obligation to 
cut off the marked trees and to drive them to Ruelle, and, if the navy did not take them , the purchaser 
would become the owner) for a cubage at such price; therefore he would have no interest in not 
delivering them; or it would be obliged to cut, and if the navy did not take them, these woods would 
belong to the administration, which would sell them by a new auction. It could also have the advantage 
that in the woods rejected by the navy, artillery and engineering could take what would be convenient 
for them. His Majesty, therefore, thinks that a change is necessary in this respect, because, on the other 
hand, the forest administration is making very high the damage done to it by the hammering of the navy. 

One feels that there is some inaccuracy in this way of operating. 

A bidder bids an acre where there are two marked trees; they are supposed to be good: if they are 
refused) it is clear that the successful bidder wins; so this chance is favorable to him. If he then increases 
this chance by a bribe, there is only a series of abuses. On the connection that, when the successful 
tenderer makes his bid on the principle that the marked woods do not belong to him, he will not be 
interested; he will be obliged to the transport, then he will remove from the price of the acre the value of 
the marked woods and the expenses of their transport. The navy does not take these woods, it is a new 
adjudication. 

To return to the question, the navy does not have the means, for its officers, to cut the woods; the 
forest administration can not do it either. An error made in the forest of Fontainebleau has given rise to 
many cisoners. There is therefore no other way than the adjudication. We should hammer the woods, 
and 


176 


Page 177 


the invitation would designate the contractors who would be in charge of cutting and driving the timber 
reserves to Ruelle; it would be a simple adjudication of labor. If the navy refused the woods, it would be 
a special sale by auction.

18451. - TO THE GENERAL LACUEE, COUNT DE CESSAC, 
MINISTER DIRECTOR OF THE ADMINISTRATION OF THE WAR, IN PARIS. 
Paris, January 24, 1812. 


Monsieur le Comte de Cessac, I write you the letter for you alone. I want her not to come out of 
your hands, so that the contents remain completely secret. 

My intention is, when the conscription of 1812 is gone and at the moment when the war will be 
declared, that is towards the end of March, to raise 120,000 men, under the title of first ban of the 
National Guard. These 120,000 men would be taken from the conscriptions of 1809, 1810, 1811, and 
1812, which remitted 30,000 men by conscription. The senatus-consulte would give them the assurance 
of not leaving the frontiers of France, but they should serve for as long as the war would last. This lifting 
will be done quickly, because the men would remain in the localities, the Dutch in Holland, the 
Flemings in Flanders, the Britons in Brittany. I suppose then that in April and May I will need all that is 
necessary for the clothing of these 120,000 men. It would be advisable to take some precautions now to 
have sheets. These 120,000 men would not actually move from within, in order to have the guarantee of 
the tranquility and inviolability of the territory during the war. I will probably train from these 120,000 
men one hundred and twenty battalions. 

NAPOLEON
