18454. -OBSERVATIONS 
DICTATES IN ADVICE OF BRIDGES AND PAVEMENTS. 
Palace of the Tuileries, January 21, 1812. 


Of all the communications from the Baltic to the Rhine, the best, the shortest, the most 
economic, is the sea. But, the sea being forbidden by superior forces, thence arises the idea and comes 
the necessity of an internal communication from the Baltic to the Rhine, The first idea that presents itself 
is to leave Hamburg, to go down the Elbe, to follow the Wadden to Delfzyl. It is true that this navigation 
is only good for vessels drawing four feet of water, and that this navigation, like the first, has the 
disadvantage of being intercepted by the enemy. 

So the most natural idea is to go down the Elbe to Cuxhaven, and join the Elbe with the Weser to 
Bremerlehe via a side channel without locks. 

The navigation from Hamburg to Cuxhaven can be practiced by huge buildings, as well as that of 
Cuxhaven to the Weser by *6 





186 


Page 187 


the canal; at Bremerlehe we would take the new canal, which would lead to Delfxyl, 

This project has not been studied; it was for want of positive information that the Emperor had 
adopted the proposed project of a canal passing through the Oste. Here there is a sharing of water, which 
is always a difficult thing. It is true that the Oste is navigable as far as Bremerwoede, where it would be 
necessary to break the load as far as the Weser. 

Thus the Emperor does not stop this project until it has been studied. From next year the project 
will be made for the joining of the Elbe to the Weser, and the point will be determined where the canal 
will join the Elbe. The Emperor will be proposed with the appointment of a joint commission of land 
engineers, naval officers, and highway engineers to determine this project. 

The first point is to have the work of Mr. Beautemps-Beaupré checked by a commission of naval 
and engineering officers; the second, to determine the point where the basin will be made, since the 
vessels engaged in the Elbe might perish by the ice; we must ensure the possibility of establishing the 
basin in the location to be designated; third point: two forts are necessary on the right and on the left of 
this great establishment, in order to be always master of 2,000 toises of harbor, and then one would 
establish along the sea, with 7 or 800 toises, a fort like the fort Lasalle of the Helder, costing about a 
million, or 1,000,000, 500 men could sustain a very long siege, because one can be attacked only by the 
dikes. 

If this work could be studied by April, we could start this fort in the next campaign and have it in 
the year, known Fort Lasalle. 

The Minister of the Navy will hold a council where General Haxo, MM. Tarbé, Blanken, 
Sganzin, Cachin and Beautemps-Beaupré, to make a first project that will be submitted to His Majesty, 
and then we will send on the spot to study the land. 

According to the copy. Naval Archives.

18456. - TO MARSHAL BESSIERE, DUKE OF ISTHIE, 
COMMANDING THE IMPERIAL GUARD, IN PARIS. 
Paris. January 27, 1812. 


Cousin, report to me on the staff of my Guard. I begin with the Polish light horse: General 
Krasinski is the colonel. I have appointed Brigadier-General Konopka, who has long commanded a 
regiment of lancers to the army of the south of Spain, who is the second major? The 2nd regiment of 
light lancers is commanded by General Colbert; there is, I believe, a Dutch major; who is the second 
major? can I trust the Dutch major? 

General Guyot commands the chasseurs on horseback; Colonel Lion is one of the majors; I 
appointed General Exelmans Major in this regiment. Daumesnil being wounded can not remain major; it 
is necessary to report to me on this officer, that my intention is to employ militarily. Could we not give 
him the command of Vincennes, with a higher rank and a good salary? Vincennes being a state prison 
and one of the quarters of my Guard, I need a reliable man. 

General Saint-Sulpice commands the dragons; Colonel Letort is one of the majors; I do not know 
the second; make me a report that lets me know ... 

General Walther commands my grenadiers on horseback; Generals Lepic and Chastel are majors. 

General Lepic would like to be made general of division and to go'** 





188 


Page 189 


to order a big cavalry division? As my grenadiers rarely charge, he would gain experience in the line, 
and I could then call him to the grenadier command when General Walther would withdraw. I only want 
to do what is right for him. See him and tell him about it as coming from you. 

General Chastel is given talent; the command of a cavalry brigade would give him experience; I 
will also do only that which will suit him. 

I would like to place as Major in one of my Guard's cavalry regiments, General Ornano, who, 
having always been with the army, will gain in my Guard a confidence which will be useful to him; I 
will place it after that in the line. 

If Generals Lepic and Chastel passed in the line, what brigade generals or colonels could I name 
majors in the grenadiers? 

I move to the infantry. General Dorsenne being General-in-Chief must now follow his career; I 
wish to appoint a general of division to replace him in my Guard. 

Let me know if I have enough generals and colonels to command all the rest of my Guard.

18458. - TO JEROME NAPOLEON, KING OF WESTPHALIA, 
A CASSEL. 
Paris. January 27, 1812. 


Brother, various indications had long made me fear that the Emperor of Russia would have 
ceased to be in the sentiments of Tilsit. A ukase, published in December, 1810, injured the interests of 
France and the Confederation chiefly; it was advantageous to England; it was against the Tilsit treaty. 
However, I had abstained from any kind of complaint, confining myself to friendly representations. At 
Blois the following April, the Emperor of Russia had his ministers at the various courts issue a protest 
relative to the Oldenburg. I must have been all the more astonished at so singular a step that, anticipating 
the wishes of Russia, I had, from the beginning, offered a proper indemnity for the Duke de Oldenburg. 
I thought only of repeating this offer. As Russia did not appear to approve the object proposed for 
compensation, I urged her to make known what she desired. Finally, I put everything in use to stop the 
consequences of a public act which, although it spoke of the preservation of the alliance, naturally had to 
make succeed the mistrust of the good harmony which had reigned between the two courts. Instead of 
explaining itself, Russia weakened her army of the Danube, evacuated the right of this river, removed 
from Finland part of the troops which occupied the province so recently conquered, and gathered all her 
available forces on the frontiers of the Duchy of Warsaw. 

The territory of the Confederation was thus threatened, so much so that I was obliged to demote 
the troops of the duchy on the Vistula, in order to be able to support them in the event of a sudden 
attack. From the commencement of these Russian movements, my first care had been to provide for the 
defense of Danzig, which is one of the boulevards of the Confederation, and to render the garrison 
respectable; which milks me in the case of requiring then part of the contingents and writing for this 
purpose to your Majesty, who sent one of his regiments into that place. 

Shortly thereafter, a Brazilian envoy, transported on an English frigate, was received at St. 
Petersburg as minister of a friendly power, though, under the alliance of Tilsit, Russia must be in a state 
of war with the House of Braganza. I desired peace; I had an interest in preserving it, since a part of my 
troops was in Spain; but, when Russia supported the violation of the treaties by the apparatus of arms, I 
had to resort also to arms.'”° 


190 


Page 191 


This precaution is more than justified today by the extraordinary lifting of 4 men out of 500, which has 
just been ordered throughout the whole of the Russian empire, without Russia having explained itself on 
its protest or on its ukase without her troops having left the positions she had made them take in the 
vicinity of the duchy. 

I had to gather my armies, train them and restore my war material. These preparations used a 
year. Now, 300,000 men are going to cross Germany and go to the frontiers of the Confederation, not in 
hostile feelings, but for my armies to be as close to the Vistula as the Russian armies. 

When it is time for my minister to answer the protest against the Oldenburg, I will instruct: that 
the affairs of this country are really foreign to Russia; that the duke, who was required, during the last 
war, to furnish his contingent, had not done so; that, having not fulfilled the duties of a confederate, he 
had lost his rights; that, however, and for the sake of peace, I have offered him a suitable indemnity, and 
that I am still ready to give it to him. 

While adopting the principle, Russia did not say what she wanted, and I must have thought that it 
was her intention to ask Danzig and any part of the territory of the Confederation. If, indeed, she had not 
had to make proposals contrary to the treaty of Tilsit and to my principles, and that I could not hear dirty 
answer to them by the weapons, would she have armed, and since one year she would refuse to explain? 
I am far from having lost the hope of peace. But since it is admitted to me the fatal process of 
negotiating at the head of a powerful and numerous army, it is my honor to negotiate also at the head of 
a large and powerful army. I do not want to begin hostilities, but I want to put myself in a position to 
repulse them. I do not want to violate Russian territory, but I want to be ready to repent anyone who 
violates the territory of the Confederation. 

I desire, therefore, that your Majesty's contingent should meet and be ready to enter the 
campaign on February 15th. I ask her to get me the status of her contingent as general officers, staff 
officers, infantry, cavalry, artillery with caissons and crews, and as it is intended to organize. 

NAPOLEON 

According to the copy comm. by S. A. I. Prince Jerome.

18460. — NOTE 
DICTATED IN ADVICE OF FORTIFICATIONS. 
Tuileries Palace. January 28, 1812. 


About Fort Tromp (Goeree Island) vis-a-vis Hellevoetsluis. His Majesty says that Fort Tromp does not 
seem to him well determined to decide to build it in its present location. The idea of Fort Tromp was to 
make the existence of ships in Flakkee harbor depend on the capture of a fort which required eight days 
of open trench, and not a few easy batteries to take. 





1 The regiments of Saxony Ducale (4th Regiment), Anhalt and Lippe (Sth), Schrwarzburg, Wuldeck and 
Reuss (6th).!”” 


192 


Page 193 


This goal seems quite well filled by Fort Tromp, which is less than 900 fathoms from Pamplis. But it is 
necessary to make on the Meuse researches like those which His Majesty had done on the Texel; for 
that, one must know the probes of the Meuse, which the navy must have. This research will reveal 
whether it is possible to anchor outside the Meuse bar. At the next council, we will present to His 
Majesty the probes of the river, and we shall call Mr. Beautemps-Beaupré, hydrographic engineer. This 
is a very important maritime issue, because if the ships could anchor out of the pass, it would be 
convenient to place the strong Tromp in such a way as to protect this outer harbor. If, on the contrary, 
we can not draw any advantage from this outer harbor, we might then consider the batteries which are at 
the tip of the island to be useless, and concentrate the whole defense in Fort Tromp, except to have only 
12 batteries to protect cabotage. 

The Schouwen Island watershed should be placed on the Grevelingen Channel, which separates 
Goeree Island from Schouwen Island; for a reduction, whatever strength it may have, is susceptible only 
to a few days of defense; if one can not come to his aid, he can only capitulate, and it is a lost garrison. 
Instead of a rifle on the canal not allowing the enemy to block it, Tholen and Bers-op-Zoom would be 
flown in to help him; if he can defend himself for eight or ten days, he is almost certain to be rescued. 

Then there must be a fort at the tip of the island of Zierickee, to defend the passage of Keete, it is 
a question of another nature. 

On the island of Goeree, we made the reduction, not to defend the passage, but to preserve a 
point where we can not be blocked; that is what determined to make Fort Duquesne; it is large enough 
that, in one night, five or six thousand men may be thrown into it and clear the whole island. This is the 
same system that must be applied to Schouwen Island. The best way to fortify an island is to facilitate 
communication: that is how, for the island of Walcheren, we had the project of making a dike on the 
Sloe. What was not practicable for this island, is for the island of Schouwen, the canal having only 3 or 
400 toises. If we can have an arrow, a bridge that reaches Tholen, and, if that is not possible, that we 
have boats insured to carry a lot of people, we will have given the greatest possible strength to 
Schouwen Island. 

According to the copy. Archives of the Navy.!”°

18461. - TO MARSHAL DAVOUT, PRINCE OF ECKMUHL, 
COMMANDING THE Ist CORPS OF OBSERVATION OF THE ELBE, HAMBURG. 
Paris, January 28, 1812. 


Cousin, I look forward to your report on the colonial goods you have found in Pomerania. You 
have no doubt sent a detachment from your customs officers. 

I intend General Damas, who commands the troops of the Grand Duchy of Berg, to command a 
division, which will consist of eight battalions of Berg, four of Hesse-Darmstadt, which will make 
twelve battalions, of a cavalry regiment. Berg and a regiment of Hessian cavalry, and finally artillery 
troops belonging to these two contingents. Two battalions of the Grand Duchy of Berg are already at 
Stettin. I ordered that three battalions, forming 2,400 men, be ready to leave for Diisseldorf under the 
orders of a brigadier general. An equal amount of troops will be ready from Hesse-Darmstadt. You can 
therefore go directly to Diisseldorf to set Berg's Brigade in motion and direct it to Hamburg, where it 
will take up your troops as soon as you have to walk further. 

Since you are entering Pomerania, it is necessary that you seal all the passages between Sweden 
and the mainland hermetically, and that, without doing anything ostensible, you put a kind of embargo 
such that nothing can enter or leave, if it is not the couriers of cabinet that the government of Sweden 
would like to send to France; but no trunk of commerce should pass. You will also stop all 
correspondence with Sweden that one would like to pass through Denmark.

18463. - TO GENERAL CLARKE, DUKE OF FELTRE, 
MINISTER OF WAR, IN PARIS 
Paris. January 29, 1812. 


Duke de Feltre, I send you a report from my orderly officer Athalin on Delfzyl. I would like you 
to give me, on next Tuesday's council, what is relative to that place, the projects that have been done and 
the opinion of the committee. 

Delfzyl is considered the most beautiful harbor that exists from the Scheldt to Hamburg. It is 
destined to play, in the future, a very great role. The harbor seems to leave nothing to be desired; we 
must provide for the defense of the place. 

It seems necessary first to occupy in a solid way the island of Borkum, since one passes a 
thousand fathoms of this island, and to establish an important fort at the point of Bierum, in order to 
prevent the enemy to make a simple landing and remove the batteries. This fort would defend the bay at 
1,800 toises; Holwierde's strong-battery would defend the pass at 1,500 fathoms, and finally the walls of 
Delfzyl would complete the protection of the squadron, which can retire to Termunterzy] (1), that is to 
say more than 400 fathoms from Delfzyl, at the bottom of the harbor, and about equal distance from 
Delfzyl to the first fort, at the height of Bierum. 

There is no doubt that a military establishment becomes indispensable at Delfzyl, with a pool 
sheltered from the ice. Where should this establishment be done? is it in Delfzyl itself or in 
Termunterzyl? You will consult the Minister of the Navy on this last question, for it is especially under 
the maritime point of view that it must be considered. 

What are the walls and the current establishments of Delfzyl worth? What defense could they 
do? What part is there for the future and for the current year? Even if the navy corps and the engineers 
would be of opinion to make establishments at Termunterzyl, it would be a thing to do only in a few 
years and which one could not think of for this year. It is therefore necessary to have at the point of 
Bierum a strong battery of eight pieces of 36 or 24 and four mortars, and such a battery at Howierde. It 
is also necessary to shelter Delfzyl's place with a hand, so that my fleets are protected and this place can 
defend itself. There is no doubt that, if the enemy wanted to operate on the coasts, he would seize, in 
preference to everything, 





1) Today Termunten,'” 





Page 196 


Delfzyl, which would make him a place of deposit and the most beautiful harbor of all these places. 

I also want you to give me, on Tuesday, what is relative to the Place de Groningen, the other 
forts of the Ems and the places of the Yssel. Would it be advisable to keep these places or to withdraw 
the artillery, as has been done at Breda, and to drive this artillery to Wesel? 

NAPOLEON. 

According to the copy. Deposit of the war. 


18464. - TO THE GENERAL LACUEE, COUNT DE CESSAC,

Count de Cessac, I receive your letter of January 28th. Could we reduce the weight of the 
wagons being built in Antwerp, Sampigny and Italy, from the model of last July, and can withstand a 
weight reduction according to your report, that is to say that weighing 1,200 kilograms they weighed 
only 983 kilograms; what would make a reduction of 217 kilograms or 434 pounds? Order that this 
operation be done on all the cars to which it is rotted to apply it. Send instructions to the Navy, 
Sampigny, Plaisance, the Viceroy, and the artillery. Recommend that, for each service, you write on 
each wagons its weight, in order to easily distinguish between them. 

I see in your report that the wagons of the new model weigh 983 kilograms, and those of the old 
model 915; the difference is 68 kilograms: we can therefore consider these two models of caissons as the 
same weight. It would be very good if we could, from the three models of caissons, make one for the 
future. These wagons would have the benefit of having a lid, which I do. Looks like an important thing, 
to be as light as possible and to carry the same weight as the new model wagons; it would be that which 
one would build at Sampigny and at Plaisance. 

I think I have told you that it was useless to make Danzig the 160 new model wagons, and that 
the carts were to be built beforehand in the Comtoise.

18468. - NOTE FOR THE GENERAL MAJOR. 
Paris, January 30, 1812. 


The Emperor sends to the major general the states of the Grand Army handed over by the 
minister of war; His Majesty does not find them precise enough to give orders. That night he got up and 
wanted to work; which he could not do, having not found the necessary information. 

State No. 5 carries the 2nd Light Cavalry Division (7th and 8th Brigades), that is, the 11th 
chasseurs Regiment at Verdun on the 22nd, and the other regiments at Saint-Mihiel, Stenay and 
Schelestadt: what are these regiments doing in the past? of the 22nd? This assumes that I did not give 
any orders to the 2nd Light Cavalry Division, which I do not think is correct. I believe that I have 
ordered that this meet on Mainz; it is possible that, given the proximity, I did not give order; but I think I 
gave general orders to the Minister of War. 

In State No. 3, I see, at the artillery, the battalion of the train destined for the 10th division still in 
Besancon: did not I give him an order? The 10th division must however be reunited on February 15th at 
Mainz; she will not have any artillery? I may not have ordered the minister in detail, but it had to work 
together. 


The artillery park of the ocean observation corps has no'”® 


Page 199 


order? There are companies at Strasburg, at the camp at Boulogne; All this must be given orders. 

The pontooners who are in Bonn, Wesel, also seem to have no orders. 

The major-general will send to the office of the movement to take all these details, so that I shall 
have morning in the order followed for the armies of Spain. 

All that has no orders must receive it. 

It is possible that all this comes from the fact that the artillery, the engineers and the troops do 
not depend on the same office. 

I believe that the troops are badly directed: when I see that, from the Hague and Utrecht, they are 
made to pass Bois-le-Duc, there can be only one mistake; if there is time yet, change their course. It was 
more natural to take the Rhine over Wesel and Diisseldorf, which would have shortened considerably. 

Finally, I want to see, on the chart handed to me by the Major General, all the corps that make up 
the Grand Army, their march day by day, to their destination, and, in observation and also by a particular 
state, which are corps or fragments of corps, either of infantry, cavalry, artillery, crews of the train, 
crews of the military transports, which have no order to join the division to the destination of meeting 
prescribed by my orders.

Monsieur le Comte de la Riboisiere, I send you a letter from the Prince d'Eckmihl; I am 
attaching a report made to it by the Major General. It is necessary that you become aware of all this, so 
that you now order it as commander-in-chief of the artillery of the army. 

I notice first that, if the cars of the 6th Division arrive at Miinster hitched, that is good; but, if 
they can not reach it, this movement is impracticable; for before the 20th of February, the 6th, 8th, and 
9th Divisions will make a movement. It is therefore necessary that their artillery be hitched up. 

It is necessary that on the Ist of March the headquarters crew of Magdeburg, which might be 
destined against Spandau or Kolberg, be in good condition; that at the same time the siege crew of 
Danzig, which might be destined against Graudenz, be in good condition; that in the supposition that I 
am dealing with Prussia. I do not need to inform you that the War Ministry must ignore these 
provisions; the major-general is not instructed; you alone are in secret. Thinking it useless to say 
anything of that to the engineers or the artillery, you must get the state of the Magdeburg and Danzig 
siege parks to see if they can fulfill my purpose. You will report this to me confidentially. I recommend 
that this letter be read by no one, and that the names Spandau, Kolberg and Graudenz do not come out of 
your hands, because in this”

18485. -NOTE 
FOR MINISTERS OF INTERIOR AND TRADE 
Paris February 8, 1812, 


We are in a vicious circle, we must leave. I have prescribed that it should be distributed by the 
Paris charity committees 30,000 pounds of bread and 30,000 economic soups, which will disinterested 
the poor; if this help is not enough, I will increase it. I ordered distributions to Versailles, Saint-Cloud, 
Saint-Germain, Compiegne, Rambouillet, and Fontainebleau, to the title of principal owner of these 
cantons. Having thus disinterested the most needy mass, my intention would be to bring Tuesday the 
bread to 18 cents and the flour of the reserve to 85 francs, to prohibit any purchase of flour above 85 
francs, so that the reserve would offer flour only 85 francs to the flourers. The flourers need to sell; we 
are not in a hurry, since a large quantity of wheat is coming. I am waiting for the minutes of the last 
meeting of the council of the living to know where our purchases are. These three steps in front of one 
another seem useful, always maintaining that the reserve does not make any credit. 

NAPOLEON.

18186. - AT THE VICE-AMIRAL COUNTY DECRES, 
MINISTER OF THE NAVY, IN PARIS. 
Paris, February 8, 1812. 


Count Decres, I have read with attention your report of January 29th on the Boulogne and 
Schelde fleets. My intention is to raise in the course of March the 9,000 men of the conscription of 
1813. [have granted you the 1,400 sailors of 1810 of Holland; I suppose you made me raise the 1,500

registration; so there will be nothing disturbed by my decree of November 14, and everything will be 
organized according to its form and content. 

Let me know if you have made me sign the appointments of staffs and crews. 

We must not have regard to the claim of Vice Admiral Emeriau, but always increase the number 
of crews. 

I really want the 69 gunboats to exist in the Scheldt. I wish that there should also be forty-six 
barges, so that each vessel had, to fight against the English, three gunboats, two barges, which would be 
supported by four good frigates, four corvettes and two brigs. If the two frigates of Saint-Malo could go 
there, we would have six frigates, which I would consider very advantageous. 

You must put before me the precautions taken last year for the defense of the islands of 
Walcheren, Goeree, and Schouwen. The same measures must be taken for this year. It is my intention 
that twenty-three gunboats, commanded by a captain and placed under the command of the commander 
of the island of Walcheren, be intended for the defense of Vlissingen and to hold a line of embossing in 
front of this port. I also attach importance to having the Texel, if not the hundred twenty gunboats, at 
least eighty gunboats and forty cannoneers or big barges, in order to be able to fight with advantage 
against the fleets that the enemy could send to attack the various passes of the Zuiderzee. Even if the 
crews of the fleet could not serve all these gunboats, if they were in good condition at Nieuwe-Diep, the 
admiral, according to the circumstances, would decide to disarm some frigates and reinforce the fleets. 
You know how useful it will be in the Zuiderzee this flotilla always maneuvering, exercising the crews 
and defending passes. 

As for Boulogne, it is my intention that the 17th Battalion continue to remain there; but that the 
12th and 14th leave it without delay under Rear Admiral Baste. They will mount forty gunboats, twenty- 
three barges of new model, nine prames and four bombards. You will organize the divisions as you will 
hear, to facilitate the passage. They will go to Cherbourg. In Cherbourg I shall have twelve prames, sixty 
gunboats, and fifty barges. I see in this movement several advantages. In the port of Cherbourg, these 
buildings will be able to exercise better; they can go out every day; I will have 480 sailors”’°

must go there from Le Havre on the five ships leaving for this port, 2,000 seamen who are now 
embarked in the port of Cherbourg, and finally those of the 12th and 14th crew: I will thus have nearly 
5,000 sailors in Cherbourg. Rear Admiral Troude would command all the harbor. Rear-Admiral Baste, 
under his command, would command the flotilla. It would remain in Boulogne the 17th crew, which 
would have five prames, twenty-seven gunboats and one hundred and thirty-two boats gunners, 
including the gunners of Dunkirk. 

In this way I will have assembled defense fleets in the three most vulnerable points, Holland, 
Scheldt and Cherbourg, and, in case of events, this large quantity of small boats will be able to offer for 
the defense, especially for that of Cherbourg, either a flotilla or soldiers. 

It will be convenient, on this occasion, to diminish the administration of Boulogne as you 
propose, to order, however, that the embossing line often goes out to remove the bombardment, and 
finally to remove from this city, by directing it on Calais and Saint-Omer, all that is useless in its 
defense, so that, Boulogne falling into the power of the enemy, I experience the least possible loss. 

You can use transport or service vessels for the service of the Scheldt or the transport of timber, 
according to the needs of your department. It will be enough for me to have at Boulogne thirty 
buildings, prames or gunboats, one hundred and fifty gunboats and a hundred barges. By bringing 
together two or three hundred fishing boats, when we want to make this flotilla play the game it must 
play in a general operation, we will always have the means to land 30 to 40,000 men and a few horses 
on a single point. Besides, the flotilla of Cherbourg can easily refer to Boulogne, or from Cherbourg, if 
there were a camp there, to operate under the protection of the squadron which would dominate the 
Channel. I therefore consider it advantageous from every point of view to have a hundred flotilla ships 
in Cherbourg. 

Present me a draft letter to write to Rear-Admiral Basie for these arrangements, a draft letter to 
the Vice-admirals, Missiessy and Dewinler for organizing the Scheldt and Zuiderzee defense, and finally 
a read to Vice Admiral Ver Huell to provide for all the cases of the North defense. 

In case of war, my intention is that my gunboats and my fleets find refuge in the Elbe under the 
batteries of Cuxhaven, and in the Ems under the place of Delfzyl; which would lead me to think that it 
would be necessary to have in Delfzyl a marine commissioner”!

18488.- TO PRINCE OF NEUCHATEL AND WAGRAM, 
MAJOR GENERAL OF THE GREAT ARMY, IN PARIS. 
Paris. February 8, 1812, 


My cousin, order the viceroy to send the Italian guard from Milan to Brescia, where it is 
necessary that it be returned to you as soon as possible. Order the Viceroy to send all his army corps to 
Ralisbonne from the 16th to the 20th. For this purpose, the 1st Division, with its artillery and a cavalry 
brigade to which it will keep the head, will leave from the 16th to the 20th, in two columns, the artillery 
divided between the two columns and with provisions for four days; the 2nd division, with its artillery 
and cavalry, will leave Trent on two columns. At the same time the Italian division will leave in two 
columns and the royal guard in one column. The rest of the cavalry will leave in two columns. The park 
will be well escorted. The movement must be as fast as possible; it is therefore necessary that what is at 
Bassano, Castelfranco, & c. concentrates. The observation corps of Italy will start with four days of 
food. 

You will inform the King of Bavaria, when addressing your letter to my minister at Munich, that 
the army of Italy, 80,000 strong,” 


212 


Page 213 


will cross the Tyrol in nine columns; that it starts from the 16th to the 20th of February; that it is 
necessary that he give his orders to have Mount Brenner clean up the snow and to supply the troops with 
what is necessary; that it is important to keep the secret as long as possible, so that the troops have time 
to reach the Vistula before the Russians know anything about it, and can come and ravage the Grand 
Duchy of Warsaw, as the Austrians have done made in Bavaria in the previous war. 

You will write to the Viceroy that you have warned the King of Bavaria; that the snows of the 
Brenner do not mean anything; that he must send many sappers, and, with money, reunite the 
mountaineers to clean this pass, and that we must collect as much snow as we can to relieve the horses 
on the way. 

The viceroy will send his horses and his crew, but he will not move from Milan. He can send 
General d'Anthouard as the most interested, and make him understand that I do not hear that the snows 
of the Brenner are twelve hours late. Reiterate that his movement must be as fast as possible; that it is 
better for him to delay it by one day, but that, once unmasked, he must descend like a torrent towards the 
Danube.

18496. - TO MARSHAL MARCONT, DUKE OF RAGUSA, 
COMMANDING THE ARMY OF PORTUGAL (1). 
Paris. February 11, 1812. 


The Emperor regrets, Monsieur le Duke, that with the Souham division and the three other 
divisions you had assembled you did not return to Salamanca to see what was happening. This would 
have given a lot to think of the English and could have been useful in Ciudad-Rodrigo. 

The way to rescue the army of the South in the position you are in, is to place your headquarters 
in Salamanca, to concentrate your army by detaching only a division on the Tagus, to reoccupy Asturias 
and to compel the enemy to remain at Almeida and in the north, by the fear of an invasion. You can 
even push posts, march on Ciudad Rodrigo, if you have the necessary artillery of siege, and, your honor 
is attached to it, to take this place, or, if the want of food or artillery forces you to postpone this 
operation until the harvest, you could at least make an incursion into Portugal and bring you to the 
Douro and Almeida. That threat would contain the enemy. 

The army of the South is very strong. The Valencia army, which today has its outposts on 
Alicante, clears its right. 

The position you must take must therefore be offensive, from Salamanca to Almeida. As long as 
the English will gather you in force in Salamanca, they will make no movement. But if you go from 
your person to Valladolid, if your troops are sent to get lost on the rear, if especially your cavalry is not 
able after the rainy season, you will expose all the north of Spain to disasters. 

It is essential to reoccupy Asturias, because it takes more people to keep the edge of the plain to 
Biscay than to keep Asturias. 

Since the English divided into two corps, one on the south 





1) This letter, sent in figures and signed by the Major General, was dictated by the Emperor; the minute is, in several places, 
corrected by the hand of Napoleon.”” 





220 


Page: 121 


and the other on you, they are not strong, and you must be much stronger than them. The letter I wrote 
you, and which you received on the 13th of December, made you know what you should do: threaten the 
English, and if you think that for the moment you can not take back Ciudad-Rodrigo, have them 
repaired. paths leading to Almeida, have Salamanca strengthened, gather your siege crews, send large 
detachments to Ciudad - Rodrigo; that will contain the English, will not tire your troops, and will have 
much less inconvenience than to disseminate you as you propose. 

I suppose Montbrun has arrived and you have finally assembled your army. 

The capture of Valencia has greatly strengthened the army of the South, and you must assume 
the English crazy to believe they can walk on Badajoz leaving you in Salamanca, that is to say by letting 
you arrive in Lisbon before them. They will go to the south if, by badly calculated measures, you detach 
two or three divisions on the Tagus, because, by this, you reassure them and tell them that you do not 
want to do anything against them. 

I repeat it to you, the intention of the Emperor is that you do not leave Salamanca, that you make 
reoccupy Asturias, that even army relies on the position of Salamanca and that you threaten the English 
there. 

By order of the Emperor, 

Major General ALEXANDRE, Prince of Neuchatel and Wagram,

18408. - NOTE DICTED IN THE COUNCIL OF MINISTERS. 
Palace of Tuileries, February 12, 1812. 


It is necessary that the great judge send letters patent to allow these six people to remain in the 
service of the king of Westphalia, but not to allow them to be naturalized Westphalians. He will write to 
the Minister of Justice of the Kingdom of Westphalia a letter by which, by sending him these six letters 
patent, he will inform him that the Emperor refuses to grant any letters of naturalization in Westphalia, 
as in Spain, at Naples, and in Italy, since the sovereigns of these countries themselves have not ceased to 
be French, which results from the right they have retained in the throne, from the dignity with which 
they are clothed in the Empire, and from the regulations which that they are treated in this quality as 
French; that being so, these sovereigns do not need the French they employ to cease to be French, since 
on the contrary they find in this very quality a guarantee of their fidelity; it is sufficient that they have 
the authorization to pass to their service, that consequently His Majesty has sent the six letters patent in 
the form prescribed by the decree of August 26, 1811. 

The great judge will also submit to the Emperor letters patent for some of the French employed 
in Madrid and Naples, in order to fix the principles. 

He will write to the Minister of Foreign Relations to inform him of these principles, so that he 
may write to the Emperor's ministers at the different powers. 

As to the princes of the Rhine Confederation, Russia, Prussia, and Denmark, questions of this 
nature can be answered only individually. 

In general, His Majesty will grant letters of naturalization only in cases where there is no interest 
for France to do otherwise. For example, a Frenchman is established as a merchant in Odessa; he finds 
great advantages therein, and these advantages can be preserved only by naturalization: there is no 
inconvenience” 





222 


Page 223 


to allow it to be naturalized. An individual, driven by events in a court, has obtained a great charge, 
which he would lose if he were not naturalized: he may, by exception, be allowed to do so, because 
France has no interest in what we defend him. 

But all the Frenchmen who, by the services which they render to a foreign prince, can make the 
law to these princes, like myself, for example, a minister, a general difficult to replace, do not need that 
His Majesty allow the naturalization, since the prince needs them: it is enough to allow them to remain 
in his service. 

The foreign princes who are French have more need of their French servants than these 
Frenchmen need to remain in their service. Moreover, if the sovereign demanded that they make 
themselves natural foreigners, this requirement would be ridiculous, since it is precisely by their quality 
of French that they have one more title to his confidence; so that, if they took away the heart of the 
French, by depriving them of their quality, they would diminish the advantage the prince can derive 
from it. 

It is not the same with a Frenchman brought by circumstances to the court of a non-French 
foreign prince, who is clad in court. 

It will be necessary for the Minister of Foreign Affairs to develop all these considerations, by 
writing to the Ministers in the Courts of Naples, Madrid, and Westphalia, in order to make the question 
clear, because the difficulties in this respect arise only from the fact that the question is not clear; which 
is the result of the lack of analysis.

18501. - TO GENERAL CLARKE, DUKE OF FELTRE, 
MINISTER OF WAR, IN PARIS. 
Paris. February 18, 1812. 


Duke de Feltre, I have issued a decree for the arming of the Mecklenburg coast, the 32nd 
military division, the 31st and the 17th; send it to the commanders of the engineers and artillery without 
delay. 

It is necessary that the generals actively monitor the work and report on their progress. 

I keep only six batteries in the 32nd Military Division. There must be three coastguard 
companies; it is necessary to add two companies of creeper artillery, placing them essentially at the 
mouth of the Elbe, and sending detachments to the different batteries; 6 to 700 infantrymen seem to me 
sufficient for the batteries. The commanding generals will visit them every week; the general of the 
division will visit from March 15th to April Ist and will make sure everything is in order. 

The General of the 32nd Military Division will have three reserves: the first in range of the Elbe, 
the other of the Weser, the last of the Jahde. Assuming each of these reserves of 5 to 600 men with a 
hundred horses and two pieces harnessed, it would follow that with 2,000 men the ribs would be 
guarded; and as it is my intention to employ 8,000 men in the defense of the 32nd Division, there will 
remain 6,000 men and twelve pieces to contain Hamburg, and to carry where necessary. The Danes can 
also, in case of event, provide 8 to 10 thousand men. The general commanding the 31st division will 
have 500 men on the islands and 100 men on the battery of the Jahde; he will have 500 men on the 
coasts of his department: 1,000 men are therefore of an absolute necessity, with 1,000 men in 
Groningen, to reinforce Delfzyl and to carry wherever it is necessary.”

I have destined 3,000 men for the 31st military division. I also ordered the formation of three 
cohorts of 500 men. There are also three coastguard companies. A line company is essential for Delfzyl.

reserve of 2,000 men and a brigadier general. He will hold the campaign with the rest to join the

Delfzyl and Coeverden are the only two strongholds in this division; each brigadier general must

The general commander of the Ist military division has a much more important task to fulfill.

COMMANDER SQUARDON OF ESCAUT, ANTWERP. 
Paris, February 18, 1812. 


Mr. Vice-Admiral Count Missiessy, we inform you that it is our intention that our squadron 
under your command will press its rearmament with all diligence, and that it will descend the Scheldt on 
the 1st of March next, so as to give the anxiety to our enemies by its presence at the mouth of the river, 
where it will have to be wet and able to sail by the 10th of March at the latest; a disposition which, 
independently of the other results we propose, will force the enemy to bear the gale of the equinox at 
sea. 

We particularly recommend that you print the greatest activity to the vessels under your 
command, and carry their reconnaissance out of the passes, so that they become familiar to the 
Commodores, captains and officers. 

We want the exit of our squadron to cease to depend exclusively on the employment of the river 
pilots, hearing that several officers of each vessel, and in particular our captains, acquire in this 
campaign the necessary knowledge to replace these pilots when necessary and to bring out our ships by 
themselves, with the proper precautions. 

Our letters patent of August 9, 1810, and the instructions, orders, and decrees which our Minister 
of the Navy has sent to you in the course of last year, have made known to us our intentions as to the 
measures you have to take in order to defense of the islands and the mouths of the rivers included in the 
extent of your command; but we find it useful to trace you : 





Page 236 


in this letter the various provisions which we have definitively decided upon these important objects. 

The meeting of our squadron of the Meuse in the Western Scheldt naturally determines us to 
assemble under your command all the part of the coasts whose defense was assigned to this squadron. 

As aresult, your authority with respect to maritime operations will extend from Brielle in the 
north to, and south of, the left bank of the Ecluse Canal. 

For this purpose, we order that it be assigned to our fleet of the Scheldt ninety-two gunboats or 
barges or boats gunners, which will be armed by detachments of the twenty-three crews of high-edge 
under your orders, which consequently, will be successively raised to a manpower of 600 men by the 
incorporation in these crews of the 13th of flotilla and the men we would have destined to form new 
ones. 

We have been disposed to this incorporation by this consideration that the sailors of these, being 
continually scattered on scattered buildings, are too deprived of the care and supervision of their 
superior chiefs, a disadvantage which will cease to exist to the same degree of the moment that 
belonging to a crew of high board they will not be more, as they will not be it indeed, only temporarily 
detached on gunboats, to be recalled to the corps at definite times, and whenever the interest of 
administration and discipline will demand it. 

Each crew under your command will have to arm three gunboats. 

The ninety-two gunboats or gunboats or barges, thus armed, will form three divisions, each 
vessel to supply a rowboat to each division. 

The Ist division will take the name of fleet division of the Scheldt; the second, that of division of 
the Meuse; the 3rd, the Wing Division. 


OF THE DIVISION OF THE ESCUT AND DEFENSE OF THE ISLANDS OF WALCHEREN AND 
SCHOUWEN. 


The Scheldt Flotilla Division will be responsible for the service of the passes of the two Scheldt, 
that of the islands of Walcheren, Cadzand and part of Schouwen. 

It will be commanded by a captain appointed by our Minister of the Navy. 

It will be divided between the Western Scheldt and the Eastern Scheldt.”°° 





236 


Page 237 


Six of the gunners of this division will be particularly placed under the command of the general 
of division commanding at Walcheren, to be employed by him to light the coast as he wishes, and to 
advance upon the points which the enemy would threaten. These six gunboats will provide this general 
officer with his private and independent means of communicating with the island of Cadzand and the 
island of Schouwen. 

The seventeen other gunners of this division will be under your command when you are at the 
mouth of the river; but, when you ascend east of Borssele, the whole division, as well as the brigs and 
corvettes, must be left near Walcheren, and remain there for as long as time permits, to enter the ports of 
Walcheren, and especially in that of Flushing, in case of need, this division being specially assigned to 
the defense of this place, and not having, whatever event may happen, having any other fate than that of 
the place itself. 

You will give instructions accordingly to the captain commanding this division (1). He will be 
put by our naval minister to the command of the commander of the island of Cadzand a naval officer 
with two cannoneers, three Caiques and three barges. 

There will be a corvette stationed between the mouth of the Eastern Scheldt and Zierikzee, and, 
in addition, six gunboats and six barges armed, but not equipped, at the disposal of the commander of 
this corvette, to be by him employed in as required by the circumstances. 

The commander of this corvette will make sure of all the means of transport which exist at 
Zierikzee, Nord-Beveland and all the coast, to be able quickly to reunite in the canal the number of boats 
necessary to go to the aid of Schouwen and Walcheren, if these islands were attacked. 

The commander of this corvette will send every day a report to the commanding general at 
Schouwen, and will assist the garrison with all his means. He will also send you frequent reports, being 
under your orders for the maritime operations, 

If the island of Schouwen was attacked, Tholen would have to go to his aid, and in this case the 
whole fleet of the two Scheldt

DIVISION OF THE MEUSE AND THE DEFENSE OF THE SCHOUWEN AND GOEREE 
ISLANDS. 


The division of the Meuse will be charged with a part of the service of Schouwen and that of 
Goeree. 

It will be commanded by a Captain, appointed by our Minister of the Navy. 

You will divide it between Brouwershaven-Gat and the mouth of Haring- Vliet, so that one part is 
still between Schouwen and Goeree, and the other north of Goeree. 

This division will be under the command of the commanding general at Goeree, with regard to 
the particular service of this island, and under yours for the general movements. 

The superior naval officer who will command it will correspond daily with the commander of 
Goeree, and for this purpose, a gunboat will always be within reach to receive his orders. 

The military commander at Hellevoetsluis will also be expected to correspond with him and have 
at his disposal the means necessary to send to Goeree all the help that this island needs. 

A strong corvette will be stationed between Willemstad and Fort Duquesne, so as to protect the 
passage on the island of Goeree; this building, in case of attack, would be protected by the two batteries 
of forts Ruyter and Duquesne. It will serve as a cut in case of need to the Goeree garrison until Fort 
Duquesne is established. 

This vessel shall have under its command four gunboats and three boats for the service of the 
garrison of Goeree, and for the details of this service it shall be under the command of the general 
commanding the island, but under the command of the commander of the fleet of the Scheldt for general 
service. 

The officer commanding this corvette will also command the port and navy of Willemstad. 

It will be ensured in advance of all the means of transport that can offer the boats of the country 
to be able to carry as quickly as possible from Willemstad to Goeree. 

If the enemy threatens the island of Goeree, the military leader of Hellevoetsluis will take his 
measures to make it pass without delay all?*® 


238 


Page 239 


the troops that the commanding general at Rotterdam could send, as the commander of the corvette of 
Willemstad will pass all the troops of the 24th and 25th military division at Fort Duquesne at 
Ooltgensplaat. The commander of the flotilla will have to maneuver to facilitate these movements, and, 
if the enemy seized the island, to receive on board the whole garrison. 

In Willemstad there must be six gunboats and six barges, ready to be armed when needed by the 
country's sailors and the crew of the corvette, to be carried wherever necessary. 

If the island of Schouwen were threatened, the flotilla of the Meuse would be carried on this 
island, as that of the Scheldt would be on Goeree, if this one was threatened. 

If Hellevoetsluis was threatened, the flotilla of the Meuse must go to this place, shut up and 
follow his fate. 


OF THE DIVISION FLOTILLA OF THE WING, 


The fleet division of the squadron will be composed as the first, plus twenty-three barges; its 
destination is to exercise the seamen whenever the vessels and frigates are prevented from sailing; and in 
this case, it is advisable to keep them under sail whenever possible, especially with fresh winds and 
rough seas, in order to seize every opportunity to get young sailors accustomed to the movement of the 
sea and the exercise of maneuvers, 

These twenty-three gunboats and twenty-three barges will be a flotilla reserve at your disposal, 
to be employed, as circumstances warrant, wherever his presence may be useful, and to designate one or 
more senior officers of the squadron to command it, whenever it has to execute movements of 
instruction, attack or defense, 

You will use the barges to keep those of the enemy away from the coasts of Cedzand and 
Walcheren. 

Irrespective of the accounts to be given to you by the commanders of the two first divisions and 
those of the stations of Willemstad and Zierikzee, each of them will have to send directly to our Minister 
of Marine a weekly report on all matters of interest to the service. 

We reiterate to you, Vice-Admiral, the order to see that all the vessels of this flotilla are 


continually sailed, so that the crews may acquire all the instruction which this kind of navigation.”*” 





Page 240 


You will kindly give each of the Flotilla and Stationary Commanders all the detailed instructions 
which must follow from this, and you shall send a copy to our Minister of the Navy for presentation. 

We have not hereby intended to prescribe all the provisions which you will have to make for the 
defense of the coasts under your command, since they must depend on circumstances which can not be 
foreseen; but we expect that, some events which may occur, you will be able to employ the forces which 
will be entrusted to you in the manner most in accordance with the interest of our service and the honor 
of our arms.

18505, - TO M. MARET, DUKE OF BASSANO, 
MINISTER OF EXTERNAL RELATIONS, PARIS. 
Paris, February 19, 1812, 


The Duke of Bassano, you will receive a decree by which I order the demolition of houses and 
other buildings that hinder the fortifications of Magdeburg, You will send this decree to the King of 
Westphalia. It is necessary that the execution is prompt, because that the security of the place is 
compromised. It is necessary that the inhabitants have dislodged and that the roofs are discovered in the 
beginning of March, and that one destroys all these houses at the same time. The King will cede, as 
compensation to the owners, estates situated in the province of Magdeburg; I inserted this obligation in 
my decree. 

NAPOLEON. 

From the original. Foreign Affairs Archives.

Count Mollien, I authorize you to negotiate your shares of the Canal du Midi at the rate of 
12,000 francs per share. At this rate, sell as many as there are buyers. Make exactly the payments to the 
treasure of the Crown, so that it does not form an embarrassment. Also set the price that can be made to 
give shares of the Loing Canal.

18507. - TO MARSHAL BESSIERE, DUKE OF ISTRIA, 
COMMANDING THE IMPERIAL GUARD, IN PARIS. 
Paris. February 19, 1812. 


Cousin, you have not answered my fourth question: What is an ambulance division of the Guard? 
You tell me that it is composed of what is necessary for a division of 10,000 men; this is not enough; 
give me the details. 

For the 7th battalion of the crew train, is the clothing of the conscripts ready, so that the 
conscripts can have their clothes and their masses of linen and shoes forty-eight hours after their arrival? 

Do the 500 conscripts of the Guard's military crews have their clothes, and forty-eight hours after 
their arrival can they be provided? 

It appears that the 7th Battalion must receive 240 wagons. Write to the Minister of 
Administration to find out where these wagons are to be taken; it is necessary that they be returned to 
Metz or Mainz on | March, 

I refer you the answer of the authorizing officer, so that you put in the margins what exists and 
what must be the complete in men, in horses, in harnesses and in wagons of any kind.

18508, - TO MARSHAL BESSIERES, DUKE OF ISTRIA,

My Cousin, let the 3rd grenadier regiment march from my Guard, tomorrow, the 20th, for Metz, 
without passing it through Paris. This regiment will take with it its artillery and caissons. 

Order the Polish light horse to go to Compiegne tomorrow 20. You will send them to Compiegne 
the order to go to Mainz by the shortest route, without however passing through Metz, this road being 
sufficiently congested. Keep the secret so that the Poles do not know where they are going. I do not need 
to say that they will take with them their forges, caissons and everything that belongs to them.

battalions of the Daendels division, who will not come to Stettin until the moment to go forward 
will have arrived. 

The 85th, which is at Glogau, will be ready to go to Posen as soon as the Dessaix division

18512. - TO PRINCE OF NEUCHATEL AND WAGRAM, 
MAJOR GENERAL OF THE GREAT ARMY, IN PARIS. 
Paris, February 21, 1812, 


The Major General will write to the Duke of Ragusa that he misunderstood my intentions 
on Valencia; that I ordered to make march on that place 12,000 men, including the troops of the 
army of the Center; that I heard that this movement would be made by Cuenca; that there were 
already at Cuenca 4,000 men; that the King would give 3,000 others, and that it was, therefore, 3 
or 4,000 men of the army of Portugal to be sent to Cuenca; that his complaints are unfounded; 
that it would have been foolish for the King to go from Cuenca to Albacete; that this move would 
have allowed him the enemy, who was a 





244 


Page 245 


Requefia, to march on Madrid; that it was evident that this operation of Albacete could not be 
done without immense forces, since it required a great line of operation, and that it would not 
have given any result for the capture of Valencia; for if Marshal Suchet had been beaten at the 
passage of the lines, this operation meant nothing; that the art of war does not consist in dividing 
one's troops; that the operation of Cuenca by Requefia, communicating by the left with Marshal 
Suchet before attacking the enemy, was a real military operation; that 3,000 more men with 
General Darmagnac would not have weakened the army of Portugal; that the English would not 
have noticed it; that this operation could even have been accomplished by sending troops from 
the Central Army and replacing by troops of the Army of Portugal the troops which would have 
gone to Cuenca; that, doubtless, the road to Cuenca is not good for the artillery, but that there 
was no need for artillery against the insurgents, and that Marshal Suchet had some; that it is a 
fault of the Duke of Ragusa which is not justifiable, since he was before the enemy, and it is 
evident that he exposed all the north of Spain; that, had it been necessary to make a great army 
operation, it would have been preferable to have it done by the Duke of Dalmatia, and it would 
have been foreseen that the English might have marched on Madrid or Salamanca. 

According to the minute. Deposit of the war. 


18513. - TO THE PRINCE OF NEUCHATEL AND WAGRAM, 
MAJOR GENERAL OF THE GREAT ARMY, IN PARIS. 
Paris, February 21, 1812. 


The Major General will write to the Duke of Ragusa that I have read his letters of the 6th 
of February; that I am extremely sorry that he sent Bonet's division to the army of the North; that 
this division is the only one which can occupy with advantage Asturias, because the soldier 
knows Spain and the inhabitants; that it was better not to send anything to the army of the North, 
and to send Bonet's division to Asturias; that it is my intention that, wherever she may be, she 
return to that province; that for the North it is better to have Bonet's division in Asturias than in 
Burgos; that the army of Portugal is in the air; and that communication with Irun is not tenable, if 
one does not have Asturias; that Asturias must be occupied when we are at the height of 
Salamanca, and occupy the line of Potes and? 





245 


Page 246 


Reynosa when one is at the height of Valladolid or Burnos; but that to leave the peasants masters 
of the mountains, communicating with the sea, is the greatest misfortune that can happen in 
Spain; that the population of Galicia will return to the provinces occupied by the army; that 
experience has proved this theory, that when the Duke of Istria evacuated Asturias, the whole 
country was in motion; that it takes 6,000 men to keep the mountains, that they are placed in 
Asturias or Santander. it is the same thing, with this difference that by placing them at Santander 
they do not cover the kingdom of Leon and do not occupy that province, which is the most 
important for the insurgents; that I place at his disposal the Bonet division for this purpose; let 
him direct it to Asturias by the way General Bonet will judge the best; that you have informed 
him that his Majesty does not approve the dissemination of his army; that she sees in her conduct 
only trial and error. How, in Valladolid, does he claim to be informed in time of what the enemy 
will do? This is not possible in any country and especially in an insurgent country. How will it 
prejudge what the enemy will do in Valladolid? That you can only repeat to him that his Majesty 
sees an honorable operation for his arms as to occupy Salamanca, to have light vanguards firing 
on the frontiers of Portugal and with Ciudad-Rodriao, to have his army centralized around him at 
four or five steps, that, until the Army of the Center was able to set up troops, at Almaraz, that 
the army of Portugal should occupy Salamanca and that the Operation of the Duke of Dalmatia 
on Merida and Badajoz has influence over the enemy and made himself felt, he can leave a light 
division, ready to join him on Tulavera, occupying Almaraz; that when he has occupied 
Salamanca, that his outposts will have taken this direction, and that this kind of military blister 
will have had an effect on the enemy, he may have the division which he has left on the Tagus, 
and that the Army of the Center will be able to give troops to guard the valley; that he deals too 
much with that which does not concern him, and not enough with that which regards him; that 
his mission was to defend Almeida and Ciudad-Rodrigo, and that he allowed these places to be 
taken; that he has the north to maintain and administer, and that he abandons Asturias, that is to 
say, the only means of governing and containing it; that he will embarrass himself if Lord 
Wellington sends one or two divisions on Badajoz, when Badajoz is a very strong place and that 
the Duke of Dalmatia has 80,000 men, when he can be rescued by Marshal Suchet, finally when, 
if Lord Wellington walked on Badajoz, he has a sure, prompt and**° 


246 


Page 247 


triumphant to remind him, to walk on Ciudad-Rodrigo and Almeida. 

That his army is composed of eight divisions; that a division must remain in Asturias; 
that he must count only to make her march on Galicia; that, even if after a battle with the English 
he should be defeated, he must not evacuate Asturias by this division, but make it pass by the 
mountains to his rights, that the shots will arrive in a few days at Mondragon, if we do not 
occupy the mountains; that the division of Asturias is a division which, in case of evacuation of 
Salamanca, from Valladolid, should follow the movement in the mountains, otherwise the 
position of Burgos would not be tenable, not even that of Vitoria; that besides, once more, he has 
to fight not only against the English army, but also against Galicia; that these 6,000 men, who 
would march forward through the outlets of Galicia, will contain this province; that it may be 
said that 6,000 men in Asturias amount to 18,000 more than at Astorga and on the coast; that the 
insurgents, without communication after the capture of Valencia, were in despair; that the arrival 
of the bands at Potes and Oviedo and the reestablishment of their communications with the sea 
has restored their courage; and all this by default of reflection and knowledge of localities. 

That in summary, from his eight divisions one must be in Asturias and not move; that the 
other seven must be gathered around Salamanca; which made him an army of 50,000 
Frenchmen, with an artillery of a hundred pieces of cannon, which in the studied soil, covered 
with arrowheads, having their provisions assured and their support at Salamanca, would not be 
conquered by 80,000 men. ; that, however, one must be careful not to make an entrenched camp 
at Salamanca; that the English would believe it on the defensive, and have no more fears, and 
that it is a stronghold which must be had in Salamanca. 

According to the minute. Deposit of the war. 


18514. - TO PRINCE OF NEUCHATEL AND WAGRAM, 
MAJOR GENERAL OF THE GREAT ARMY, IN PARIS. 
Paris, February 22, 1812. 


My cousin, order the Duke of Elchingen to carry his headquarters to Erfurt, from the 5th 
to the 10th of March. The 2nd Reserve Cavalry Corps, composed of General Wattier's Light 
Cavalry Division” 





247 


Page 248 


and the two cuirassier divisions of Generals Sebastiani and Defrance, will be under his 
command. 

The division of light cavalry commanded by General Wattier will set in motion, so as to 
cross the Rhine at Mainz on the 27th, and proceed to Weimar. This division will have its 
batteries of light artillery with it, and its movement will take place by brigade. The Sebastiani 
division will be able to cross the Rhine at Coblenz and head for Weimar. The Defrance division 
will be able to cross the Rhine in Diisseldorf and go to Paderborn and from there to Leipzig. All 
the artillery of these two divisions of cuirassiers which is at Wesel will leave it on the 28th with 
the park of the cavalry reserve, and will march on Paderborn, where it will meet at the division 
of cuirassiers of the general Defrance, and will march under its protection up to Leipzig. The 
infantry division at Mainz, with the Army Corps Park, will set out on the 28th and will move to 
Erfurt. The park will stay in Gotha. 

The infantry division at Dusseldorf and the Portuguese regiment at Coblenz, which will 
join the division at Dusseldorf, will proceed to Paderborn and thence to Leipzig. 

It is necessary that the Duke of Elchingen send the situation of each regiment and its 
artillery, military crews and all the artillery of the corps. You will make known to this marshal 
that his corps must pass the Elbe to Wittenberg. Recommend to him to march his troops gently, 
so as not to tire his horses.

18516. - TO PRINCE OF NEUCHATEL AND WAGRAM, 
MAJOR GENERAL OF THE GREAT ARMY, IN PARIS. 
Paris. February 22, 1812. 


Cousin, write to Prince Eckmiihl that he should not allow the two regiments in Pomerania 
to return to Sweden; that he must not allow Colonel Peyron to return to Sweden; that he must not 
receive the new governor who comes from Sweden; that the reason for this is very simple is that 
all communication with Sweden is forbidden; that any individual who comes from Sweden to 
Pomerania should be sent to his headquarters; that apart from the allied troops he must 
temporarily leave a French regiment in Pomerania; that the division which is in Pomerania must 
be the last to move, since it is nearest to Stettin; that even when she walks, he must always leave 
a brigade in Pomerania. You will instruct the Prince of Eckmiihl to reiterate the instruction not to 
suffer in Pomerania any communication whatsoever with Sweden. 

NAPOLEON. 

From the original. Deposit of the war.

Magdeburg. The Duke of Reggio will have in his hand the divisions Legrand and Verdiere, and a

18318. - TO THE GENERAL COUNT DE LA RIBOISIERE, 
COMMANDING THE ARTILLERY OF THE GREAT ARMY, IN PARIS. 
Paris, February 23, 1812. 


Count de la Riboisiére, commander of the artillery of the Grande Armée, I need to know 
if the artillery is ready to satisfy the different orders that I give to the corps d'armee. 

The Ist corps of the Elbe, with the Ist corps of the cavalry reserve, sets in motion at the 
end of the month to arrive in the early days of March on the Oder. Minden Park follows this 
movement and goes to Stettin. 

The 2nd corps, with the division of cuirassiers which belongs to the 3rd corps of the 
cavalry reserve, is also set in motion at the end of this month, and is proceeding to Magdeburg. 

The 3rd Corps or Observation Corps of the Ocean, commanded by the Duke of 
Elchingen, crosses the Rhine at the end of this month and heads for Leipzig and Erfurt. The 2nd 
corps of the cavalry reserve follows this movement. The park has to go to Gotha. 

The 4th corps opens with Innsbruck with the 8th corps of the cavalry reserve, and in the 
first days of March it will be on Regensburg. 

Ihave not yet given any orders to the Army General Park or to the deck crew. I wish to 
receive from the artillery a report which informs me if all the preparatory movements of the 
equipment, the personnel and the teams have been made so that everything is at his post and that 
the service can be done according to the rigor of the organization. 


250 


Page 251 


If there are some wagons to leave behind not hitched, I want to know what is the number, what 
kind of wagons and when they will be hitched to join. Is there a general park, or have we all 
confused with each corps? Is there a general park for the cavalry reserve, as has been the case in 
previous wars, or is there only one park attached to each corps of the cavalry reserve? Finally, 
when will the deck crew and teams be able to cross the Rhine? how many horses will there be? 
how many wagons? what will be loaded on these wagons? when will they be able to pass the 
Rhine? Is the equipment of the siege crews ready in Danzig and Magdeburg, as well as the staff? 
Where will they be on April 1? 

NAPOLEON. 

From the original comm. by the Count de la Riboisiére.

NAPOLEON. 


NOTE TO MY ORDER OFFICER HAUTPOUL. 

See you in Metz. You will visit the personnel, equipment and artillery teams that are to 
be attached to the Guard reserve. You will also visit the battalions of military crews who are in 
Metz. You will go to Sampigny. You will see this establishment in detail, and you will let me 
know how many trolleys there are; what are the cadres of battalions of military crews, and

situation of the General Park of the Army, either artillery or engineering, equipment, personnel 
and teams. As the Duke of Elchingen's corps is going to make a movement, see in what situation 
the various divisions of artillery leave, 

You will write to me every day, from Mainz, what will come to your knowledge about 
the strength of the troops, the way they are equipped, their health, theirs! armament, etc.

18524. - TO THE PRINCE OF NEUCHATEL AND WAGRAM, 
MAJOR GENERAL OF THE GREAT ARMY, IN PARIS. 
Paris, February 26, 1812. 


Cousin, I send you a letter from Prince Eckmiihl. Tell him that he seems to have heard 
that Stralsund has been found. There must be some; that we do research. If it were not there, it is 
indispensable that we send about twenty guns in iron, in order to arm especially the Stralsund 
coast, to ensure the communication with the island of Rugen, It is necessary to establish in this 
island, at the point where the canal is the narrowest, a recess which can give refuse to the 
garrison if the enemy landed, to return to Stralsund, or which allows him to receive help to 
tumble the enemy who would have landed. The prince”

Page 254 


from Eckmiihl will send six or eight cannoneers there; there must be some in Lubeck; if it is not 
at Liibeck, it may be passed through Denmark, or, better still, send sailors to Stralsund, and have

him to send an engineer officer with instructions to fulfill my intentions. We must work on this 
with a busy activity. Enemy boats or barges must never be placed between Stralsund and the

18525. - TO THE GENERAL COUNT DE LA RIBOISIERE, 
COMMANDING THE ARTILLERY OF THE GREAT ARMY, IN PARIS. 
Paris, February 26, 1812. 


General Comte la Riboisiére, I receive your report of the 24th. I approve that each of the 
three cavalry corps should have their park, and that, consequently, the thirty pieces of light 
artillery attached to each of these corps should have their own double supply, regardless of the 
general fleet. 

Make me make the state of the arms, either rifles, carbines, or pistols, necessary both to 
arm the cavalry (because the cavalry is armed with carabiners and rifles) than to be able to 
provide the infantry under unforeseen circumstances. 

I do not think it's fitting that the year's bodies have only one and a half supply. I think 
they should be left with their entire supply, since the bodies can operate at a distance from each 
other such that they can not be reached with the park. 

In winter or refreshment areas, horses, both Guard and Guard Reserve, and deck crews 
and siege crews, can be used for extraordinary movements. The reserve of the Guard will 
actually form the park. Thus the park would consist of only sixty spare fire hydrants, spare 


c : ‘ ‘ . 254 
carriages, a few park caissons and a good number of infantry caissons. As you will experience i 


254 


Page. 255 


several campaigns in the same country, I will wait for your report on this before making a final 
decision. 

I want the bridge crew to talk about Strasbourg or Mayence, hitching wagons or artillery 
carts, which can then be used by the siege crews. I would like these wagons to be loaded with 
pioneering tools and rifles; we have enough powder. I see that the deck crew has horses at 
Wesel, Mainz, Strasbourg; have the condition of the artillery carts which these horses can take in 
each of these places, and the quantity of tools, arms, rifles, carbines, swords, which may be 
loaded on them. I do not hear the deck crew providing anything to the field crew, because, once 
these horses have left with the field crew, I will have nothing, and I will find it without a deck 
crew. The pioneering tools to be left at Danzig, the horses of the deck crew will leave the cars for 
the siege crew there and serve the deck crew. So I do not see much inconvenience in having 
these horses hitched up trucks, carriages, and other carriages for siege crews, although I think 
these sails should be built in Gdansk. Do you agree with General Chasseloup? 

Ihave told you that the two heavy cavalry divisions which are at Bonn and Cologne are 
going to Leipzig and Weimar, so the artillery of these two divisions must be at the same time in 
these cities. It is necessary that the park of the Ist corps of cavalry is with this corps with the 
corps of observation of the Elbe, and that the park of the 2nd corps goes to Weimar, where will 
be united the 2nd corps of cavalry. 

Give me statements of the artillery personnel, appointing the colonels, majors and 
battalion commanders, so that I know the officers who will be present on the first walls and those 
who will join only in the course of March. 

NAPOLEON 

From the original comm. by the Count de la Riboisiére,

18527. - TO GENERAL LACUEE, COUNT DE CESSAC, 
MINISTER DIRECTOR OF THE ADMINISTRATION OF THE WAR, IN PARIS. 
Paris, February 27, 1812. 


Comte de Cessac, I am responding to your report of 22 February on the returns. I see that 
you propose a new distribution for the returns to be made in Germany. It seems to me that there 
would be some inconvenience in making new arrangements before being sure that the first ones 
are executed. In Germany I asked for 8,300 horses, namely 1,300 riflemen and cuirassiers, 640 
dragons, 2,175 light horses, 4,210 hunters and hussars; total, 8,323; which, with the 300 of the 
Imperial Guard, makes 8,600 horses, just for the cavalry. For these 8,600 horses, I sent to 
Germany 5,900 men; it will therefore still be necessary to send 2,000 men on foot. I must be sure 
to get these 8,600 horses before making any changes to the arrangements made. The only 
measure to be taken at present is to send 230 Portuguese chasseurs to Hanover on foot, with their 
saddles, and, consequently, on the 500 horses which were ordered for them at Epinal, from give 
250 to other corps. What would be equally important was to make the state, what each regiment 
was to send to Germany as a consequence of the decree of the 19th of January, and of the men 
who left, with the time of their departure, so as to determine what was sent on February 15 in 
men, saddles, bridles, etc., in order to see at a glance what is lacking and what the depots of the 
regiments still have to supply in men, saddles, & c. I received the news that the King of 
Denmark had consented to the release of 6,000 horses from Holstein without paying duty. As 
soon as General Bourcier deploys all these means, and we become acquainted with the result of 
the various requests made, we will be able to see if it is necessary to make leave for Germany 
new detachments of men on foot and new shipments of harnesses. 

NAPOLEON. 


From the original. Deposit of the war.”
