18528. - NOTE FOR COUNT DARU, 
MINISTER SECRETARY OF STATE, IN PARIS. 
Paris. February 27, 1812. 


I want Count Daru to see, the Minister of War or the offices to arrive at the following 
result: 

I have a lot of Spaniards; the fact is that in the middle of Germany they are more French 
than German. I have not had to repent of the Portuguese I have, and hear nothing but the good of 
the Spaniards who have existed for a year in Italy and Germany. It is necessary to know if I did 
not create a new regiment of infantry; I think I have created a new battalion of sappers. 

This is what I would like to do. I want a handsome cavalry regiment; the soldiers exist; as 
for the officers, they would be: the colonel, French; the officers, half French, half of those who 
took the oath. I will only take men who have served in the Spanish cavalry. There is a regiment 
which has been disarmed after the Romana affair, and which must furnish subjects. As soon as 
these men were dressed in the least expensive fashion, and yet so as to recognize them at a 
glance, they would be sent to Germany, where they would go back. 

What officers, good cavalry officers, have taken the oath? 

I have very fine companies of light artillery; I do not believe 





1) On the surrender of General Dupont at Builen. 
2) See Exhibit 18497.7°’ 


257 


Page 258. 


that it would be advisable to create Spanish artillery companies, but I would have no objection to 
attaching to each regiment of artillery on horseback a sergeant and a squad of fifteen men. We 
would take ready-made gunners; they would amalgamate, and if that succeeds, we would extend 
this measure. 

The same thing could be done for all the artillery: 1 officer, 2 sergeants and 25 or 30 men 
per regiment, if we have Spanish artillery officers who have taken the oath. 

Finally, the same thing for the train battalions. To each company of the train would be 
added 10 or 12 men of the Spanish train; that would not form new corps; they would be watched 
by the mass. 

The execution of this measure would take place without delay. If that succeeds, we would 
put in every infantry company a tenth of Spaniards. I already have Romans, Tuscan, and that's a 
wonderful success. 

I prefer to start with gunners and train soldiers, because they are corps that have a spirit 
apart and desert less. 

Who would still prevent to make a battalion of Spanish military crews, by giving him 
some officers and some French supervisors? Those men accustomed to serve horses would do 
their service well and spare me from the French. 

If these measures were successful, I would find myself having a result of 80,000 men 
who would recruit my army and attach the population of Spain to me, for, having fought with the 
French, they would find themselves entirely French. 

One could even take the regiment of the Mediterranean which is in Toulon, to bring the 
frame in the North and fill it with Spaniards. The officers and non-commissioned officers would 
be French, of course; only one third of Spanish NCOs would be placed, and some Spanish 
officers would be amalgamated. One could organize the regiment of the Mediterranean and some 
battalions of that of Walcheren, and thus have six battalions; Of course, none of this would 
remain in France and everything would follow the army. 

I would like to hear a discussion on this. 

In amalgamating the Spaniards with the French, there is the inconvenience that, if that 
does not succeed, there will be deserters in all the regiments, which is unpleasant; however, 10 
men per company would make only 60 men per battalion, and by choosing them good subjects, 
the desertion would be less or would not affect. While having”* 





Page 259 


all Spanish regiments with French officers, they are regiments that one tries, on which one does 
not count. 

I asked men to organize three crews of oxen; if I wanted to put a third of Spaniards 
among those who know how to drive the oxen, I could make four battalions; that would employ 
500 Spaniards. 

I asked for two battalions in the comtoise, if I wanted to put a third of Spaniards, it would 
make me enough to form three battalions instead of two, taking among those who are 
accustomed to this trade, it would employ me 700 Spaniards. 

I have six battalions of military crews; putting 100 per battalion would make another 600 
Spaniards. This would make a total of 1,800 Spaniards among those who are used to this service. 

From unsigned original, War Repository. 


18530. - TO THE PRINCE OF NEUCHATEL AND WAGRAM, 
MAJOR GENERAL OF THE GREAT ARMY, IN PARIS. 
Paris. February 28, 1812, 


Cousin, write to the King of Westphalia that his contingent is organized so as not to be 
manageable in the war. This division into the vanguard, army corps and reserve, is not the right 
one. Tell him that he must form his army corps into two divisions of infantry and a brigade of 
cavalry: 

Ist division, nine battalions of infantry, one regiment of hussars and eighteen pieces of 
artillery, besides the artillery of the regiments; 

2nd division, nine battalions of infantry, one regiment of hussars and eighteen pieces of 
artillery; 

The Ist Cavalry Brigade will be composed of two regiments of cuirassiers, light lancers 
of the guard, bodyguards and two artillery batteries on horseback of 12 pieces. 

The train and the administrations must, as well as the military crews, be divided between 
the three divisions. Consequently, there will be four infantry brigades, two of which are four 
battalions and two of five battalions. 

By this means he will have a corps of army very simple and easy to handle. If the troops 
which he has at Danzig join him, the divisions would be of eleven battalions each; which would 
not prevent, in the circumstances, to reunite the two regiments of hussars with the other 
regiments of cavalry, and to form a fine division of 2,500 horses, and to make such an infantry 
battalion as one would like” 


259 


Page 260 


in the vanguard, But my intention is that the permanent organization be in two divisions and a 
reserve of cavalry. It is good that this reserve of cavalry should be commanded by a general of 
brigade. 

Point out to the King of Westphalia that the cavalry regiments are very feeble at 550 
men; they should each be 8 or 900 horses, and the regiment of lancers of the guard, because 
before the enemy it would be reduced to nothing,

18531. - TO GENERAL CLARKE, DUKE OF FELTRE, 
MINISTER OF WAR, IN PARIS. 
Paris, February 29, 1812. 


Duke de Feltre, I thought it appropriate to assemble in the 10th Military Division a 
reserve division composed of infantry, cavalry and artillery, which would put once for all my 
frontiers safe from the incursions of brigands. 

My intention is to entrust this command to General Travot. You will order him to leave 
within twenty-four hours after receiving your letter to go to Toulouse; he will get along with 
General L'Huillier, who commands the 11th Military Division, so that at the slightest event the 
columns of the Bayonne reserve will set in motion and make their way to Tarbes. 

When he has recognized the frontier, he will place his troops in the manner he deems 
most convenient; he will even build some defensive towers at the most important points of the 
passes, if necessary. Of course, he will not place his troops on the French territory, but on the 
back of the mountains and so as to be master of the pendant of the waters. Finally he must not 
forget that his only goal must be to defend the border. 

General Avice will command his cavalry. You will appoint an artillery colonel to 
command his artillery. You will also give him two engineer officers with a pioneering company 
and tools. 

General Gareau, who is at Mont-Louis, will be under his command. General 
Wouillemont will command his right at Saint-Girons. General Brouard will be ordered to go to 
General Travot to command his advance guard at the outlets of Ax and L'Hospitalet. 

General Travot will first carry his headquarters to Toulouse,” 


260 


Page 261 


and as soon as his arrangements are made and his troops sufficiently organized, he will go to 
Foix; he will then go to Tarbes and Mont-Louis; he will himself visit all his posts and take such 
measures as I no longer hear about the outrages made on the French territory by brigands. 

The troops under General Travot's orders will be: 

1st Two companies of artillery of line, with twelve pieces of mountain gun, which will 
be harnessed by what there is artillery train in the 10th military division; 

2nd The 4th and Sth battalions of the 116th; 

3rd The regiment which is at present part of the Bayonne reserve, which is commanded 
by the Major in the second Vallet, and which is composed of men of the 17th and 31st light and 
the 86th of the line; at which regiment you will send the order to go to Tarbes, where he will 
receive the subsequent orders of the commanding general; 

4th The 2nd Battalion of the 3rd Regiment of the Grand Duchy of Berg, to be completed 
by 840 men by the Ist Battalion; immediately after this operation, the cadre of the Ist battalion 
will return fully to the Grand Duchy of Berg, and the 2nd battalion thus completed will go to 
Tarbes; 

5th The Ist and 2nd battalions of the 29th of the line, to be completed by 800 men, for 
which purpose all the detachments will be recalled, all that is available in the 5th battalion will 
be the first two battalions, all that would be embarked will be disembarked, and this regiment 
will start without delay from Toulon to Toulouse with its artillery, its equipment and its teams; 

6th The cadre of the Ist, 2nd, 3rd and 5th battalions of the 2nd regiment of the 
Mediterranean; all the refractory conscripts who would be in these battalions will be placed in 
the 4th, which alone will remain in the islands of Hyeres; These four battalions will march to 
Toulouse with their colonel, their majors, their labor masters, and the depot; the minister of the 
administration of war will decide whether they will have to carry off some of the clothing they 
would have in their stores; Arrived at Toulouse, these cadres will receive 3,500 conscripts from 
the first ban of the National Guard of the 10th Military Division; 

7. Finally the battalion of Wurzburg and the other troops which are at Mont-Louis; which 
will make 8 to 9,000 men of infantry. 

The cavalry will be composed of a provisional brigade, which will be commanded by 
General Avice. He will have under him: 

1st A provisional regiment of hussars, which will consist of 120 horses of the 4th 
hussars, 120 of the Ist, 120 of the 3rd, 50 of the 2nd and 70th of the*”’ 


261 


Page 262 


10th; total of the regiment of march, 480, forming four companies; this regiment will be 
commanded by a second-in-command, whom you will appoint without delay; as soon as half of 
these men are on horseback, they will leave their depot to go to Foix; 

2nd A provisional regiment of chasseurs, composed of 100 men of the 29th chasseurs, 
100 men of the 15th, 200 of the 13th, 100 of the 22nd; total 500 men or five companies; as soon 
as half of them have gone up, they will go to Tarbes or Foix; this regiment will be commanded 
by a second-in-command; 

3rd Finally a regiment of dragoons, which will also be commanded by a major in second 
and which will be composed of 30 horses of the 16" of dragons, 30 of the 21st, 30 of the 26th, 30 
of the 27th, 80 of the 25th, 80 of the 24th; total, 280 horses. 

This provisional brigade will thus be 1,260 cavalry men. 

Infantry forces may be increased, if necessary, by the cohorts of the National Guard of 
the 9th and 11th Divisions, as well as by some new battalions from the Bayonne Reserve, as 
soon as the conscription has furnished new means to the corps that are in the military division 
Island. 

Always give orders for departure of the four battalions of the Mediterranean; before they 
arrived in Toulouse, the arrangements I made for the first ban of the National Guard will be 
known to you. 

National guards who are trained and those organized under the name of Chasseurs des 
montagnes will always be kept. 

There must be at the Repository information as to what is to be done to rectify this 
frontier; have them search. My intention is that the whole of the water and the good positions are 
ours, and that we build ovens on the passes where it will be necessary. You will propose to me a 
decree of meeting to the frontier departments of all the pendants of the waters. 

You will recommend to General Travot not to place the men of the Grand Duchy of Berg 
in the front line. They are good troops who fight well, but do not scatter the outposts to not 
expose them to the temptation to desert. He can hold them in hand at Castres or at Foix, and they

18532. - TO THE PRINCE OF NEUCHATEL AND WAGRAM, 
MAJOR GENERAL OF THE GREAT ARMY, IN PARIS. 
Paris, February 29, 1812 


Cousin, I see with pleasure that the million of powder to be shipped from Wesel to 
Magdeburg and the 500 thousand to be sent from Mainz are gone; Prussia has offered me a 
million. So this important point is. 

I believe that the dispatch of the 43 guns, 18,000 balls of 20, 11,000 of 18 and 1,725 7- 
inch bombs, etc., which were to be sent from Wesel, must be suspended. I approve what the 
general of artillery proposes to me, to modify the armament of the places so that the pieces of 12 
replace those of 18, and that one is not obliged to carry this large quantity of balls. Finally, I 
approve that we use the 76,000 shells of 7 inches, 7 lines, 27,000 6-inch shells, and lines which 
are at Magdeburg, by sending pieces which are at Metz. Finally, when these modifications are 
made, if anything becomes necessary, Prussia would furnish it. Write in this direction to the 
artillery general and the minister of war, so that nothing is sent from the French forts for the 
arming of the Oder and Vistula squares, unless it is a few carriages and objects of little 
importance. It is necessary, however, that the first inspector take measures so that the places are 
in a good state of armament.

18533. - TO THE VICE-AMIRAL COUNT DECRES, 
MINISTER OF THE NAVY, IN PARIS. 
Paris, February 29, 1812. 


Count Decres, you will receive a decree by which, without changing the present 
regiments of the marine artillery, I have ordered that the 1st regiment should supply the ports of 
Brest, Rochefort, and Lorient; the 2nd, at the port of Toulon; the 3rd, at the port of Cherbourg, 
and the 4th, at Antwerp. The Ist regiment will have the headquarters of a battalion at Lorient and 
that of another battalion at Rochefort. By this means, there will be artillery staffs in all major 
ports. I left the Ist regiment (that of Brest) to four battalions, that of Toulon to five battalions, 
and the 3rd and the 4th regiment each to two battalions. I left them the current composition; only 
the formation of the company will henceforth be as follows: the officers, according to the present 
organization; | sergeant major, 6 sergeants, 1 quartermaster, 12 corporals, 40 Ist class gunners, 
40 2nd class gunners, 148 cannon-gunners, 2 drummers; total, 254 men; which makes more than 
1,500 men per battalion, and for thirteen battalions about 20,000 men. The number of men 
currently composing these battalions being 10,000 men, so you are short of 9 to 10,000 to arrive 
at the complete new organization. Now, by my decree, I took 6,000 on the maritime conscription 
of 1813; which, out of 9,000 conscripts of the navy, leaves you 3,000 to recruit the crews as 
sailors. I also grant you 2,000 men on the conscription of land, which is currently in motion. 
These 2,000 men are supplied by the levy of 14 men on the contingent of each regiment. It is 
essential that, in the day of tomorrow, you make the distribution between the ports of Toulon, 
Brest, Antwerp and Cherbourg, so that the director general of the conscription can give in time to 
the prefects the order of take these 14 conscripts from each contingent on the march. These 2,000 
men will all have arrived in the various ports before the 15th of March, because the director- 
general will preferentially appoint Provencals for the Toulon regiment, Bretons and Poitevins for 
that of Brest, & c. It will be essential, therefore, that you give the order to the staff and depot of 
the 4th Regiment to proceed to Antwerp without delay, and to those of the 3rd to proceed to 
Cherbourg. Some officers will even have to go there, because the conscripts will arrive before 
the deposit, and it takes some officers” 


264 


Page 265 


to receive them. You can even order to land some in Antwerp and Cherbourg to receive the 
conscripts provisionally. With these provisions, you can return to Cherbourg, Antwerp, Brest and 
Toulon, in the course of April, all garrison companies that you have there. 

I saw only disadvantages in changing the current organization, and that new 
embarrassments for accounting. Nothing can prevent the men of the Toulon regiment, once 
embarked, from being found in the harbor of Brest, and those of Brest not found in the harbor of 
Toulon; this is therefore without remedy. The main thing is that there is a staff and an artillery 
depot in each major port. The bad air of Amsterdam and the dearness of everything in this 
country prevented me from placing a deposit there. When we have enough ships to have Spezia, 
we can demand that a staff resides in La Spezia. So you have no new officer to ask; you only 
have to appoint a few sergeants and corporals. By this means all these perpetual discussions with 
the war will be over. In the event of an extraordinary sortie, it will always be possible to resort to 
the extraordinary means of placing some fine company of grenadiers or voltigeurs aboard the 
vessel commander; but the usual service will be able to do without the help of the two ministries. 
This will be a great benefit for the service; it will also be a great economy, because you will have 
one less officer on board. Only one officer can command the garrison and the gunners. You will 
have a more marinated garrison and more skillful in the service of the cannon, and finally the 
colonel or the chief of battalion who will remain in the depot will be there more useful. 

NAPOLEON. 

From the original comm. by Madame la Duchesse Decres.

18535. - TO GENERAL CLARKE, DUKE OF FELTRE, 
MINISTER OF WAR, IN PARIS. 
Paris, March Ist, 1812. 


Duke de Feltre, I refer you to the route of the Helder. I do not see what use the citadel 
might be; it is an expense which will give no property in the place, Fort Morland, Fort Lasalle, 
the precinct of the place, all these works have only one goal, it is to cover the batteries which 
defend the harbor. Once these batteries are taken, what does it matter to a citadel that does not 
defend the entrance to the harbor, since it would be 1,200 toises? The citadel we would like to 
put on the side of Fort Dugonunier, we must put it at the entrance of the Nieuwe-Diep. It must be 
a stone citadel, vaulted, with casemates, making me perfectly master of the dike, protecting the 
batteries and armed with thirty to forty pieces of cannon, so that the enemy, having seized Fort 
Morland, the fort Lasalle, of Fort Dugommier, of the enclosure, has still nothing as long as he 
will not be master of the citadel, The forty guns will prevent his squadron from entering the 
roadstead, and from then on my ships will be7”’ 


271 


Page 272 


always safe. This citadel, which can easily have a resistance of fifteen to twenty days, can thus 
give fifteen or twenty days more to arrive and save the squadron. I can have twenty warships 
there; consider the immense advantage of having this property more. 

In general, the enclosure of the place seems to me very great. I would prefer it 100 
fathoms behind, so that there were only four fronts on the front, and on the side of the harbor 
three fronts at most; that would make the place better defended, would require less garrison and 
could be much better looked after. 

The unsafe of the place must be taken into consideration; It is difficult to have a large 
garrison, and it is difficult for a large garrison to maintain it for a long time. 

The obligation to defend the forts Morland, Lasalle, the Lock and Dugommier, already 
comprises 3,000 garrison men. 

A place that is dressed is expensive, and the economy of a few fronts is important. In a 
place not covered, there is also an advantage in saving a few fronts; this makes the guard easier 
and better protected from surprises. Instead of six fronts I would like, if possible, only four on 
the front. 

What I especially want is at the citadel or reduced to the entrance of the Nieuwe-Diep. 
There is between the place where the navy wants to build its basin and the Nieuwe-Diep 250 
toises; when one took him a hundred yards to the fort, there would still be enough left. It would 
be a matter of principle, as long as the fort is there, that the navy will not build anything between 
the fort and its basin and the sea, so that the citadel could play all its game on the basin and on 
the ships, and was not dominated by the buildings. 

NAPOLEON. 

According to the copy, Depot of War.

18541. - TO PRINCE KOURAKINE, 
AMBASSADOR OF THE EMPEROR OF RUSSIA, IN PARIS (1), 
Paris, March 3, 1812, 


Mr. Ambassador, I have placed under His Majesty's eyes the letters you have done me 
the honor to write to me concerning M. Jean Custinguer (2). 

His Majesty was painfully affected by the conduct of Count Czernitchef; he saw with 
astonishment that a man whom she had always treated well, who was in Paris, not as a political 
agent, but as an aide-de-camp to the Emperor of Russia, accredited by a letter to the Emperor, 
having a character of confidence even more intimate than that of an ambassador, took advantage 
of this character to abuse the most sacred of men. 

His Majesty flatters himself that the Emperor Alexander will be as painfully affected as 
himself to recognize, in the conduct of M. de Czernitchef, the role of an agent of corruption, 
equally condemned by the law of nations and by the laws of honor. 

H.M. the Emperor complains that, under a title that called trust, spies were placed near 
him and in times of peace, which is permitted only with respect to an enemy and in times of war; 
he complains that spies have been chosen, not in the last class of society, but among the men 
whom their position also attaches to the sovereign. 

I know too much, Ambassador, the sentiments of honor which have distinguished you 
throughout a long career to believe that you are personally afflicted with something so contrary 
to the dignity of the sovereigns. "If Prince Kurakin," said the Emperor, "could have entered such 
maneuvers, 





1) This letter, signed by the Duke of Bassano, Minister of Foreign Relations, was dictated by the Emperor. 

2) Custinguer, the concierge of the Russian legation, had been the intermediary with which M. de 
Czernitchef had used himself to gain an officer of the offices of the war, and thus obtain information on the 
preparations ordered by the Emperor for the purpose of a next campaign against Russia,” 


275 


Page 276 


the would excuse; but it is not the same with a colonel clothed with the confidence of his master 
and attached so closely to his person." 

His Majesty had just given the Count of Czernitchef a great proof of confidence by

18542. - TO THE COUNT BIGOT DE PREAMENEU, 
MINISTER OF RELIGIONS, IN PARIS. 
Paris. March 3, 1812. 


Count Bigot de Préameneu, it is time to end this scandal of the Sisters of Charity in revolt 
against their superiors. My intention is to suppress houses which, twenty-four hours after the 
warning you give them, would not have entered subordination. You will replace the suppressed 
houses, not by sisters of the same Order, but by another Order of Charity. The Sisters of Charity 
of Paris will lose their influence; it will be good. You will substitute for them sisters of an Order 
of which one is the happiest and who has not given subjects of complaint. 

NAPOLEON.

18544. - TO THE PRINCE OF NEUCHATEL AND WAGRAM,

Paris, March 3, 1812, 


My Cousin, the Polish Army Corps will form the 5" Corps of the Grand Army. The Ist 
Division will carry No. 16; 2nd Division, No. 17; and the 3rd division, No. 18. This corps will be 
commanded by Prince Poniatowski. 

The 6th Corps of the Grand Army will be composed of Bavarians. The 1st division will 
carry the number 19, and the 2nd division the number 20. This corps will be commanded by the 
general Saint-Cyr. 

The 7th corps will be formed by the Saxons, the Ist division will carry the No. 21, and 
the 2nd division will carry the No. 22. 

The 8th corps will be formed by the Westphalians. The Ist Division will be No. 23, and 
the 2nd Division will be No. 24. 

The Wurtemberg corps will form only one division, which will carry No. 25. 

The division composed of the brigades of Berg, Hesse-Darmstadt and Baden, which 
General Daendels commands, will form only one division and will carry No. 26. 

From April Ist, the denominations of Corps of observation of the Elbe, of 2nd Corps of 
the Elbe, of the Corps of the Ocean, will be suppressed, the Corps of observation of the Elbe will 
take the name of 1st Corps eit 





277 


Page 278 


of the Grande Armée; it is composed of the Ist, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, Sth and 7th divisions, and will be 
commanded by the Prince of Eckmihl. The 2nd Corps of the Elbe will take the name of 2nd 
Corps of the Grand Army; it will be composed of the 6th, 8th and 9th divisions, and will be 
commanded by the Duke of Reggio. The observation corps of the Ocean will take the name of 
the 3rd corps of the Grand Army; it will be composed of the 10th, 11th, 12th and 25th divisions,

to leave on the 21st. 

Order General Tharreau to go to Cassel to take command of one of the divisions of the

General Tharreau to command one of his divisions; that General Chabert, having served only as 
a major, has not the necessary aptitude; that I choose a brigadier general capable of being his 
chief of staff; that he should send his baggage and his military house to Halle, and that he should 
come from his person, with very few people, to Paris. He will come incognito; there will only 
remain two or three days; after which he will rejoin his army corps.

18546. - NOTE, 
Paris. March 3, 1812. 


Count Daru and the Minister of the Interior will call upon them the architect Fontaine and 
two other architects to examine the following questions. 

The Imperial Archives are very badly placed. This year it is proposed an expenditure of 
300,000 francs. It is to be feared that they are burning; but they lock it up, as it were, into the 
archives of Europe. The Emperor's project was to put them in the Louvre. 

1st question. - Can we put in the Louvre the Imperial Library and the Archives? 

2nd question, - The second floor of Luxembourg is empty. Make accommodations in a 
palace is unsuitable; Senate officers who are not there for life would be poorly housed there; 
hence the idea of putting the library of St. Genevieve there; this would offer the advantage of 
making the location of this library free for the high school. 

But the Archives are of an entirely different importance. 

Is it advisable to put only the Imperial Library at the Louvre, with the manuscripts, the 
medals, the furniture, and all the precious things? If there was room, which would prevent, for 
example, to put in the Louvre models of artillery? All this adorns a palace and is appropriately 
placed there. 

If it were important to place the Archives in Luxembourg immediately, or the Sainte- 
Genevieve library, is there enough room for the Archives? Will they be safe? If we put the 
Archives in the Louvre, could we start this year? 

We will report to the Emperor on this object in the week (1). 

According to the minute. Archives of the Empire. 





1) A decree of March 12, 1812, ordered the construction, on the left bank of the Seine, between the punished of 
Lena and Concorde, of a building intended to receive the archives of the Empire. The work, begun shortly thereafter, 
was abandoned in 1814.78°

18547. - TO EUGENE NAPOLEON, VICE-KING OF ITALY, AT MILAN. 
Paris. March 3, 1812. 


My Son, I learned about the Rivoli disaster. You did not, in this circumstance, justify 
what I expected from you. I asked you, first, to be of your own at Venice, at the moment of the 
departure of the vessel; Secondly, to await the return of the couriers you were to send to Pola, 
and the reports of a cloud of avisos, which would have taught you with certainty whether the 
Adriatic was free; 3rd, to bring out with the Rivoli, the Princess of Bologna or another frigate. 
You have not done anything of it. If only a frigate had gone out with the ship, you would have 
been victorious. If you had sent letters to Pola and notices everywhere, you would have known 
that there was an English vessel in the Adriatic. Re-read the letters I have written to you, and you 
will see that I can only attribute the Rivoli catch to the care you have taken in carrying out the 
instructions I gave. 

NAPOLEON. 

According to the copy comm. by S. A, L Mm, the Duchess of Leuchtenberg,

This decree seems to me, as well as all states.7°!

I do not want legions; the last rank will be battalion commander. You need a title of 
administration; this one is not developed enough. All the cohorts will meet at the chief town of 
the division, where they will be dressed and equipped by the board of directors, which will have 
at its disposal all the depot, an officer of clothing, a quarter-master, tailors, shoemakers and a 
number of workers; all this counting in the deposit. 

The prefect is chairman of the board of directors; the sub-prefect of the chief town is 
specially charged with the details. The board of directors is composed of the prefect, the sub- 
prefect, the director of the division, the quartermaster, the captain of the clothing and two 
captains taken from the depot. 

Specify that the mass of the clothing is paid to the deposit, that of linen and shoe to the 
cohort. 

Each cohort will have a board of directors that will correspond with the board of directors 
of the department. 

The reserves will be centralized. 

The Minister of War Administration will pay the board of directors what is his first bet 
and ruin of clothing, whereby the board of directors will provide for everything. 

In the decree, it is not enough to feel that the National Guard must be for the defense of 
odds. 

I think we have to go back to the proposed decree, or change it as follows: 5th division, 
instead of three cohorts, four; 10th division, instead of two cohorts, four; 11th division, instead 
of two cohorts, three; 20th division, instead of one cohort, two; total, thirteen, instead of eight; 
which will make thirteen cohorts, which will be destined for the defense of the Pyrenees; a 
cohort for the coasts of the 9th division; one for Bordeaux; put one fault for the other ribs, there 
will always be ten cohorts. The four cohorts of the 10th Division will all be formed by the cadres 
of the four battalions of the Mediterranean regiment, Ist, 2nd, 3rd and 5th Battalion, arriving at 
Toulouse. 

In the decree, it might be useful, without commitment to anything, to indicate the place 
where cohorts should meet. 

1st and 2nd military division, to form a reserve in Paris, eight cohorts; 3rd, one; 4th, one;

It should be said in the report that it is the creation of a new army of the interior.

18550. - NOTE DICTED IN THE COUNCIL OF MINISTERS. 
Paris, March 6, 1812, 


The basins of Antwerp and Flushing are sufficient for the Scheldt Navy. It is a harbor that 
is to have. 

At Terneuse, a channel similar to that of Nieuwe-Diep, at Terneuse, in the canal of the 
Ecluse, or in the Sas-de-Ghent canal, is required. 

A replacement sketch of Fort Nieuwe-Diep will be sent to the Minister of War, who will 
order the Director of Engineering to travel to the site and present a project for this fort. It must be 
at least 900 toises from the end of the bench. 

The Director of Engineering will sound the line with the utmost accuracy. He will consult 
with Admiral Ver Huell to mark the number of vessels that can anchor in this harbor and the 
points where they can approach the fort. 

It had been settled in the engineers' councils that two large batteries would be made to 
protect the work of the fort. This year we will work on these two batteries, placing mortars and 
pieces of 36; and, while waiting for the fort to be finished, which can only be the next campaign, 
a camp will be pitched there; which will enable the admiral to get his frigates out and to keep 
them in the harbor.

Cousin, I send you the letters of Prince Eckmiihl. Tell him that he must place his army 
corps in the following way, as of March 15: 

General Bruyere, with his light cavalry, at a march in front of Stargard, cutting the three 
directions of Kolberg, Danzig, and Bromberg. This general will have his artillery and his 
headquarters a day's journey closer to the Vistula than Stargard, so that this division, with its 
light artillery, may in six or seven days be reunited on the Vistula. 

The 2nd Cavalry Brigade of the Ist Corps will carry its headquarters to Landsberg. She 
will be under the command of Major General Dessaix. She will have positions on the Bromberg 
and Posen directions.”*°

The corps headquarters, with an infantry division, will be at Stettin. 

The other two divisions will be on the left bank of the Oder, well quartered, so that a

Count Hedouville, we wish you to go without delay to your Senate, to visit the 
departments of Rome and Trasimeno. 

Your mission; like that of the senators in their senate, must be all of observation; During 
your stay you will be surrounded by public officials and the most important people in the 
country. Their communications with you will have the effect of spreading the true spirit of the 
Government and sending to your knowledge the observations, both on men and things, of which 
it would be important for the good of our service that we were informed. 

We authorize you to write to us directly from all the chief towns where you go, to 
communicate to us your observations and the information which you have collected.

which you think you will have to present to us, as regards the present public officials and the

18553. - TO THE GENERAL LACUEE, COUNT DE CESSAC, 
MINISTER DIRECTOR OF THE ADMINISTRATION OF THE WAR, IN PARIS. 
Paris, March 7th, 1812. 


Count de Cessac, I authorize you to make the second order of 1,150 horses for the 
Spanish army. It is important that the 4,800 horses that must form the depot of the Spanish army 
exist in the course of April, in order to recruit the armies of Spain, to have a good number of men 
on the borders of Spain, and to be able to place a platoon of cavalry at all the outlets of the 
valleys, and finally to have, for the service of the coasts and the interior, the value of 2,400 men 
ready to go where the need would require it. 

Prussia must supply me with 15,000 horses, of which 6,000 are light cavalry, 3,000 are 
heavy cavalry, 6,000 are artillery or crew, quarter by quarter, from month to month. I therefore 
agree that you bear the 1,700 horses whose orders are not made in France on the supplies of 
Prussia; consequently, they will spend the Berlin depot. As for the 6,000 artillery horses or 
military crews, my intention is that we take it to assign to battalions for which the purchase of 
horses is not yet ordered, but whose frames are made and men provided by conscription. We 
should have the wings made in Berlin; the men would march with the harnesses, as soon as they 
were armed, dressed and equipped, they would find wagons and horses in Berlin; that would 
make a considerable saving. 

Thus it will be necessary to give me a statement, Ist orders made in Germany at the 
Hanover depot, 2nd orders made inside, 3rd orders made at the Potsdam depot. The depot of 
Berlin and that of Posen will be under the orders of a particular officer; they will return to the 
accounts of General Bourcier, when his present mission will be over and allow him to go there. 
Dilute all the saddles, because I see that there are 5,000 men in Hanover and that there will soon 
be 5,000 horses that can not be used if we have enough to equip them. I also ordered the 
purchase of 3,000 horses in the Duchy of Warsaw, and ordered?”

that 250 men of Portuguese chasseurs would be sent there; but these horses are intended to 
replace the losses resulting from the war. It is necessary to indicate well in the state the place

18563, - TO THE GENERAL LACUEE, COUNT DE CESSAC, 
DIRECTOR MINISTER OF ADMINISTRATION OF THE WAR, PARIS. 
Paris, March 10, 1812, 


Count de Cessac, I receive the situation of the hospitals on the Ist of February. I see there 
are 49,000 patients on the Ist of February, and only 42,000 on the Ist of January; which would 
make an increase of 7,000 patients during January. This first result frightened me at first; but, on 
closer examination, I see that the 32d division is carried for 6,400 patients on the Ist of February, 
and that it was carried for nil on the Ist of January; that Danzig is included for 1,500 patients in 
the state of February, and that it appeared for zero in the state of January: here is a difference of 
8,000 which comes from the manner of disposing the figures. Thus the number of patients was 
nearly the same in the two months of January and February; they decreased in Italy, in Ilyria, in 
the Ionian Islands; they increased by 100 men in the Sth military division; they decreased in the 
8th division, in the 10th and in the 11th division, although he passed many prisoners; they also 
decreased in the 12th, in the 16th division, in the 17th military division; finally they have 
diminished almost everywhere. Your result is not accurate; there were fewer sick in February 
than in January, despite the extraordinary movements of troops and the increase of 20,000 
Spanish prisoners who entered the country.

18568. - NOTE DICTATED IN THE COUNCIL OF MINISTERS. 
Paris. March 11, 1812. 


His Majesty is made aware of the resource which the Rumford soups offer for the relief 
of the indigent class of the people. She notices that Rumford soups do not require wheat. The 
fact is that we lack wheat in France. The administration of the towns and the prefects should be 
ordered to have a large quantity of stoves built for the Rumford soups everywhere, not only to 
deliver gratuitously, but also to sell. It should first be established in the communes around Paris, 
especially Saint-Denis. The Ministers of the Interior and Manufactures will take care of the 
execution of these provisions. The Minister of the Interior will write to all the prefects to inform 
them that the Emperor has seen with discontent that in the countries where the bread is good and 
the food is scarce, they have not taken steps to establish Rumford soups by entrepreneurs who 
would sell them to the public. He will calculate that a soup costs so much and feeds like so much 
bread; Thus, in times of scarcity, this resource offers the people a way to feed themselves as if 
the bread cost only so much. He will send them instructions on how to build the stoves and how 
to make soups. 

We could then give them at half price. At Saint-Denis and in the neighborhood of Paris, it 
would be necessary that the prefect had the soups made by contractors and had them displayed. It 
would also be necessary for Paris to introduce the use of selling them, which should be 
absolutely separate from free distribution. Moreover, the worker who has a little ease may blush 
to go to charity, while he may find it convenient, especially for his children, to buy it cheaply. 
There is more advantage for the people to establish them for sale than for 


Page 303 


give free, because the free distribution can only be limited, instead that in countries where wheat 
is expensive it could take a big extension. 

The administration could, moreover, help by furnishing the furnaces and by ensuring that 
the soups were given at the best possible price. 

The Emperor adds to these observations the following questions: 

What is the manner of obtaining ten millions to meet the needs of the indigent class of 
France, which, for April, May, June, July and August, would make two millions a month? The 
resources seem to be the revenue of the communes. 

If there are funds from departments, either in non-securities or reserve companies, not 
only of the current year, but of all the backlogs, or finally savings that can be made on the 
budgets, in postponing less urgent expenses and granting something on the treasure, if it is 
necessary? 

Once funds are found, what is the way to use them, so that it is not a source of abuse 
more harmful than useful? These ten millions must be used to relieve the indigent class, to 
compensate it for the rise of the wheat. We must therefore know the departments where the price 
is the highest and who suffer, and finally determine what should be the distribution of these 
funds between departments, and the process to follow to reach the goal. 

We must walk in the direction which has been given to Paris; thirty thousand pounds of 
bread and forty thousand soups have been distributed to Rumford. It can be bragged today that 
no inhabitant of the capital suffers from hunger. 

Ministers of Interior and Manufactures, Minister of the Treasury, State Councilors 
Constituting the Council of Ministers and Ministers of State Regnaud and Defermon to Meet at 
Home Minister's Office with Minister of Police and the State Councilor General Manager of 
Municipal Accounts, to take care of this project. 

According to the copy. Empire Archives,

18570. - TO GENERAL CLARKE, DUKE OF FELTI, 
MINISTER OF WAR, IN PARIS. 
Paris. March 11, 1812, 


Duke de Feltre, my intention is to have six battalions of 840 men each, made up of 
Spanish prisoners, of good will, in accordance with the decree I have taken; which will make 
three regiments. 

The 3rd battalion of the Walcheren regiment is at Strasburg, and I have ordered by my 
decree that he would take 800 prisoners. The 4th battalion of Walcheren is on the island of Ré 
with 900 refractory conscripts. My intention is for this battalion to come to Paris; he will 
continue his route to Paris on the army, where he will be incorporated into the infantry of the 
line, and the cadre will return to Strasbourg to take Spanish prisoners. You will order the Major 
of the Walcheren Regiment to go to Strasbourg to preside over the formation and dress of these 
two battalions. 

It is necessary that the officers of the 4th battalion should not know that their soldiers 
should be incorporated into the army regiments, because they would be less zealous in arriving 
there intact. 

Order the cadre of the 3rd battalion of the Belle-Ile regiment, supplemented by officers 
and non-commissioned officers, to leave under the command of the major of the regiment and 
with the 4th battalion completed to 900 refractory conscripts, to go to Paris. The cadre of the 3rd 
battalion will double that of the 4th battalion until their arrival in Paris. You will remove from 
the 4th battalion all the malignant men, the bad subjects, and those who are not sure. 

Arrived in Paris, the 3rd Battalion's cadre will travel to Strasbourg to take Spaniards, and 
the 4th Battalion will join the Grande Armée. When he arrives, he will be incorporated into the 
light infantry, and the cadre will return to Strasbourg to take Spanish prisoners. 


304 


Page 305 


Order that the cadres of the 3rd and 4th battalions of the regiment of the island of Ré, 
under the command of the major, go to Strasbourg to receive Spaniards. 

Only the Ist, 2nd and 5th battalions will remain at Walcheren, Belle-Ile and island of Ré 
regiments. 

I will thus have in Strasbourg three regiments composed of Spaniards, commanded by the 
majors. 

The accounts will be related to those of the Walcheren, Belle-Ile and island of Ré 
regiments. 

Charge General Kindelan, whom I shall appoint inspector of the Spaniards, and to whom 
I shall give the rank of general of division, to go over the review of the depots of Spanish 
prisoners, and to choose the best subjects, by executing all that is prescribed by my decree. You 
will order that the men of these new battalions who desert, and that it would not be judged 
appropriate to shoot for example, be conducted to the island of Walcheren. 

The Spaniards who will be incorporated into the battalion of Belle-Ile will take the light 
infantry uniform assigned to this regiment. Those who will be incorporated into the regiments of 
Walcheren and the Isle of Re will wear the line infantry uniform of these regiments, except that, 
in each regiment, they will have blue cuffs and lapels with a yellow nock, so that they can easily 
be distinguished from any French arm. 

I will not oppose the fact that, when there is a vacations, we put in these battalions a few 
safe Spanish officers and NCOs. 

As a result of these provisions, my intention is to report the decree that creates the 
Regiment of Catalonia. 

NAPOLEON. 

According to the copy. Deposit of the war.

18573. - TO THE PRINCE OF NEUCHATEL AND WAGRAM 
MAJOR GENERAL OF THE GREAT ARMY, IN PARIS. 
Paris, March 12, 1812. 


Cousin, send today the aide-de-camp of the Duke of Ragusa. Send to this marshal that 
you have put before me his last letter; that the meeting of his forces in Salamanca is not 
sufficient for the purpose he has to fulfill; that it is necessary that he bridge the Agueda and have 
a bridgehead so that, if the enemy leaves less than five divisions on the right bank of the 
Tagus, 


306 


Page 307 


can be carried on the Coa, on Almeida, and ravage all the north of Portugal; that the rainy season 
must end; that if Badajoz is taken by two simple English divisions, and that he, Duke of Ragusa, 
has retained five English divisions on the right bank, the capture of Badajoz can not be imputed 
to him, and will fall entirely upon the army of the South; that if, on the contrary, the enemy 
weakens by more than five divisions and leaves only two or even three or four on the right bank, 
it will be the fault of the army of Portugal if it does not work. on the corps of the enemy, does not 
invest Almeida, does not ravage all the north of Portugal and does not throw parties until the 
Mondego; that finally the main role of the army of Portugal is reduced to this: to hold in check 
six divisions of the English army or at least five, to take the offensive in the North, or if the 
enemy took the initiative or, if any other circumstance orders it, send the Tagus to Almaraz, to 
raise the siege of Badajoz, as many divisions as Lord Wellington has done. 

When you have sent this letter, you will tell the aide-de-camp to come to the Elysee at 
eight o'clock; I will say a word to him. 

NAPOLEON. 
From the original. Deposit of the war. 


18574. - TO PRINCE OF NEUCHATEL AND WAGRAM 
MAJOR GENERAL OF THE GREAT ARMY, IN PARIS. 
Paris, March 13, 1812. 


Cousin, tell the Duke of Reggio that I will probably send him orders to be executed on 
the 20th; that Iam not yet decided on this movement, but that I thought it my duty to warn him, 
so that, receiving the orders, he could execute them twenty-four hours later. The brigade 
Corbineau and the division of cuirassiers with twelve pieces of light artillery, forming 3 or 4,000 
horses, will pass first the bridge of Magdeburg to go on Berlin. He, with his person, with his 
headquarters and the Legrand division, would come a day later. The division Verdier would 
leave the same day of Brunswick, the park of the army would leave with the division Verdier. 
The Belliard division would centralize in Magdeburg. The marshal would enter Berlin with his 
4,000 cavalry and Legrand division. The Verdier division would remain in Magdeburg. The park 
would stay there too. Things would stay that way until further notice. It is therefore necessary 
that the troops of the Verdier division take position between Brunswick and Magdeburg,*”” 





Page 308 


and that the companies are placed in such a way as to be able to open in twenty-four hours. The 
marshal will have an instruction on how to behave and what he must do; he still has only to 
prepare himself and not let anything transpire from this movement. Its arrangements must be 
made in such a way as to be honored by the handsome dress of the army. He may stop, if 
necessary, one day at Brandenburg. It will have to avoid Potsdam, where, by the convention, one 
must not pass. I suppose that all his fleet will be well hitched, that each division will have its 
ambulances, that the army will have its military crews, and that nothing will be conducted by 
requisition. Send the Marshal an extraordinary dispatch on this subject, and that, by the return, he 
will let you know what will be the situation of his whole army in cavalry, infantry, engineers, 
artillery, sappers, etc., at the moment of his Entrance. His infantry might march in brigade, each 
brigade having, independently of its guns and caissons of regiments, to know: the Ist brigade, the 
artillery batteries on horseback, and the 2nd brigade, the batteries of artillery on foot. Generals, 
staff officers, ordering officers, etc., everyone will remain at his post and will only work with the 
troop. General Doumerc will command all the cavalry.

18578. - TO GENERAL CLARKE, DUKE OF FELTRE, 
MINISTER OF WAR, IN PARIS. 
Paris. March 14, 1812. 


Duke de Feltre, show my discontent to the general who commands the island of Elba the 
little education of the 7th battalion of the 6th line and the 14th light; these men scarcely know 
how to handle weapons; it is the fault of this general: if he had made them exercise, and if he had 
passed the magazine himself every week these men, who had almost nothing to do, would be 
today perfectly educated. Make him the same reproach for the men drawn from the battalions of 
the Mediterranean. 

Testify my discontent to the general who commands in Corsica the poor quality of the 
supplies made to the soldiers by the administration of the regiment of the Mediterranean. The 
shirts and shoes are so bad that the soldier could not use them. Have an investigation done to find 
the perpetrators of the infidelities and wrongdoings that have been committed. 

Write to the Grand Duchess so that all the troops that are on the island of Elba are 
reunited with the battalion every day, so that within a month, clicks can begin the exercise on fire 
and be perfectly educated. Recommend that he send officers to oversee the execution of his 
orders. 

If the battalion commander of the 3rd foreign battalion, who arrived at Livorno, is not 
good, we must put another one. 

The secretary of the commandments of the Grand Duchess must not correspond with you; 
write that it is not suitable; that he can make the letters, but that everything must be signed by the 
Grand Duchess or by her husband; that this way of doing things is ridiculous and contrary to the 
dignity of my ministers and to the good of the service; that in the army there is no rank; the King 
of Spain must himself write to the Minister of War, as he writes to the Major-General when he 
reports to him the command I have given him. 

NAPOLEON. 

According to the copy. Deposit of the war. 


18579. - TO THE GENERAL COUNT DE LA RIBOISIERE, 
COMMANDING THE ARTILLERY OF THE GREAT ARMY, IN PARIS. 
Paris, March 14, 1812. 


Count de la Riboisiére, I send you this letter by

Page 311 


one of my pages, to be sure that it will be delivered to you personally, and so that it does not 
come out of your hands. The object of this letter is to let you know (and I put you alone in my 
secret) that my intention is to begin in the countryside by the siege of Dinabourg and that of 
Riga. I intend the Danzig siege crew for Riga and the Magdeburg siege crew for Dinabourg. 
Take indirect and secret information on these two places, and let me know, by a note written in 
your own hand, the composition of one and the other of these places. Let me know how many 
ships it would take to embark the crew of Magdeburg; there is no time to lose, wanting it to be 
embarked on April 1, to be transported by the Vistula. Let me know how many days it takes for 
this crew to arrive in Bromberg, it would have to be there on May Ist. He will have to descend 
and continue navigation on the Haff, enter the Haff of Memel, and go up the Niemen to Vilna, 
where it will be carried on the ground in front of the place of Dinabourg, which is a journey of 
about forty leagues. Could the same boats suffice for this whole trip, or should they break the 
load, and how many times? It will be necessary for this crew to arrive on | June in Vilna, in 
order to open the trench in mid-June. 

In the material you have to carry, put the material of the engineers, not judging it 
necessary to put the general of engineers in my confidence. 

How many boats are needed to carry the crew of Danzig? From Danzia, this crew will 
have to be transported, either on Memel or on Tilsit, from there to go on the ground in front of 
Riga; it is a journey of about sixty leagues. Can the same boats go to Tilsit or Memel? What day 
must the loading take place at Danzig, and how many days it is necessary to operate the 
transport? It is essential that it be done only at the right moment, so as not to expose anything; 
the loading of the crew of Magdeburg will not expose anything, since it can be supposed 
intended for the armament of Danzig or Thorn. Finally, let me know how many wagons it will 
take to transport one and the other of these crews from Vilna to Dinabourg and from Memel to 
Riga. I suppose that the siege of these places will not stop me more than fifteen days, namely: 
five days for the investment, the opening of the trench, the construction of the batteries and the 
beginning of the fire, and ten days of open trench. It is therefore necessary that the supplies 
should nae arrived in a fortnight, at the rate of one convoy a day, from Memel and Vilna. What 
portion

will the army be able to supply for this cart, and what portion will it be necessary to take in the 
country?

18584. - TO PRINCE OF NEUCHATEL AND WAGRAM, 
MAJOR GENERAL OF THE GREAT ARMY, IN PARIS. 
Paris, March 16, 1812, 


Cousin, let Prince Eckmiihl know that I have sent him orders of movement for the Ist of 
April, on the supposition that the Russians will not leave their frontier and will not begin 
aggression; that in this case all that I ordered will be executed literally, and that the main thing 
will be to rest the troops, to have them well nourished, to organize the bridges and bridgeheads 
of the Vistula, and to be in a word, master from there to begin the campaign with activity, if 
hostilities take place. If, on the other hand, the Russians begin hostilities and enter Prussia or the 
states of the Grand Duchy, the 5th corps, which is about 40,000 men, commanded by Prince 
Poniatowski, would be supported by the 7th, who is 20,000 strong, and the 8th, which is also 
20,000 strong. The King of Westphalia, who will be sent to Krossen on the Ist of April, at the 
head of his contingent, and who will follow his march to Warsaw, will then take command of 
these three corps, which will be commanded by Prince Poniatowski and by General Vandamme 
and Reynier, and with these three corps would see to cover Warsaw. The Ist corps advancing on 
the Alle, on Osterode, Allenstein, and Guttstadt, would threaten to turn the corps which would 
lead to Warsaw by Grodno and force the enemy to keep the Niemen. Moreover, on the first news 
of 





314 


Page 315 


Prince of Eckmiihl, the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th Corps, would march on Krossen, Berlin, Kiistrin, and 
Glogau, and all three would march to Thorn, bringing together 250,000 men on the left. I desired 
that the Prince of Eckmiihl should know these general ideas, so that he behaved accordingly. 

It is necessary to ignore until the last moment that the king of Westphalia must command 
my right. 

If, on the contrary, the Russians make no movement, then Prince Poniatowski will place 
the Saxons and Westphalians between Kalisz and Warsaw to feed them more easily. The Ist 
Corps will make its movement as I ordered, and the 2nd, 3rd and 4th corps and the Guard will 
advance successively and methodically in the course of April. The general headquarters will be 
in Berlin on April Ist. 

The Prince of Eckmiihl must, on the contrary, be announced at Warsaw with all his army 
corps, as if he were destined to go there. 

NAPOLEON. 

From the original. Deposit of the war,

in Brandenburg with the Army Park. The Belliard division will pass the Elbe on the 27th or the 
28th, and will be confined between Magdeburg and Brandenburg. 

You will communicate to the Duke of Reggio the extracts of the treaty with Prussia 
relating to the non-occupation of Potsdam. He must, therefore, take a different route from 
Brandenburg than that of Potsdam, where his troops can not enter. He must also not occupy the 
Charlouenburg Palace nor the King's Palace in Berlin. 1,500 Prussians have to go to Potsdam; a 
company must stay to keep Charlottenburg; another Prussian company must also remain to guard 
the Berlin Palace. There must be no troops at Spandau; the Prussians will only have invalids 
there. The Duke of Reggio will let me know in what situation this place is. Without occupying 
the fortress, it is necessary to place a battalion in the city. Order General Headquarters to stay 
two or three days in Erfurt; afterwards, he will continue his journey to Berlin, where it is 
necessary that he does not arrive before April 1, that is to say that he must arrive there only two 
days after the Marshal Duke of Reggio will have entered it. Submit to my approval the road that 
the headquarters must make every day. Write to Count Saint-Marsan to tell him roughly the 
movement of the 2nd corps, commanded by the Duke of Reggio. 

NAPOLEON. 

From the original. Deposit of the war. 


18587. - TO THE PRINCE OF NEUCHATEL AND WAGRAM, 
MAJOR GENERAL OF THE GREAT ARMY, IN PARIS. 
Paris, March 16, 1812. 


Cousin, inform the Prince of Eckmithl that, on the 28th of March, the 2nd corps enters 
Berlin; that the 3rd Corps, under the Duke of Elchingen, will be in the first days of April on the 
Oder at Krossen; that the Bavarians and the 4th corps or the army of Italy arrive at Glogau;*’° 





316 


Page 317 


that henceforth I can not give orders of detail; that I can only give instructions, since we are 
approaching the frontiers of the enemy; that it is my intention that General Dessaix leave on the 
1st of April from Kiistrin, with the 2nd Light Cavalry Brigade of the Ist Army Corps and the two 
regiments of his division which are at Kiistrin, to proceed to Posen, that the regiment of his 
division which is at Glogau also moves to Posen, so that before the 10th of April this general, 
with his division, with the artillery of his division, and the brigade of light cavalry, reunited at 
Poseu. He will send forward wars commissioners to ensure that the food is ensured to his troop. 
On leaving Kiistriu, he will distribute the bread for four days, and he will carry it for four days 
with him, so that his march will not slow down and that the soldier will lack nothing. General 
Bruyére's cavalry division and Gudin's division will be on Thorn, where they can also be from 
the 10th to the 12th. A division of the corps will be able to move by the road, along the sea, to 
arrive more quickly to Danzig, without however passing to Kolberg, which we must not occupy. 
The big cavalry will march on Marienwerder. The Prince of Eckmiihl will carry his headquarters 
and the park of his year to Thorn. From the 10th to the 15th of April, he will occupy Marienburg 
and work without delay to establish the bridges at Dirschau and Marienburg, if, however, the 
debacle took place. He will have the works of Marienburg work to raise them and put them in 
condition, so that fifteen days later they can be armed. He will also raise the bridgehead of 
Marienwerder and restore the bridge. At the same day, Ist April, Prince Eckmiihl will order the 
Saxons to leave Krossen (1) on the 30th to march on Kalisz; to Prince Poniatowski to unite all 
the Poles in Warsaw, by bringing to Warsaw all that might be on Posen's side, and also 
withdrawing all that would be at Thorn; so that, in the event of an event, Prince Poniatowski had 
to defend the Duchy the three Polish divisions and the Saxon corps, which from Kalisz could 
quickly reach Warsaw. 

Thus, from the 10th to the 12th, if the Russians did not make any movement which 
obliged the prince of Eckmiihl to change these dispositions, the headquarters will be at Thorn, 
having in quarterings in front, but not very far, the light cavalry and the whole Ist cavalry corps; 
having at Thorn a division; in with another in Posen; the 7th division united at Marienburg, and 
the three others lying, one on Marienwerder and the environs, and two on Danzig; Polish

18588. - TO PRINCE OF NEUCHATEL AND WAGRAM, 
MAJOR GENERAL OF THE GREAT ARMY, IN PARIS. 
Paris, March 16, 1812. 


My Cousin, there is a mistake of writing in my last dispatches. The Saxon corps is in 
Guben and not in Krossen. You must therefore give him the order simply to leave his current 
cantonments to go to Kalisz, leaving him master to pass the Oder where he deems it suitable. 
You must lead the Westphalians, not on Krossen, but on Sorau and Spremberg. Make them go on 
little walks and give them stays every three days; they will take two days off around Sorau and 
Spremberg. You will inform me of the day when they will arrive on these two points, so that I 
give orders to make them continue their movement on Glogau and Kalisz. So, instead of arriving 
at Glogau on the 3rd, they would only arrive on the 5th or 6th. 

NAPOLEON. 
P. S. Tell me, then, when the Bavarians and the Army of Italy arrive at Glogau.

The service of the army is divided into districts: between the Rhine and the Elbe, between

As for the communication routes of the army, a road will leave Mainz and go to

Another route will go from Wesel to Magdeburg, Berlin, Stettin and Danzig; a fork will 
fall on Dirschau and Marienburg. Another route will go from Hamburg to Stettin. Finally another 
route will go from Mainz to Wurzburg, Bamberg, Kronach, Leipzig, Torgau, Glogau, and from 
there to Posen, from Glogau a branch will go to Kalisz and Warsaw. 

Another route will go from Innsbriick, Augsburg, Nuremberg, and join the former to

In Magdeburg, there will be a French commander and a French administration. In

18591. - TO COUNT DARU, MINISTER SECRETARY OF STATE, IN PARIS. 
Paris. March 17, 1812. 


Count Daru, the Minister of the Interior has been sick for three months, and my business 
is suffering. Go to his house to see how he is doing. It would be appropriate for him to ask me to 
appoint someone to manage the ministry, as Count Cretet did. Eight days ago a council of 
subsistence must take place; during this time the people suffer from an evil to which no remedy 
is put. Whatever may be the zeal of the Minister of the Interior, no one can overcome nature; he 
will recover more quickly by taking two months rest, I would like the request to come from him, 
so that he does not believe that I want to take away his ministry. 

Before going to the Minister of the Interior, bring his doctor to his house to find out what 
kind of illness he has, and if it will last for a long time. 

NAPOLEON. 


According to the copy comm. by M, Count Daru.*”°

18594. - TO EUGENE NAPOLEON, VICE-KING OF ITALY, AT MILAN. 
Paris. March 19, 1812. 


My Son, on the 13th, 15th and 17th of February, the 5th battalion of the 6th of the line, 
the 5th battalion of the 14th light infantry and the marching battalion of the Ist regiment of the 
Mediterranean left from the island of Elba, together making 1,800 men. They passed in Florence 
on the 20th, the 22nd and the 24th; so they had to arrive before March 2 in Mantua.*”’ 





327 


Page 328 


I am surprised that you do not mention it in your letter of the 4th. You can put in sustenance in 
the 5th battalions of the light and sixth of the line the 500 men of the battalion of the 
Mediterranean, from which you can thus send back the setting on the island of Elba. The 5th 
battalions of the 14th and 6th will then be strong each of 900 men. Have both battalions started 
to continue their journey; send a review of their armaments and clothing to Verona; give them 
cartridges and go to your bodies. You will distribute these 1,800 men among your regiments who 
are at the Grande Armée; it will fill about half of the deficit that your regiments are experiencing. 
Be careful to incorporate light infantry men into light infantry regiments, and line-in-line 
regiments. I am told that clothing is in bad condition; rectify all this before leaving Mantua. I am 
very anxious that all the regiments that have left Italy should be worn by 140 men per company 
and be kept there. The 4th Battalion of the 8th Light must have arrived; as with the detachment 
of the 14th Light, the 8th and 18th Light will be strong enough, my intention is that the 4th 
Battalion of the 8th Light be sent to Trieste, where he will garrison. This will be the increase of 
one battalion for the Illyrian province; there are two, it will be three and can only be very useful. 
Take care that these men who come to you have two pairs of shoes in the bag and a good pair at 
their feet; have them complete this supply in Verona. 

It is indecent that the military road passes through Munich; it embarrasses the king; pass 
it through Augsburg, Nuremberg, Donauwetth, and thence to Glogau, where your army must be. 

You did not tell me about the arrival of the 300 men of the 92nd; in which regiments did 
you incorporate them? I send you the report of the ministers on the movement of the men of the 
6th and 14th. 

NAPOLEON. 
According to the copy comm. by S. A. I. the Duchess of Leuchtenberg.

Duke de Feltre, there is no problem in writing these letters to the generals commanding 
the 17th and 31st military divisions. 

It will be necessary to give a new instruction to General Molitor, as soon as it is decided 
which troops should guard Holland.*”* 





328 


Page 329 


He is going to have two cohorts of the National Guards of the country, strong together of 1,600 
men; a battalion of departmental reserve companies; two battalions of the paid guards of 
Amsterdam and Rotterdam; which will make a good brigade of nearly 4,000 men. Independently 
of this, he has, I believe, had companies of artillery and foreign regiments, the strength of about 
3,000 men. General Molitor would have from that moment 7,000 men. In addition there will be 
in Holland six cohorts of National Guards of the Interior, who will meet at Utrecht; which will 
still make a brigade of 5,000 men. There will also be a brigade of six 4th battalions. Thus four 
brigades or 18 or 20,000 men will be in Holland. Antwerp, Bruges, Wesel, even Hamburg and 
Boulogne, will soon furnish another reinforcement of 25 to 30,000 men. 

It is necessary that the general of division know in advance the use he must make of these 
troops, not to order anything, but only to have an eye on their training, review and censor their

18600, - SPEECHES OF THE EMPEROR, 
Palace of the Tuileries, March 22, 1812, 


TO THE DEPUTATION OF THE ALLIER. 


I thank you for the sentiments you express on behalf of the electoral college of the 
department of Allier. My people will always see me ready to do anything to consolidate the 
destinies of this empire on immutable bases, and to make France triumph over the hatred of 
England. I have the confidence that no sacrifice will appear painful to the French, when I judge it 
necessary for the accomplishment of these great designs. 


TO THE DEPUTATION OF THE ARDENNES. 


The wishes you make for the future will be fulfilled: it must consolidate what was 
founded by the bravery of the French. The Ardennes department will always be at the forefront 
of its zeal and good spirit. I thank you for the sentiments you express on behalf of me. 


AT THE DEPUTATION OF INDRE-ET-LOIRE. 


The city of Tours, although one of the most beautiful of the Empire, suffers from the 
mediocrity of the harvest. Nine years of abundance succeed in France to a mediocre year. My 
people can not prove to me better the love they have for me than by showing the calm and 
resignation that circumstances require. I agree with your feelings. 


AT THE DEPUTATION OF LOIR-ET-CHER. 
The sentiments expressed by my people, in the different circumstances in which they are 
called near me, are dear and necessary to my heart. The government of the greatest empire in the 
world bears with it the worries which the love of the French alone can wipe off. 


AT THE DEPUTATION OF THE HAUTE-MARNE. 


I spent my first years in the midst of my Champagne peoples; I know how good they are 
and attached to what is estimable.**! 





331 


Page: 332 


I approve of the wishes that you form for me: they make me happy; I know they are real. 
Excerpt from the Moniteur of March 23, 1812. 


18601 - TO THE PRINCE OF NEUCHATEL AND WAGRAM, 
MAJOR GENERAL OF THE GREAT ARMY, IN PARIS. 
Paris. March 24, 1812. 


My Cousin, the division of General Bruyere, or the Ist of the light cavalry of the reserve, 
will be composed of two French brigades and a Polish brigade composed of three regiments of 
light cavalry, which Prince Poniatowski has already received, train and meet at Thorn. The 2nd 
Division, or the Wattier Division, will be composed of two French brigades and a brigade 
commanded by General Ornano, of the Wiirttemberg Light Horse Regiment, which has already 
served in the Prussian Campaign with the Cavalry Reserve, and two Prussian light horse 
regiments. The 3rd Division, or Kellermann's division, will be composed of two French and two 
Bavarian light cavalry regiments, and one Saxon light horse regiment, under the command of 
Brigadier General Dommanget. The 3rd Brigade of the Bruyére Division will take No. 15; the 
3rd of the Wattier Division will wear No. 16, and the 3rd of the Kellermann Division No. 17. 
Thus, each of these light cavalry divisions will be of a total of 6,000 men and a present of at least 
4,000. 

There will be a 4th corps of the reserve, composed of the 4th division of light cavalry and 
a 7th division of heavy cavalry. The 4th Light Cavalry Division will consist of two brigades, 
each of three Polish regiments, with a line of six Polish brigade artillery guns. A Polish 
divisional general and two Polish brigadier generals will command this division. The 7th Heavy 
Cavalry Division will be composed of a brigade of Saxon cuirassiers and a brigade of 
Westphalian cuirassiers, also having twelve pieces of light artillery. General Lorge will 
command this division. 

General Latour-Maubourg will have the command of the cavalry of all the right. 

The 5th corps will have three brigades of light cavalry, each composed of two Polish 
regiments; which will still employ six Polish regiments. 


Thus the sixteen regiments of Polish cavalry will be employed,**

and six with the three brigades of the 5th corps. These last three brigades will carry Nos. 18, 19 
and 20. 

The six light Saxon cavalry regiments will be employed in the following manner: two

18609. - NOTE DICTED IN THE COUNCIL OF MINISTERS. 
Tuileries Palace. March 25, 1812. 


The Minister of the Navy reports a despatch he received from the Transportation Office 
regarding the exchange of prisoners. His Majesty thus indicates that he follows the answer to be 
made: 

I received your letter of the 10th of this month; I put it in front of the Minister of the 
Navy. The negotiation which took place by the channel of Mr. Mackensie, in the course of 1810, 
so simplified this question of the exchange, that, if the British government really wants the 
general exchange of the French and the allies of France against the English and the allies of 
England, this negotiation may be very nearly finished. The two governments agree in principle, 
but do not seem to agree in their intentions. The English government really wants to have only 
the English prisoners, and to be the master, when it has made this exchange, to continue the 
exchange of the rest of the French prisoners against the allies of England. The French 
Government does not wish to depend on a change of dispositions in the English Government, 
and it wants the mode of execution to assure the reality of the execution of the principle. 

According to the copy comm. by Madame la Duchesse Decres.*“°

18610. - TO THE VICE-AMIRAL COUNT DECRES, 
MINISTER OF THE NAVY, IN PARIS. 
Paris. March 26, 1812. 


Count Decres, the construction of the ships of line, not only of 74, but also of 80 and 
even three bridges, on the Loire, is of the highest importance: then Brest becomes only a place of 
armament, and ships are built at the mouth of the Loire. 

It has been many years since I have a presentiment that vessels can be built at the mouth 
of the Loire. The reports of the commission which I had established then did not seem to me 
convincing. Since frigates armed with six months of food and water and shooting 18 to 19 feet 
can go out to the Indies, how can light or armed vessels in flute and drawing 14 feet of water can 
not exit? Now, when it is proved that my ships can only go out in flute and pulling 15 or 16 feet, 
they will find themselves in the same position as the loaded frigates. It is to be presumed that 
they can only come out definitively in time of peace; but it will already be a great result of 
having seven or eight vessels on the shipyard in wartime, using precious woods that are rotting in 
Nantes, and would put us in a position to have at peace a great number of ships on all sides. 

Would we have to wait for peace? Who would prevent the launching of ships following 
the procedure that took place in Venice? The vessel was raised 5 feet 6 inches and passed with a 
draft of 13 feet 6 inches. 

We could, by bringing the unarmed ships in Mindin's harbor, arm them there, place them 
on the camels, and then, fully armed, shooting at most 14 feet of water, they would shoot 4 feet 
less than the frigates, for to go to the high seas. Thus a ship of 80, only firing with the camels 
less than 16 feet of water, would be in a condition at least inferior to the frigate. 

From Paimboeuf to Mindin there are two leagues; the vessel placed at Paimboeuf on 
camels could be set up so as to fire only 9 or 10 feet of water, and from then on could take the 
time necessary to reach Mindin's bay. But finally, if it were true that there were difficulties 
Paimboeut to Mindin, why not build in Mindin or Saint-Nazaire? From Saint-Nazaire to 
Mindin" 


341 


Page 342 


there are 1,000 toises; we can consider the mouth as perfectly defended. 

I think that M. Tupinier must be ordered to go to Paris with all due diligence, while 
writing to him the letter which you propose to make his observations and reports, his answer. He 
will go to Paimboeuf, Saint-Nazaire and Mindin, and will thus be able to make a good memory 
on this question, to which I attach so much importance, At the mouth of the Loire, one finds 
wood, hemp, masts, irons, artillery; everything is easy, while everything is difficult in Brest. 

As for the construction of a basin, I would like you to give Engineer Cachin the 
commission to go to Saint-Nazaire and Mindin. The small harbor touches the rock of Simeon; 
which would prevent the digging of a basin for three vessels between Saint-Nazaire and the point 
of Penhouet, and even to build a form in the manner of the Dutch engineer, that is to say to 
establish pumps for fire for the water game? Three established forms would give me two ships a 
year. The engineer Cachin can go there from Cherbourg without making an absence of more than 
eight to ten days, and give me the first ideas on this project. 

NAPOLEON. 

From the original comm. by the Duchess Decrés, 


18611. - TO THE PRINCE OF NEUCHATEL AND WAGRAM, 
MAJOR GENERAL OF THE GREAT ARMY, IN PARIS.

My Cousin, the Ist Division of the Grand Duchy of Warsaw, has its headquarters in 
Warsaw, The 2nd Division has its headquarters in Bromberg, the troops occupying Posen, Kulm,
