18618. - TO EUGENE NAPOLEON, VICE-KING OF ITALY, AT MILAN. 
Paris. March 28, 1812. 


My Son, I receive the organization of the troops that remain in the interior of Italy, in 
accordance with the instruction I have given you. 

The Ist division will be composed of General Schilt's brigade, four battalions of the 13th 
line with two pieces of artillery, which will meet at Udine, and a brigade commanded by General 
Zucchi, meeting at Padua, composed of six Italian battalions and four pieces of artillery; which 
forms a division of ten battalions, six regimental artillery pieces, four squadrons, and six pieces 
of horse artillery, with a force of nearly 8,000 men. I will immediately name a general of 
division. 

The 2nd division will be commanded by General Barbou. It will be composed of the 
Renard Brigade, which meets at Ancona, having two pieces of artillery, a squadron of chasseurs 
and a squadron of dragoons, and forming 2,000 men of infantry and 400 horses. The 2nd Brigade 
will be composed of two battalions of the 112th, which are still at Florence, and which will 
receive orders to go to Bologna; which will bring this division to 4,000 men. There will be 
attached a battery of six pieces of artillery, served by an Italian artillery company on foot. 

Independently of these two divisions, there will be the observation corps of southern 
Italy, commanded by General Grenier, stationed at Perugia, in a situation of being on Ancona, 
Livorno, and Naples, according to the circumstances. 

The Ist and 2nd divisions will, according to circumstances, be carried on Venice, the 
Illyrian provinces, the Tyrol, Ancona, Livorno, and Genoa. There will therefore be in Italy an 
active force of 20,000 men, which may be carried wherever it may be, without understanding 
what would be in Piedmont. 

I approve of the composition of the garrisons of Palmanova, Osoppo, Venice, Mantua, 
Legnago, Peschiera, Rocca d'Anfo, and Verona Castle. It is necessary that you take all the 
measures to complete the frameworks of the*”® 





346 


Page 347 


Italian corps; French executives will be. Whole artillery companies at Palmanova, Venice, 
Mantua, will be available. 

Arrange everything to give things that direction; accelerate the totality of the deposits and 
the rise of the 5 squadrons, in order to have, this summer, 1,500 available horses. 

I suppose that everything that has to leave for the Grand Army is already gone. 

It is necessary that you consult with the Bavarians to know the quantity of troops which 
they will leave in Tyrol. It is proper to leave some troops at Trent. A column of infantry, with 
some cavalry, and six pieces of cannon, are indispensable to keep watch over the whole of the 
Italian Tyrol, to smother all movement at once, and to maintain tranquility. 

General Vignolle will remain in Italy as chief of staff; I will appoint a general to 
command. 

As for the civil government, I imagine that it will be the same as at the time of the 
campaign of Vienna; you will leave the Duke of Lodi the presidency of the Council of Ministers; 
I suppose he is in a position to act. 

Prepare everything for your departure, for in three or four days I will write to you to 
come to Paris, and perhaps from Paris you will go directly to Glogau, and from there to your 
army corps. 

I do not want to let you know that I have for several months concluded an alliance with 
Austria, which is a common cause with me, and provides me with a contingent of 40,000 men. 

NAPOLEON.

18622. - TO THE PRINCE OF NEUCHATEL AND WAGRAM, 
MAJOR GENERAL OF THE GREAT ARMY, IN PARIS. 
Paris, March 30, 1812. 


Cousin, let Prince Eckmiihl know that I suppose the Russians will be careful not to make 
any movement; that they can not ignore that Prussia, Austria, and probably Sweden are with me; 
that, hostilities recommencing in Turkey, the Turks will make new efforts; that the Sultan 
himself is going to surrender to the army, and that all this seems likely to prevent them from 
braving me easily; that I think that on Ist April the 1st Army Corps, with six divisions of 
infantry, and the Ist Corps of Cavalry will be between Thorn and Danzig, occupying Marienburg 
and Marienwerder, having for vanguard the Prussian corps occupying Pillau. and having 
detachments on their borders; that at the same time the Westphalians, Saxons and Poles will be 
near Warsaw. and the Bavarians at Posen; that the Verdier division and a division of the Guard 
will be at Stettin; that the 3rd Army Corps, with the 2nd Cavalry Corps, will be at Frankfort-on- 
the-Oder; finally that the body of Italy will be at Glogau. If the Busses do not make any 
movement, my intention is to spend the whole month of April, contenting myself with working 
with the greatest activity to raise the head of the bridge of Marienburg and to arm it; to fortify the 
Marienwerder Bridge,”

Page 350 


attaching it to pilots and not just anchors; to have good bridges in Marienburg and Dirschau; to 
establish a good bridgehead at Dirschau on the right bank of the Vistula, on the island of Nogat,

Nehrung, opposite Pillau; to supply Thorn's store; to grind as much flour as possible in Gdansk; 
to prepare boats to embark from 50 to 60,000 quintals of flour; to prepare boats to take on the

The Prince of Eckmiihl will place his reserve park near Dirschau on the island of Nogat.

The prince of Eckmiihl will gradually approach his right Marienwerder, since the corps of

18624. - TO THE PRINCE OF NEUCHATEL AND WAGRAM, 
MAJOR GENERAL OF THE GREAT ARMY, IN PARIS. 
Paris, March 31, 1812, 


My Cousin, the Mainz route to Berlin by Magdeburg is twenty days*”! 





351 


Page 352 


If, from Eisenach, the road was headed by Leipzig and Wittenberg, one would have only 
seventeen days walk and three stays, in all twenty days; it would be three days of spared. These 
two roads must be drawn; the Magdeburg would be too tired, and for all that goes to Berlin, 
Wittenberg's roll seems more suitable. It must however be ascertained whether from Wittenberg 
to Berlin and to Lutterbock the road is practicable, in order to avoid Potsdam. Besides, as there 
are really no roads in this country, there can be little obstacle to pass either to the right or to the 
left of Potsdam; there will be at most a few mending bridges and some hedges to be felled. I 
want you to draw these roads on a map, as well as that of Wesel in Berlin by Magdeburg, that of 
Hamburg to Stettin, that of Mainz to Dresden by Wiirzburg (it is necessary to know if that by

Schneidemiihl, of Berlin at Kiistrin, of Berlin at Frankfurt, of Glogau at Posen, of Dresden, Po 
sen by Glogau, from Dresden to Warsaw by Kalisz, from Dresden to Plock on the Vistula by

18627. - TO MARSHAL BESSIERE, DUKE OF ISTRIA,

18630. - TO THE PRINCE OF NEUCHATEL AND WAGRAM, 
MAJOR GENERAL OF THE GREAT ARMY, IN PARIS. 
Saint Cloud. April 3, 1812. 


My Cousin, my Guard is composed of the division Delaborde, with twelve battalions; of 
the Roguet division, of ten battalions; from the division of the ten battalions of old Guards 
commanded by General Curial, and from a Polish division commanded by General Claparede, 
from nine to ten battalions. I would not be far from forming two commands, one composed of 
the Delaborde division and the Claparede division, which, with some regiments of cavalry and 
artillery, would make a corps of at least 15,000 men, what would the Duke of Treviso command? 
the other, composed of the Roguet division, which is formed of my riflemen and the Ist 
regiments of skirmishers and voltigeurs, and the division of the ten battalions of my old Guard; 
which, with the reserve of artillery, would form a body of real importance, which could be 
commanded by the Duke of Danzig, who has energy on fire, from the experience of war. He 
asked me; know if he asked for it seriously; First, is he in a position to wage war? Chat with him, 
but do not commit me, because I'm not quite decided. 

I also plan to form a 9th corps, which will be composed of the 12th Division, the

18632. - TO THE PRINCE OF NEUCHATEL AND WAGRAM, 
MAJOR GENERAL OF THE GREAT ARMY, IN PARIS. 
St. Cloud, April 3, 1812. 


Cousin, write to Marshal Suchet that I deem it necessary for General Reille to go to 
Aragon to take under his command the command of this interesting province. 

My intention is that General Reille leave under the orders of General Maurice Mathieu 
6,000 men of his troops, namely: a French brigade and an Italian brigade and at least 300 horses, 
and that he goes to Aragon with a French brigade and a Italian brigade. General Reille must also 
leave in Catalonia what belongs to the corps garrisoned in Tarragona, Lerida and Barcelona. All 
Catalonia, except Tortosa and Mequinenza, will be under the orders of General Decaen, so that 
there is more together. 

General Reille, placed at Saragossa, will be able to prevent the evil from growing in the 
Araaon, and he will be able to get along with General Maurice Mathieu and with General 
Caffarelli to pursue the brigands in concert. 

Send to the Duke of Ragusa, that his aide-de-camp will make him known to him, I leave 
him carte blanche; that, given the need to centralize*~° 





356 


Page 357 


the service, I entrusted the King of Spain with the command of the armies of Portugal, the South, 
and Valencia to direct them to one and the same purpose; that the occupation of Asturias is the 
greatest economy of troops that can be made, otherwise the scoundrel will fly on San Sebastian 
and on the rear, and it will employ against it six times more people than to occupy Asturias. 

Send to the King of Spain, in numerical terms, that I entrusted to him the political and 
military direction of all the affairs of Spain; that the army Portugal, which is composed of eight 
divisions of infantry, is in charge of holding a division in Asturias, and, as things stand, needs to 
hold two divisions in the North to contain Galicia and northern Portugal; that it would therefore 
have only five and at most six divisions available to help Badajoz; but that, in this case, he may 
dispose of the division of his guard, of the division of dragoons, which, combined with the forces 
which the Duke of Dalmatia will assemble, will put in the case of defeating the operation of the 
English; that perhaps the Duke of Albufera could threaten Alicante and occupy Murcia; that if 
the Duke of Ragusa has turned to Almeida, a place not yet safe from a hand, and has pushed 
parties in all directions, I consider it unlikely that Lord Wellington exposes to see, in seven or 
eight marches, the French enter Lisbon; but that, if, on the contrary, the Duke of Ragusa remains 
in Salamanca, did not organize the war on the Agueda and let General Wellington take the 
initiative or by default of subsistence or by any other local difficulty, he is obliged to follow the 
initiative of the enemy; then he will be able to assemble, the siege of Badajoz undertaken, five or 
six divisions of the Army of Portugal, what is available to the Army of the Center, and, with the 
Army of the South, to be superior of the double to the English army, for the English have not 
more than 25 to 30,000 men and reunite to the Portuguese more than 50,000 men. There is more 
in Spain today than the English army: either it is necessary to take the initiative on it by 
organizing the defense of Salamanca, having a head of bridge on the Agueda and maintaining the 
war in the north of Portugal, follow the enemy, which would take the initiative on him; or, if it is 
not executed, follow the initiative of the enemy and go wherever he goes; then, without 
contradiction, it is necessary that several divisions of the army of Portugal are carried on the 
Tagus, leaving sufficient forces to Salamanca to fortify this important point and to contain the 
North. 

Besides, it seems that the English have 1,500 men in Cartagena, as much in Alicante, 3 or 
4,000 men in Cadiz,*>’

Page 358 


30,000 men in Portugal, and, moreover, 20 or 25,000 Portuguese under arms, disciplined.

18633. - TO FRANCOIS II, EMPEROR OF AUSTRIA, 
IN VIENNA. 
St. Cloud, April 3, 1812. 


Dear Brother and dear Father, the letter from your Imperial Majesty, which was given to 
me by the Prince of Schwarzenberg, contains the assurances of a friendship which will always 
be precious to me, and that I dare say deserved by that that I myself carry to your Majesty. To 
multiply and make closer the bonds which attach me to her was one of my most lively and 
constant desires; and it is with real satisfaction that I have seen the relations which were between 
us producing analogous relations between our peoples, and establishing between them a union 
which time, far from being able to weaken it, will only increase. In all that can cement it, your 
Majesty will always find me ready to concur with it, as well as to give it on every occasion 
proofs of the sincere attachment and high consideration with which I am, my dear Brother and 
dear Father, Your Majesty, the good Brother and son-in-law. 

NAPOLEON. 

According to the copy comm. by the government of the Emperor of Austria,

St. Cloud, April 8, 1812. 


Count de Cessac, I am responding to your report of April 4th. I see that on 1,400 new 
model carts, ordered,*> a

know, 360 in Antwerp, 80 in Metz, 40 in Strasbourg, 40 in Auxonné, 20 in Delft, 20 in Douai, 10

88 in Paris, 196 in the 10th and 11th military divisions, 680 were provided, 150 are in Mainz,

I want you to have a new caisson model, much lighter than ordinary caisson and designed 
to carry only 20 quintals. However, we should not change the dimensions width and length; as 
far as possible, changes should only consist in lightening the pieces. Then the Sampigny park, 
which still has 140 wagons to go, and the arsenals of marine and land would stop making wagons 
of the old model to make new. There will be three types of wagons: the old model, which is the 
heaviest; the corrected model, which has been lightened from 4 to 5 quintals, and finally the new 
model, which will be lightened more. Henceforth, to agree, it will be necessary to call the 
heaviest model the first model, the model lightened the second model, and the new model the 
third model. 

I ordered that all Italy, either at Turin or at Piacenza, should be sent to Verona, where 
these sails will be used to load all the articles of clothing which the army of Italy must send in 
the course of May. The 150 trolleys that will be available in Mainz will serve the same purpose. 

I see that the 2nd, 9th, 10th and 12th battalions are complete; I see that the 6th battalion 
has only 60 wagons for its first three companies and that 60 are missing: take the 60 that are 
missing from these companies on the 400 of the old model existing at Sampigny; take from this 
number the 200 missing from the 7th battalion; it will therefore use 260 wagons out of the 400 
that exist in Sampigny. Experience alone can prove what should be done in this matter. I am told 
from Italy that we are much more satisfied with the corrected caisson, which I call Model No. 2; 
we will be even more satisfied with the model No. 3, and they offer the advantage of being able 
to better carry the caisson and all kinds of congestion. 

I will have 880 caisson and 680 carts, total 1,560 wagons, and therefore I will be 
complete. I will have more than 100 wagons, models 1 and 2, which will be in Verona and

they men, harnesses, cars or animals? What we need first are the men, then the harnesses, then 
the animals. By driving them high up, I will find wagons everywhere; I will even find horses; but 
they are French drivers, well organized, who will provide me a good service. 

So I would like all these crews to the comtoise and oxen**!

18644. - TO THE PRINCE OF NECCHATEL AND WAGRAM,

My Cousin, the 2nd corps will have its first depot at Kiistrin, Consequently, all the men 
who are lame, sickly or in need of rest, who belong to the 6th, 8th and 9th divisions and the 
brigades of light cavalry attached to the 2nd corps, will be led on Kiistrin. The Duke of Reggio 
will appoint an officer to command this deposit. All the battalions destined for the 2nd corps, as 
soon as they receive orders to leave Magdeburg, will march on Kiistrin. The 3rd Corps deposit

of march on their respective depots. 

The army will have second depots on the Vistula, namely, the Ist Corps at Danzig, the 
2nd Corps at Marienburg, the 3rd Corps, and the 4th at Thorn. But you will first know only what 
is relative to the 1st Corps; for the other Corps, you will wait until they have unmasked their

18646. - TO JEROME NAPOLEON, KING OF WESTPHALIA, 
A KALISZ. 
Saint Cloud. April 10, 1812. 


Brother, I receive your letter by which you inform me that you are leaving and that you 
will have returned to Kalisz on the 12th. If, upon your arrival, there is nothing new, if, having 
established your quota, and having provided for all that is relative to the supply, there is nothing 
to suggest that the Russians are attacking, you could go, very incognito and as if to make a 
military reconnaissance, at Krakow and Sandomir. The local knowledge that one takes oneself is 
always very precious. You can even visit the mines of Wieliczka. If you make this race; which 
has no other purpose than your instruction, try to keep the incognito well, and that you do not 
know that it is only after you have left. You will visit the citadel of Krakow, and you will 
recognize the different situations of the river. You might also have an officer in Warsaw who 
could come to warn you quickly in Krakow if there was anything new, at the same time as he 
would send the order to your contingent to start. By the way, I guess this race will be short. My 
Guard is completely gone. I do not think the Russians make any move. The last news of 
Petersburg, of the 29th of March, showed that they were set in motion, but that they always 
protested that they did not want to attack. 

NAPOLEON.

18647. - TO GENERAL CLARKE, DUKE OF FELTRE, 
MINISTER OF WAR, IN PARIS. 
St. Cloud, April 12, 1812. 


Duke de Feltre, the garrison of the Saint-Marcouf Islands is accustomed to lodge out of 
the tower, some in a blockhouse, the others in barracks. My intention is that you give the most 
precise orders so that from May Ist the commander, the officers, the soldiers, the employees, the 
stores, the artillery, the enginers, all be enclosed in the tower, which will be closed at night, and 
It will open only after the sun has risen and with the usual precautions, so that it is safe from a 
surprise. The tower can be armed with forty pieces of cannon; there are only twenty-two. There 
are, however, in the Saint-Marcouf Islands forty-five guns. Would it not be proper to enclose the 
most liable in the tower? All powders must be in the casemates of the tower. Let me know if it 
would be appropriate to reduce the defense of the island in defense of the tower. This tower can 
not be attacked regularly; she can only be surprised. The buildings and works on Island of Large 
could be razed and the cuttings used to form a glaze that would envelop the tower. This glacis 
would be separated by a wide moat. In this ditch flanks would be obtained by means of 
crenellated and vaulted double caponiers. The counterscarp would be made of dry stones. To the 
east one could establish a covered way. What should we do with the island of Earth? Would not 
a simple little battery be enough, and would it not be appropriate to destroy everything else? 
Give me a report on that. On May Ist have the semaphore established in the tower; it has been 
unreasonably placed in the island of Large. 

NAPOLEON. 

From the original. Deposit of the war.

18652, - TO LORD CASTLEREAG, 
SECRETARY OF STATE FOR FOREIGN AFFAIRS, LONDON (1). 
Paris, April 17, 1812. 


Sir, the Emperor and King, always animated by the same sentiments of moderation and 
peace, wished to make an authentic and solemn step again to put an end to the misfortunes of 
war. The greatness and force of the circumstances in which the world finds itself today determine 
His Majesty; he authorizes me, sir, to speak to you of his disposition and views. 

Many changes have taken place in Europe for the last ten years; they have been the 
necessary consequence of the war which had begun between France and England; many changes 
will happen again, and they will result from the same cause. The peculiar character of the war 
may add to the extent and duration of these results. Exclusive and arbitrary principles can only 
be 





1) This letter was dictated by the Emperor of Bassano.*”! 


371 


Page 372 


an opposition without measure and without term, and the system of preservation and resistance 
must have the same character of universality, perseverance and vigor. 

The peace of Amiens, if it had been maintained, would have prevented many upheavals. I 
renew the wish that the experience of the past is not lost for the future. 

His Majesty has often stopped at the prospect of the most certain triumphs, and has 
turned his gaze away to invoke peace. In 1805, confident as he was of the advantages of his 
position, and some confidence that he owed to omens that fortune was soon to realize, he made 
proposals to the British H.M. government, which were evaded on the ground that the Russia had 
to be consulted. In 1808, new proposals were made, in concert with Russia: England asserted the 
necessity of an intervention which could only be the result of the negotiation itself. 

In 1810, His Majesty, being unable to conceal himself any longer than the decisions of 
the British Council of 1807, made the conduct of the war incompatible with the independence of 
Holland, authorized indirect overtures which also tended to peace. no effect, and new provinces 
had to be united to the Empire. 

The present moment brings together all the circumstances of the various epochs in which 
His Majesty showed the pacific sentiments which she commands me to manifest to-day. 

The calamities which afflict the Peninsula and the vast lands of Spanish America must 
excite the interest of all nations and animate them with equal solicitude to see them cease. 

I will express myself, Sir, in a manner which Your Excellency will find in accordance 
with the frankness of the step I am charged to make, and nothing will show better in it the 
grandeur and loyalty than the precise terms of the language which it I am allowed to hold. In 
what views and for what motives would I form myself in forms which are only suitable for 
weakness, which alone is the interest to deceive? 

The affairs of the Peninsula and the Two Sicilies are the disputes which seem most 
difficult to reconcile; I am authorized to propose that you set it up on the following bases: 

The integrity of Spain would be guaranteed; France would renounce any extension of its 
limits on the side of the Pyrenees; the present dynasty would be declared independent, and Spain 
governed by a national constitution of the Cortes.*”” 





372 


Page 373 


The independence and integrity of Portugal would also be guaranteed, and the House of 
Braganza would reign. 

The kingdom of Naples would remain with the King of Naples. The kingdom of Sicily 
would be guaranteed at the current House of Sicily. 

As a result of these stipulations, Spain, Portugal and Sicily would be evacuated by the 
French and English troops of land and sea. 

As for the other objects of discussion, they can be negotiated on this basis, that each 
power will keep what the other can not take away from it by the war. 

Such, sir, are the bases of conciliation and reconciliation offered to St. Regent Prince 
Regis. 

The Emperor and King calculate, in this step, neither the advantages nor the losses which 
the war, if prolonged for a long time, can presage to his Empire. It is determined by the sole 
consideration of the interests of humanity and the repose of peoples; and, if this fourth attempt is 
to be unsuccessful, like those which preceded it, France will at least have the consolation of 
thinking that the blood which might yet flow will fall entirely upon England. 

The Minister of External Relations, 
DUKE OF BASSANO.

the third store is Marienburg, which I consider a stronghold or at least as safe from a helping 
hand.

18661. - TO THE PRINCE OF NEUCHATEL AND WAGRAM, 
MAJOR GENERAL OF THE GREAT ARMY, IN PARIS. 
Saint Cloud. April 23, 1812. 


My Cousin, you will give the following instructions to the Duke of Bellune. The corps of 
which he will take the command consists of the 12th division or that of General Partouneaux, of 
the 25th division composed of three Polish regiments which were in Andalusia, the 4th, 7th and 
9th; they have now passed Bayonne and are marching for Sedan. That will make a force of more 
than 30,000 men. The 12th Division is running from Wesel on Magdeburg. My intention is to 
unite it at Spandau and Berlin; she will be there in the first half of May. The Daendels division is 
in Mecklenburg, Swedish Pomerania and Stettin. The Polish division can not be in Berlin until 
the end of May. Thus, during the month of May, time necessary for the formation of this corps 
d'armee, it is destined to keep garrison in Berlin and to assure the communications of the army 
and the tranquility of the country. At the beginning of June, three divisions of the reserve, which 
meet at Cologne and Wesel, and which will form about 40,000 men, will take up positions at 
Magdeburg, Berlin, and on the coasts. Then the 9th corps will be*”® 





378 


Page 379 


formed, well organized, and will be on the Vistula to enter online. 

Thus, during the month of May, the Duke of Bellune has no other operation to do than to 
organize his corps to contain Prussia and to supervise the whole country between the Vistula and 
the Rhine. This determined me to decide that he would take his headquarters to Berlin, and to 
place under his command not only the troops of the 9th Corps, but also the garrisons of Stettin, 
Kiistrin, and Glogau, the princely division, whose Ist brigade occupies Hamburg and the second 
Berlin, the Magdeburg garrison and all the remaining troops in the kingdom of Westphalia, as 
well as all the battalions and squadrons of march which will march on Magdeburg and Berlin to 
join the army. 

A precise instruction is necessary for this important mission. It is my intention that the 
Duke de Bellune be returned to Berlin on the 26th or 27th, in order to take this place from the 
Duke of Reggio. You will send him a copy of the treaty made with Prussia, as well as of the 
Convention respecting subsistence, but under the secret, and to put him in a position to 
understand the question. As we advance, we are approaching the war, and we must therefore 
redouble our firmness and vigilance. The Duke of Reggio had only vague instructions to enter 
Berlin; it was then further from the war; but a month has passed since then and brought more 
decisive circumstances. Here are my instructions: 

In accordance with the spirit of the treaty, no general or Prussian officer should command 
Berlin; no Prussian troops must be there; no service should be done there except by order of the 
French general. I entrusted the command of the place of Berlin to General Durutte. He will have 
to scroll through the parade every day, give the password and order the service. The National 
Guard will be able to do the service jointly with my troops. The few men of regular troops who 
have remained in Berlin must be there only for the guard of the palace; still receive the order of 
the French commander. 

Spandau must be considered as the citadel of Berlin. I attach the greatest importance to 
having no worries about this place. It was agreed in the treaty that the King of Prussia would be 
the master of disarming it, and that he would leave there only a company of invalids; but I have 
reserved to occupy it, as well as Pillau, both of them being necessary for the safety of 
communications. I ordered that an artillery company be put in the citadel, and that we would 
use 





379 


Page 380 


stores to contain ammunition. I recommended that one or two battalions should always be 
garrisoned at Spandau, that a commander of arms of the rank of battalion commander should be 
placed there, and that all the battalions or squadrons of march coming from Magdeburg should 
pass by Spaudau, in order to always have 2 or 3,000 men. A brigadier general will be in charge 
of the superior command, and will see to it that the service is done with the greatest exactitude. 
Spandau will be under the orders of Major General Berlin. It will be avoided to keep troops in 
the citadel, except the artillery company I mentioned, until hostilities begin; but at the first shot a 
thousand men will enter the citadel. The Prussian invalids will remain there, the Prussian flag 
will continue to float there. Immediate provision will be made for the formation of a 
headquarters supply for six months; the artillery of the citadel and the place will be supplied, 
and, if necessary, the works in good condition. Up to the moment of the war, one must be 
careful, content to keep the artillery that is there, leave nothing out, admit Prussian troops only 
the company of invalids, and find themselves able to be master of the citadel, without occupying 
it, meanwhile, otherwise than by an artillery company, which will appear to be there only to heal 
the ammunition and prepare artifices. 

One must occupy the arsenal of Berlin, preserving all that is property of the king and 
taking nothing but inventory; but it is important to keep an eye on the fact that there is not in 
Berlin or in the neighborhood any depot of arms, no cannon, which the populace can seize. All 
French stores, both food and war ammunition, must, except for the moment of passage, be 
constantly at Magdeburg, Spandau, and Kustrin. There must be no troops all over Prussia, only 
1,800 men at Potsdam, and 3,000 if the king remains there, 4,000 at Kolberg, 3,000 at Graudenz, 
and 10,000 in Upper Silesia. The command of the Duke of Bellune extends over the part of 
Silesia which we have preserved on Kolberg, all the coast from Kolberg to Hamburg, on 
Pomerania and Mecklenburg, He must receive frequent reports of all these points of the Prussian 
commander of Kolberg and the French officers I established there, of the commander of 
Magdeburg and of the Westphalian Minister of War, in order to be able, in unforeseen cases, to 
know the forces at his disposal and take action depending on the circumstances. The Prussian 
gendarmerie will remain*”” 


380 


Page 381 


alone in the country. No detachment of either Potsdam or Kolberg will be able to enter it except 
at his request. 

You will order the commander of the 32nd Military Division, the Mecklenburg 
Commander, the Prussian commander of Kolberg, and the French officers who have been sent 
there to correspond with the Duke of Bellune, and to instruct him on all matters pertaining to him 
will pass; which must not prevent their ordinary relations with the General Staff. You will write 
in the same sense to the ministers of war of Westphalia and Saxony. 

If a descent took place on the coasts, the Duke de Bellune must be informed of it at once, 
to make all the proper arrangements. You will warn him that the administration of the country 
remains entirely with the agents of the King of Prussia, but that the surveillance of newspapers, 
writings, and all police means must be in his hands, so that nothing gives the people a dangerous 
impulse and that the country has no way to rebel. 

Graudenz's place will be in another system. You will inform the Duke de Bellune that I 
have ordered three or four intelligent officers to enter Kolberg and Graudenz; I reserved the right 
for it by the treaty. You will tell him that it is proper for him to go and see the mouths of the 
Oder, in order to establish batteries where necessary. Part of the Kolberg garrison could be 
established on the coasts to serve concurrently with the French troops; but the real right to keep a 
Prussian garrison is only for Kolberg, as Potsdam is the only city where French troops must not 
pass. 

It is proper, however, to accustom the people of Potsdam to see many French officers, 
and that there are those who often go to sleep there to see the city. If curiosity does not carry 
them enough, it will be necessary to engage them under this pretext. 

The best way to assure the tranquility of Prussia is to put it in the helplessness of making 
a movement, in case a descent comes to take place, or when we lose a battle. 

It seems proper to me that the Duc de Bellune, by accepting a lodging in Berlin, does not 
accept any table and that he represents on the funds which I grant him. His representation must 
be great. It is useless to recommend to him the greatest regard for the princes, the ministers, and 
the principal personages of Berlin, while seizing the police. 

Pry insult to a Frenchman must be judged by a military commission, according to our 
custom. 





381 


Page 382 


The Duke of Bellune will organize his correspondence, as I have just said, with the 
principal officers of his command. The 32nd Military Division is not part of the army for 
administration. The Duke of Bellune must give no order of detail, but be well acquainted with 
the state of things, in order to make the proper arrangements if there were movements to repress 
or descents to repel. 

The Duke of Valmy, who commands the 25th and 26th Military Divisions, will have his 
headquarters in Mainz and Wesel. 

You will give the duke of Bellune a duplicate of the treaty made with the King of 
Denmark, by which it will be learned that this prince must supply a corps of 12,000 men, if 
necessary, to carry either the Zuiderzee or the Oder, and contribute with my troops to repel a 
descent. 

The disposition of the Swedes is not yet known. Meanwhile, the embargo in Pomerania 
and the measures that have been taken must be vigorously implemented. 

The first brigade of the Partouneaux division not being able to reach Magdeburg until the 
8th or 10th of May, it decided me to order the Wurtemberge division to stay in Frankfurt-on-the- 
Oder, and not to go to the Vistula. The Duke de Bellune will only disturb her position in case of 
necessity. Thus, for the first days of May, he will have a brigade of the princely division at 
Berlin; the Daendels division in Mecklenburg, Stettin and Pomerania; the Wiirlemberg division 
at Frankfort-on-the-Oder, and finally the Imperial Guard, which arrives at Dresden. A division of 
the Imperial Guard, commanded by General Roguet, is heading for Berlin; he will arrive there 
around May 15, but only to go there. 

Works have been ordered on the island of Riigen and in Swedish Pomerania. It will take 
the mouths of the Oder. The General of the 32nd Military Division, the Commander of 
Engineering and the Commander of Mecklenburg will be able to make known the main points to 
be fortified on this coast. 

An intelligent warrant officer will be attached to the Berlin government, and will remain 
there when the Duke de Bellune leaves with his corps. 

You will order the Duke de Bellune to communicate this instruction to his successor. It is 
also necessary to organize a police force near the governor general in Berlin, in order to know 
what is going on and to have an eye open on all the activities that might take place. Being thus 
insured of Stettin, Kiistrin, Glogau, Torgau,*” 


382 


Page 383 


Spandau, Saxony, and Magdeburg, with reserve corps, keeping an eye on the fact that there are 
now no arms assemblies, with intelligent officers at Kolberg, and sometimes sending a camp of 
confidence, one will be able to fear nothing of the disloyalty of the Prussians, if, after an 
unfortunate event, they could be excited to go there. 

The French Minister at Berlin, the Count de Saint-Marsan, is a man on whom one can 
count, and who possesses to a high degree the confidence of the Prussians. The governor general 
will have to take care of it and will be able to consult with him safely. The Duke de Bellune will 
in all circumstances have to show the greatest respect for the King and the Prussian Government, 
which must even be carried to the point of assignment in all feasts and circumstances whatever. 

It would be convenient to form a district to the government of Danzig, placing the 
boundary between Danzig and Kolberg. By this means the governor of Danzig would be in a 
position to watch the coast; he could send infantry and cavalry pickets, officers, and receive 
reports. 

Tell me the point at which the command of the Duke of Bellune must finish, and give me 
tomorrow the letter which you will write to the King of Prussia and the Prussian commander at 
Kolberg, as well as the instruction which you will give to the Duke of Bellune according to this 
letter, in which I think I have foreseen everything. 

NAPOLEON. 

From the original. Deposit of the war. 


18662. - TO M. MARET, DUKE DE BASSANO, 
MINISTER OF EXTERNAL RELATIONS, PARIS. 
Saint-Cloud, April 25, 1812, 


Mr. Duke de Bassano, I asked Major General Durutte to order in Berlin. The Marshal 
Duke of Bellune will command all the Prussian provinces; he has already been to Berlin. I have 
made known to you my intention with regard to the places of Spandau and Pillau, which, 
according to the treaty, must be at my disposal, and relative to the places of Kolberg and 
Graudenz, which remain in the hands of the Prussians. I divided the Prussian coast of the Baltic 
into two parts: the first is placed under the supervision of the Duke of Bellune, and the other part, 
that of Danzig, is entrusted to the governor of Danzig, The Prussian governor of Kolberg*®* 





383 


Page 384 


may place on this line all the Prussian posts which he wishes and which he considers useless for 
the defense of his place; but the duke of Bellune and the governor of Danzig may also, as long as 
they have the means, send detachments to do the service concurrently with the Prussians and to 
hear each other; you have to agree. As far as Berlin is concerned, there must be no governor or 
Prussian commander; the service must be done only by the National Guard, in concert with the 
French troops and under the orders of the French commander. Unity is needed in military affairs. 
Moreover, this is in accordance with the treaty. I do not want any complications. There must be 
in Berlin, center of the security of my depots and my rear, only French commanders. You know 
very well that the Prussians had asked nothing for the palace and that it was I who imagined to 
leave them a guard. I desire that the officer who will command there be not of a rank higher than 
that of captain. Write in this direction to M. de Saint-Marsan. 

NAPOLEON. 

From the original. Foreign Affairs Archives. 


18663. - TO M. MARET, DUKE DE BASSANO,

Mr. Duke de Bassano, it is fitting that you speak much to M. de Krusernark of the 
command of the Duke of Bellune at Berlin, of the formation of the 9th corps and that of the 10th, 
which will be of 40,000 men, and which will consist of divisions meeting today in Cologne, 
Wesel, etc. These last troops will arrive on the Elbe towards the beginning of June; the divisions 
of the 9th corps will arrive there in the course of May. In talking with him, it is necessary that 
you give substance to his correspondence by making known to him that the hundred cohorts of 
the national guards are already formed, which will put at my disposal 100 battalions, which were 
retained to keep Holland, Boulogne, Cherbourg, Brittany and our coasts. It is good that you write 
something of this to M. de Saint-Marsan, and that you make him aware of the existence of the 
9th and 10th corps. This language is always useful. Write it also to M. Otto, to M. de Mercy at 
Munich, and finally to your principal correspondents, so that it may serve their language.

18664. - TO M. MARET, DUC DE BASSANO, 
MINISTER OF EXTERNAL RELATIONS, PARIS. 
St. Cloud, April 25, 1812. 


Mr. Duke de Bassano, I suppose you have a consul in Kolberg; However, I never receive 
letters from him. I have informed you that it was my intention that there should be a fixed one. 
This negligence is very fatal. Make sure to have a trusty man, who has a number and who writes 
to you every day. I need to have some at Elbing, Konigsberg, Memel, etc. These positions are 
important because they form an intelligence office and they are a valuable link between the 
inhabitants and the French army. You must also have a safe man in Riga, Libau and all along this 
coast. When they are forced to evacuate the country and return, they must stop at the first French 
headquarters, since the knowledge that these men will have of the country will be very useful to 
us. I need consuls more than ever at Rostock, Wismar, Stralsund, and all the different Danish 
ports, in order to have a very active correspondence on what is happening on the sea side one to 
Allona. These men have to write every day. 

NAPOLEON. 

From the original, Archives of Foreign Affairs. 


18665. - TO THE VICE-AMIRAL COUNT DECRES, 
MINISTER OF THE NAVY, IN PARIS. 
St. Cloud, April 25, 1812. 


Count Decres, I signed the decree on fishing; but does it apply only to the coasts of 
Holland, or does it extend to all the coasts of France and the Mediterranean? It seems to me that 
everywhere we are calling for fishing, because everywhere it is hindered. These claims are so 
interesting from the point of view of the navy in general, especially in terms of a livelihood 
important to a large part of the population, that they deserve all my solicitude. Let me know the 
barriers that exist on all coasts and the steps to take to lift them. 

NAPOLEON.

18666. - TO GENERAL CLARKE, DUKE OF FELTRE, 
MINISTER OF WAR, IN PARIS. 
St. Cloud, April 25, 1812. 


Duke de Feltre, reply to General Molitor, whom I see with pleasure the movement he is 
making to provide for the defense of Holland; that he has nothing to fear at this moment; that the 
English have all their troops in Spain and Portugal; that it is sufficient to keep in the lake of 
Haarlem a single gunboat, so that the officers of the engineers, the artillery; from the staff can 
use this boat, and traverse the lake to learn to know him well; that I attach great importance to 
the completion of the little vaulted guard-house which I have ordered on the lock, so that some 
fifty men who are shut up there may be able to master this important point; that all the 
precautions, besides, are so taken in France, that in a few days he would have 50 or 60,000 men 
advancing to his aid; that he must not take cannon-boats, because they are necessary in the 
Zuiderzee, where the sailors exercise themselves better; that he must ensure that Naarden Fort is 
armed and in good condition; that I wish that, after May 15, he returns to visit forts Lasalle and 
Dugommier, the forts of the island of Texel, the place of Brielle, Hellevoeisluis and the forts of 
the island of Goeree. It is necessary that at the end of May, at the latest, the fort of the island of 
Goeree be armed and in good condition, as well as the forts of Texel and Helder. 

Write to General Chambarlhac that it is necessary that in the last fortnight of May he 
should pass the review of the stores, armaments and defense of the place of Ysendyke, the fort 
Napoleon and the fort Imperial of the island of Cadzand, Walcheren Island, Fort Montebello, 
Fort Saint-Hilaire, Rammekens, Zierikzee and Willemstad; and let him come back to Fort Bath, 
Lillo, and Antwerp. He will report to you every evening what he has seen, both in terms of 
fortifications and siege supplies, and also the situation of the troops. 

NAPOLEON, 

According to the copy. Deposit of the war.

18670. - TO GENERAL CLARKE, DUKE OF FELTRE, 
MINISTER OF WAR, IN PARIS. 
Saint Cloud. April 30, 1812. 


Monsieur le Duke de Feltre, I reply to your letter of the 29th. My intention is that we do 
not send any Spaniards, if he does not commit himself, and I do not hear that we want to send 
them to the battalions of war in the hope that they will arrive there. Your letter makes me choose 
to keep, recruited by Spaniards, only the battalion of sappers, the company of workers and the 
battalion of Walcheren. You will see by my letter of this day that I give a job to the other three 
cadres who are on the Rhine, and who are destined to receive Spaniards. 

However, I do not oppose the fact that you carry up to 1,200 men the battalion of 
Walcheren, taking Spaniards of good will, because if this measure succeeded, I would send 
another cadre. 

NAPOLEON. 

According to the copy. Deposit of the war. 


18671. - TO THE GENERAL LACUEE, COUNT DE CESSAC,

St. Cloud, April 30, 1812. 


Monsieur le Comte de Cessac, I have with interest your report on the caissons. Here is 
how I classified them in my memory. The first**® 





388 


Page 389 


model weighs 2,460 pounds; the second improved model, 2,038 pounds; the ordinary box, 1,900 
pounds. The difference between the ordinary box and the second model is therefore only 138 
pounds, which can not be important. 

You present a third model that weighs only 1,640 pounds, 260 pounds lighter than the 
regular caisson. If this cart can carry 20 quintals, it has many advantages. Order that they be 
made at Sampigny, at Plaisance, and that they should be made a model at Danzig, so that the 
builders and officers who are there will make their observations. But it seems to me that this 
third model has the double advantage of carrying as much as the first in objects of size and 
weigh 800 pounds less, while it can carry more space than the caisson. 

I think that the n° 3 is preferable to the n° 3 bis, since it is lighter, more solid and has the 
same capacity as the n° 2. All that remains to build in carts with Danzig, with Plaisance, with 
Sampigny, or whatever the artillery should provide, have it done on this model. 

Give me the state of what exists in caisson of various models. 

In general, it comes back to me that in Italy we were happy with the second model; we 
will be much more of the third model. 

I want the design of the new model no. 3 to be sent by tomorrow's courier to Danzig. 
General Eble, General Lepin and several artillery officers will form a commission to rectify it. 

NAPOLEON.

18679. - TO GENERAL CLARKE, DUKE OF FELTRE, 
MINISTER OF WAR, IN PARIS. 
Saint-Cloud, May Ist, 1812 


Duke de Feltre, I have read with attention the second part of your report of the 26th of 
this month on the formation of the ten battalions to be fired from the depots employed at the 
Grande Armée. You had forgotten the 29th light, the 10th light, the 36th line, the 44th, the 53rd 
and the 51st. 

The depots of the regiments, having already furnished cadres to the four demi-brigades of 
march, have but one company at the depot, and yet the conduct of the conscripts up to the Grand 
Army would require for the return journey six months, during which time these deposits would 
be depleted. I have therefore decreed that the cadres of the 2nd and 3rd battalions of Belle-Lle, 
who are light infantry, should come to Mainz to receive all the light infantry men whom you 
propose to send to this place; and that the officers of the 2nd battalion of Walcheren, the 4th 
battalion of the Mediterranean, the 3rd and 4th battalion of the Isle of Re, should receive the men 
of the infantry of the line; that the 2nd battalion of Walcheren would receive them at Wesel, the 
Ath of the Mediterranean, at Strasbourg, and the two of the Isle of Re at Mainz. Finally, in the 
table attached to my decree, I have designated the various regiments which will pay in each of 
these six frames; these are the ones you designate in your work to form the first eight battalions 
of march. 

The three companies of the 8th Light and the three of the 18th will continue to form a 
walking battalion. As for the conscripts drawn from the regiments oie 


393 


Page 394 


who are in Italy, it is a battalion which I added to the state of which the cadre of the Ist battalion 
of the 1st regiment of the Mediterranean must receive. 

The 6th battalion of the 37th line was intended to receive refractory conscripts; I first 
gave him the 200 men of the 37th, and then the various remaining conscripts who were not 
sufficient to form a company. 

There will still remain the 5th battalions of the 123rd, 124th, 125th, 126th, 127th, 128th 
and 129th and many others that have been forgotten, such as the 150th, the 3rd, etc .; You will be 
the object of a particular work. As a result of these dispositions, the 3rd Battalion of Belle-Ile

organization of the National Guards, those of the Ist, 2nd, 3rd and 5th battalions of the 2nd 
regiment of the Mediterranean. He must train new cadres, as everywhere else, and direct the four 
battalions of the 2nd regiment of the Mediterranean on Mainz. It will be appropriate, therefore, 
that the remaining conscripts be provided with the means of recruiting these four battalions. 

As all these regiments have no numbers, once they are returned to the army, I will have 
all the men incorporated in their regiments, or, according to the circumstances, I will give 
numbers to these new regiments. 

Meanwhile, the 4th division of the reserve will have five colonels and sixteen beautiful 
battalions which must meet in Strasbourg, Mainz and Wesel. 

NAPOLEON.

18686, - TO THE MOLLIEN COUNTY, MINISTER OF THE PUBLIC TREASURY, IN 
PARIS. 
St. Cloud, May 5, 1812, 


Count Mollien, by my decree of April 5, I made a distribution of funds for the Grande 
Armée. The Intendant General has employed only a part of it, and the funds granted for this 
month must be capable of considerable savings. It seemed to me that it was unnecessarily 
complicating the scriptures to have as many different credits as months. I decided to make a 
monthly distribution each month that includes the previous months; so I make one for the months 
of April and May; the next will include April, May and June; so that the one of December will 
include all the funds which will have been granted for the whole exercise. As a result, each 
decree will report past distributions. So you have to give for both ministries of war and 
administration 22 million and so much for two months. You will be guessing what you sent for 
April, and you will only have to provide the difference. 

NAPOLEON 

According to the original comm. by the Countess Mollien. 


18687. - TO THE PRINCE OF NEUCHATEL AND WAGRAM, 
MAJOR GENERAL OF THE GREAT ARMY, IN PARIS. 
St. Cloud, May 7, 1812. 


Cousin, I see from the letter of Prince Eckmiihl of April 23 that he is in error; he says in 
this letter that we are not asking to occupy Pillau, because, by the treaty, the Prussians must 
occupy it. This is wrong. Why did the prince so prejudge that by the treaty we should not occupy 
Pillau? You will therefore order Prince Eckmiihl that, as soon as the troops are in motion, he will 
have Pillau occupied by a commander and detachments of his corps. The King of Prussia had to 
give orders for that. The prince was also wrong to allow the artillery pieces which the Prussians 
had placed in the Nehrung to be removed; since they were there, they had to be kept. The pieces 
which were at Memel provided sufficient quantities for the works of Lochstedt.*”” 





397 


Page 398 


I see that, by means of the works of the Prussians, this point of the Nehrung is safe; it must be 
fortified again, for this point is very important. It is necessary to place at the end a strong battery 
beating the sea. Make known to Prince Eckmiihl that, without insulting the Prussians, but in a 
natural manner, it will be necessary as soon as possible to take possession of the citadel of Pillau. 
It may be inconvenient to do this as long as the Prussian corps covers Konigsberg, but it should 
be done when we are on the Pregel, so that it would not be offensive to our allies. 

NAPOLEON. 

From the original. Deposit of the war.

Duke de Feltre, make a circular to all the generals commanding the military divisions so

intention is to get as many men and horses away as possible. I have three aims: 1“, To bring 
relief to the army; 2", take advantage of the moment when the heat is less considerable for long 
walks; cae to rid France, and thereby save wheat and food in the months of June, July and 
August, and reduce the expenses of the administration of war, avoiding the consumption of 
fodder, cohorts of national guards can suffice for everything. 

You will charge your bureau of the movement to meet my views by proposing to put in 
motion all the men and horses that remain in France.

11th military divisions, which guard the Pyrenees; and all that belongs to the 15th, 66th, 70th, 
26th, 82nd, 86th and 47th regiments will have to be destined for Bayonne, to form a strong 
reserve. All the rest, after having completed what I have already asked, will be formed in

18692. - TO GENERAL CLARKE, DUKE OF FELTRE, 
MINISTER OF WAR, IN PARIS. 
Saint Cloud. May 8, 1812. 


Duke de Feltre, the eighty-eight cohorts will have eighty-eight companies of artillery; I 
ordered that these companies be sent to the different schools for training. This will give great 
means for the service of the interior and the defense of the coasts. Since nothing belonging to the 
cohorts should leave France, it will be necessary to employ these companies in the custody of the 
frontier posts of the Scheldt, Holland, the coasts of Brittany, the islands of Hyéres and Ré. This 
will make available a large quantity of artillery, which I will call to the army. 

It will be necessary to set in motion, depots of artillery regiments, at the beginning of 
June, about twenty recruits per company, and to train of all these men one or two battalions of 
march, so that one is assured to have replacements for all losses caused by diseases or war. 

Four artillery companies were requested for the rear of the Grand Army, to keep the lines 
of communication. My intention is to place one in Spandau, one in Swedish Pomerania, one at 
Marienburg, and one at Pillau. I believe that I have ordered the management of two of these four 
companies on Wesel and two on Hamburg; the two who are in Wesel will be directed on 
Spandau and Pillau, and the two others who are in Hamburg on Swedish Pomerania and 
Marienburg. These companies will have to be replaced by two new companies for the 32nd 
Military Division and two new companies for the Wesel fort. 

Independently of these four companies, there is a line for Erfurt, which you have already 
designated, which will make five companies for the strongholds of the army; there will be five 
more beyond the Vistula. Thus, under the title of artillery on the rear of the army, there will be 
ten companies, independently of those which are under the title of the places of Oder, Elbe and 
Danzig. 


401 


Page 402 


My intention is for you to direct, as soon as possible, some of the companies that are on 
the island of Elba, the islands of Hyeres and Toulon, to send them to Italy, where I need more 
than artillery companies; but this will only take place when they can be replaced by the six 
companies of the six cohorts who will keep garrison at Toulon. 

The ten companies of the ten cohorts destined for the Pyrenees will be able to provide for 
the defense of Cette and the service of Perpignan and Bayonne; which will still give you 
available line artillery. 

The cohort brigade to guard La Rochelle will be able to supply your six companies to the 
island of Aix, the island of Oleron and the isle de Ré (which will also make several companies 
available), as well as the companies cohorts of Brittany who will keep Brest, Belle-Ile, etc. Make 
a report on this object, which will give me the number and strength of the artillery companies 
that will become available, and what exists at the depots of the different regiments. 

It would be a great pleasure to have a few companies in the course of the summer to 
replace at Modlin, Zamosc, and Thorn the Polish artillery, which I am told to be uneducated. 

NAPOLEON. 

According to the copy. Deposit of the war. 


18693. - TO GENERAL LEBRUN, DUKE OF PLAISANCE, 
AIDE DE CAMP OF THE EMPEROR, IN PARIS. 
Saint Cloud. May 8, 1812. 


Monsieur le Duke de Plaisance, you will leave tomorrow. Meet in Aachen, Cologne and 
Diisseldorf. You will see the situation of the Ist division of the reserve, its dress, the instruction 
of the men, the number of officers which each regiment lacks. Let me know if this division has 
orders to march on Magdeburg. See also the troops of the Grand Duchy of Berg, Let me know 
when the two complete battalions can start, as well as what must leave to complete the other 
corps. 

You will go from there to Wesel. See the situation of the 4th and 5th battalions; number 
and species of men; the desertion that there would have been. See also refractory conscripts. Let 
me know when the 6th battalions of the 37th and 56th, brought to 810 men each, will be able to 
leave for Spandau. Take information on the desertion of the 29th and 4th battalions of the 10th 
Light. Visit the*”” 





402 


Page 403 


ramparts of Wesel, to see if one is arming the place; see also engineering works and anything 
that interests me. Make me a report on each of these places. 

From Wesel, you will go to Cassel; stay there two days. You will see the Queen, my 
minister. You will obtain the exact status of the 5th battalions and cavalry depots, with their 
location, rifles and artillery. You will inform yourself of what there is to fear from the spirit of 
the inhabitants, and you will make known to me what French troops would require to contain 
them if necessary; you will also take information on the situation of the gendarmerie, and if you 
do not, you will inform me of the help that might be offered from the country, supposing the 
descent of the English. 

Go from Kassel to Leipzig and Brunswick. You will stay one day in each of these cities 
to make the same observations. Go everywhere in hospitals; see how many sick Frenchmen there 
are, and if they are well treated there, and give them consolation. Then go to Magdeburg, and 
make me a detailed report on this place, the works of engineering, its weapons, the sale of 
colonial goods, and the amount of rice and brandy and other objects of the army which are there. 

From Magdeburg you will go to Spandau. Spend a day there to see the citadel and all that 
can be interesting. 

You will stay two days in Berlin. See the situation of the troops. Arrange to arrive, if 
possible, to the 20th at Posen. It is in this city that you will send me all your reports, which you 
will take care to number. 

NAPOLEON. 

From the original comm. by the Duke de Plaisance.

18701. - TO GENERAL CLARKE, DUKE OF FELTRE, 
MINISTER OF WAR, IN PARIS. 
Dresden, May 18, 1812, 


Duke de Feltre, I receive the work that was attached to your letter of May 11th. Here are 
my definitive intentions, give orders for their prompt execution. 

The Ist division of the reserve, commanded by General Lagrange, which meets in 
Coblenlz, Diisseldorf and Aachen, will be composed of the Ist demi-brigade of strong march of 
three battalions, the 2nd, 3rd and 4th demi-brigade. marching brigades also of three battalions, 
and the 6th battalions of the 19th, 37th, 56th, 93rd, and 46th, which are at Wesel and Strasburg; 
total, seventeen battalions. You will order that these seventeen battalions go to Magdeburg. You 
will let me know their order of march and the day each of these"? 


406 


Page 407 


battalions will arrive at his destination, so that I give the subsequent orders. These seventeen 
battalions, forming about 14,000 men, will be destined to temporarily hold garrisons at 
Magdeburg, Spandau, and Berlin; which will allow me to have the 9th body. I have nothing to 
change, therefore, to the training proposed in your statement, which, of course, seems to me to be 
correct. 

The 2nd division of the reserve, commanded by General Heudelet, will meet immediately 
at Miinster and Osnabriick. It will consist of the 6th demi - brigade, which will be extended to 
four battalions; the 7th, which is four battalions; from the 8th and 9th, which have four 
battalions; finally, the 17th, which will also be only four battalions. This division will therefore 
be organized in accordance with your state No. 2, except that the 5th battalion of the 17th demi- 
brigade, composed of two companies of the 5th battalion of the 28th, two of the 5th battalion of 
the 43rd and two of the 5th battalion of the 65th, instead of being part of the 17th demi-brigade, 
will form the 4th battalion of the 6th demi-brigade. I wish another change, that the 3rd battalion 
of the 17th demi - brigade be composed of only the six companies of the 4th battalion of the 25th 
light. We will pay for this purpose all that would be available in the 9th light. These five demi - 
brigades will form twenty battalions. Two brigadier generals will be attached to it. You will let 
me know the day each battalion arrives at Osnabruck and Minster, so that I may dispose of it. 
General Heudelet's headquarters will be in Miinster. 

The 3rd division, under the orders of General Merle, will be composed of the 10th demi- 
brigade, strong of four battalions, the strong island of three battalions, the 12th strong of four, 
and the 13th strong of three. I let you know that I approved the training that you propose to me in 
your stalls 1 and 2, with a few exceptions in the latter. I also approve even state n ° 3, except that 
I do not want 113 men of the 8th of line are incorporated in the 50th; and if the 5th battalions of 
the 36th, 51st, and 55th could not furnish the complete cadres of two companies, since already 
these 5th battalions supplied two companies to the demi-brigades of march, you could, before 
their departure from Boulogne, serve you a cadre of the 2nd regiment of the Mediterranean to 
understand these conscripts. For this purpose, this frame would go to Boulogne. 

The 4th Division will be composed of three Battalions of Belle - Ile, three of the Isle of 
Ré, three of the Walcheren Regiment, two of the 1st Regiment of the Mediterranean, and three of 
the 2nd Regiment of the Mediterranean; which makes fourteen battalions. I approve state # fs 


407 


Page 408 


You will take care that the men of the 8th and 18th light embark in Strasbourg for Wesel. The 
37th of the line can not have anything to provide to the 4th battalion of the 2nd regiment of the 
Mediterranean, since it must have to provide to its 6th battalion, independently of the demi- 
brigades of march. I also approve the supplement you want to give to the Ist battalion of the 2nd 
regiment of the Mediterranean, but I can not approve that you place in the 2nd battalion of the 
2nd regiment of the Mediterranean men of the 28th light, with infantry of line: it is absolutely 
necessary to separate the line infantry from the light infantry. My intention is for this 4th 
Division to meet in Spandau and Berlin. The 4th battalion of Belle-Ile, the 2nd of the island of 
Ré, the 4th of Walcheren, the 2nd of the Mediterranean, all four composed of former refractory 
conscripts, have orders to meet at Spandau and Berlin, where they will wait the passage of their 
division. The 2nd and 3rd battalions of Belle-Ile are to be formed at Mainz and Wesel as soon as 
possible. The 3rd and the 4th of the Ile de Ré are formed in Mainz, the 2nd Walcheren which 
forms at Wesel, the 3rd Walcheren to be formed in Strasbourg, where it will be composed of 
Spaniards, Ist of the 1st regiment of the Mediterranean which is formed in Verona, the Ist of the 
2nd of the Mediterranean which will be formed in Mainz, the 2nd of the same regiment which 
will be formed also in Mainz, finally the 4th battalion of the same regiment which will be formed 
in Strasbourg, all these battalions, as and when they are formed, will march, cross the Rhine at 
Wesel, Mainz or Strasbourg, and will be directed to Spandau and Berlin. General Durulle will 
command this division; and as he commands at this moment at Berlin, his division will be 
formed under his very eyes. 

This reserve will therefore consist of four divisions: 

1st division, General Lagrange, seventeen battalions, at Berlin and at Magdeburg; 2nd 
division, General Heudelet, twenty battalions, at Miinster and Osnabriick; 3rd division, General 
Merle, fourteen battalions, first at Utrecht, Boulogne, and Chambery, to be then directed to 
Miinster and Osnabriick, according to the order I will give; 4th Division, General Durutte, 
fourteen battalions, at Berlin; sixty-five battalions, thirty-one in Berlin and thirty-four in Miinster 
and Osnabriick. 

It is evident that the 1st Division will receive the first order to go to the Vistula to be 
incorporated into the respective regiments; which will make executives, who will return to

in the line. My intention is to take 150 per cohort; which will make 12,000 men who will serve to 
complete all these frames. 

I hope that all this will be in motion, and that you will inform me of the arrival times of 
each brigade and battalion, so that I may know when I will be able to dispose of each division, as 
well as the brigade of Erfurt.

18702. - TO THE PRINCE OF NEUCHATEL AND WAGRAM, 
MAJOR GENERAL OF THE GREAT ARMY, IN DRESDEN. 
Dresden. May 20, 1812. 


My Cousin, write to the Duke of Bellune that we must continue to treat the Swedish as 
friends; that consequently the Swedish troops and sailors can remain where they are; but that if, 
before things were decided, there was danger that Pomerania would be attacked, these men 
should be disarmed and sent to the interior. 

Inform the Duke of Bellune of the arrival of General Lagrange's division, composed of 
seventeen battalions, which is marching for Magdeburg. Inform him of the orders I have given 
for the meeting of a brigade at Erfurt and for the arming of the citadel. 

Order Delaborde Division (1st Guard) to leave Stettin and proceed to Danzig. It will be 
able to walk in two columns by the two roads. Instruct Prince Eckmihl with this movement. Let 
him know that I suppose that, independently of the 300 men who will remain at Danzig, there 
must be 1,600 men of the navy and depots of his army, and that the division which arrives there 
will form with all this a sufficient garrison; that, finally, it is up to him to take measures to ensure 
that this important place is never lost, by leaving a French regiment there; that I desire the allied 
troops to serve with the French, to take the pace and the spirit; that, in the course of June, there 
will be at Danzig a march division composed of French battalions, having at heart that this 
important point be occupied by my own troops. 

NAPOLEON. 

From the original. Deposit of the war.

18709. - TO CAPTAIN OF HAUTPOUL 
EMPEROR'S OFFICER OF ORDER, IN WARSAW. 
Dresden. May 21, 1812. 


Captain Hautpoul, you must be back in Warsaw since the 20th; you will have sent me 
your report on Zamosc. I am sending you an instruction on a new mission. You will turn to 
Prince Poniatowski for letters of recommendation. You will ask him for Polish officers to 
accompany you in your recognition, and you will dispatch these officers from the different points 
with your reports. It will be proper that, to avoid giving shade, you should pass for an officer of 
the staff of Prince Poniatowski, and that you should take the Polish uniform accordingly. 

NAPOLEON. 


INSTRUCTION. 

The captain of Hautpoul will proceed from Warsaw to Terespol, and will see as near as 
possible the place of Brzesc; if she is strong, how she is armed, and what resistance she can do. 
He will note well the route of Warsaw to Brzesc, He will take information on the strength of the 
Russians on this side, on what they have in the direction of Slonime, on the right of the marsh of 
Pinsk, towards Lithuania and towards left. 

He will come back on the border to recognize the Bug until Nur. He will note the width 
of the river, the location of the banks, the nature of the road, etc. He will tell Nur what the 
Russians have in Bransk and Bielsk. 

Captain d'Hautpoul will send his reports by an officer to Warsaw, from where they will 
be dispatched to Posen. 

From Nur, he will go to Tykocin, along the Polish border. He will see what the Russians 
have at Bialystok and on this frontier, and will recognize the communication of the wheels with 
Warsaw. He will send a new Tykocin Express to bring his reports to Warsaw. He will come as 
close as possible to Grodno to recognize this place and what is happening there. He will carefully 
observe the various communications with Lyk, with Augustowo, and in different directions. He 
will send from there a new express to Warsaw. He will continue his reconnaissance of the border 
until Olitta, and he will make different excursions that can give him the knowledge of the land 
between Olitta, Narew and Vistula. After which he will return to Posen.*!°

18710. - TO PRINCE BORGHESE, 
GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE DEPARTMENTS ALONG THE ALPS, .A TURIN. 
Dresden. May 21, 1812, 


Cousin, I have been in Dresden for two days with the Empress, with the Emperor and 
Empress of Austria. I intend to stay there a few more days, All my army is on the Vistula. There 
is nothing new yet. Hostilities are not started; 

Having just learned that English ships are in front of Savona, I think it is necessary to put 
the Pope in safety. As a result, you will instruct the prefect and the commander of the 
gendarmerie to send the Pope with his senses in two good wagons. The Pope will have his doctor 
in his wagon. The precautions will be taken so that it crosses Turin by night, that it stops only 
with the mount Cenis, that it crosses Chambéry and Lyon by night, and that it is thus taken to 
Fontainebleau, where the orders are given to receive it. I am referring to your prudence and that 
of the commander of the gendarmerie. Take care that the Pope's wagon is good and that*!” 





417 


Page 418 


all the proper precautions are taken. The Pope must not travel in pontifical clothes, but only in 
ecclesiastical clothes, and so that nowhere on the road, except at Mount Cenis, can he be 
recognized. Unless there is an event, this measure is not so urgent that you can not send for the 
Prefect of Montenotte to arrange with him in advance this departure. 

You will send the attached letter to the Duke of Lodi. I write to him to send you to Turin 
the Archbishop of Edessa. When this Archbishop arrives at Turin, you will inform him of my bet 
that you have a mission to confide to him, and as soon as you learn that the Pope will be at a post 
beyond Turin, you will rejoin him. He will get into the Pope's car and accompany him for the 
rest of the way. You will make known to this prelate that the situation of affairs in Europe and 
the presence of the English before Savona made the Pope's residence dangerous in that city; that 
he must be placed in the center of the Empire; that he will be received at Fontainebleau by the 
bishops of the deputation; that he will occupy the dwelling he has already lived in; that he will 
see the cardinals who are in France, & c. 

You will correspond for the execution of these measures with the Minister of Police. I 
want the greatest secret to be kept. 

NAPOLEON 

From the original comm. by the Marquis Gozani di San Giorgio.

18716. - TO GENERAL CLARKE, DUKE OF FELTRE, 
MINISTER OF WAR, IN PARIS. 
Dresden, May 23, 1812. 


Duke de Feltre, make known to the Grand Duchess that the enemy intends to attack the 
island of Elba, and that it send Prince Felix to inspect the garrison of this island, his means of 
defense, its stores, etc. 

The 7th battalion of the 6th of the line, that of the 14e light, the 3rd battalion of the 
Mediterranean, the Italian colonial battalion, form four battalions worth 3,000 men; which, with 
the two companies of artillery, the two coast-guard companies and the battalion of the island of 
Elba, forms a garrison of 4,000 men. A good commander of arms at Porto Ferrajo, a chief of 
artillery battalion, a superior engineer and a good general to command the island are needed. I 
suppose the stores are safe from the bomb, and the place is stocked with all that is needed. 

Let me know the situation of the 112th Regiment. He must have present five battalions 
and more than 4,000 men under arms; Are these men dressed, equipped, armed and able to walk? 

Tell the Grand Duchess that if the enemy attacked either Rome, Ancona, Venice, Naples 
or Genoa, the foreign battalion at Livorno, the 112th regiment, and the cohorts of National 
Guards of Tuscany , forming a corps of 6,000 men, must, under the command of a brigadier 
general, 





420 


Page 421 


with six pieces of cannon hitched on the spot by extraordinary means of the country, to set in 
motion on the point threatened. 

Instruct General Miollis, General Vianolle Commander in Italy, and Prince Borghese 
Commander in Piedmont. 

General Miollis has three battalions of the 6th line, three battalions of the 14th light, the 
2nd battalion of foreign soldiers, and the cohort of national guards of Rome, in all eight 
battalions, which would form a division of 8,000 men. General Miollis would at once organize 
twelve pieces of cannon, which he would have served by the line artillery which he had at Home, 
and this column would be carried either to Rome, or to Livorno, or to Naples, or on Ancona, or 
on Venice, if these points were attacked. It is necessary that the battalions of the 6th line and the 
14th light be worn in full. Inform her of the Grand Duchess, Marshal Perignon, the commanding 
general in Italy, and Prince Borghese. 

Prince Borghese will have the 14th temporary demi-brigade strong of four battalions, the 
15th strong of four battalions, the 4th cohort of national guards forming four battalions, the four 
battalions of the 52nd; which would make sixteen battalions or two divisions, each of 6,000 men, 
each of whom would be attached to eight pieces of cannon harnessed by the means of the 
country. These divisions would be, according to the circumstances, or on Rome, or on Venice, or 
on Ancona, on Genoa, on Nice, or even on Toulon. It is, therefore, necessary that the Grand 
Duchess, General Miollis, Marshal Perignon, and the Commanding General in Italy be 
forewarned of these provisions. 

The commanding general in Italy happens to have, by the dispositions I have taken, three 
divisions forming 18,000 men, namely, one on the Adige, one on the side of Ancona, and one on 
the side of Milan, which would also be on the Illyrian provinces with infantry, cavalry and 
artillery. 

Thus, in Italy, there are the forces of General Grenier, with 8,000 infantrymen, 500 
Neapolitan horses, fourteen Neapolitan artillery pieces, and ten regimental pieces; the division of 
Rome, with 9,000 men and twelve pieces of cannon; the division of Tuscany, with 6,000 men 
and six pieces of cannon; the three divisions of the kingdom of Italy, with 18,000 men and 1,500 
horses; the two divisions of Piedmont, 12,000 strong, 1,200 horses, and twelve pieces of cannon. 

These corps will thus form a force of 50,000 men of infantry and of 3,000 horses and 
eighty-four pieces of cannon, independently of the Neapolitan army, 40,000 strong men.”

infantry, 4,000 horses, and seventy pieces of cannon. 

You see, therefore, that we could go with nearly 100,000 men on a point that would be 
threatened, not to mention what could be drawn from Geneva and the 7th military division. It is 
necessary that you give me a work in order on this subject, after having concerted with General 
Miollis, General Vignolle, the Grand Duchess, Prince Borghese, Marshal Perignon and General 
Bertrand. 

General Bertrand, in the event of an attack on Venice, could furnish a column of 2 or 
3,000 men, which would support the Piave. It would be necessary that the King of Bavaria be 
warned by General Vignolle, he would not fail to send 3 or 4,000 men by Trent. 

If, on the other hand, the Tyrol rebelled, General Bertrand would send to Lienz 2 or 3,000 
men, General Vignolle would send 8,000 to 9,000 men to Trent, the Bavarians would send a 
dozen thousand men through Salzburg; which would make nearly 24,000 men, who would be 
quickly reunited in the Tyrol. 

What seems to me to be wanting in Italy are French artillery companies; there are no 
Palmanova, Mantua or Venice; we must inform the means of sending. 

The 4th Battalion of the 8th Light is at Zara; this battalion has 200 patients, so that it has 
only 550 men present. Get a company of 150 men from Geneva to complete it. 

I have approved that you should make Illyria the 3rd battalion of the 23rd of the line, 
which will form four French battalions or 3,000 men in the Illyrian provinces; the fourth Italian 
light there are three battalions; which makes seven. There will therefore be in the Illyrian 
provinces, independently of the Croats, seven battalions of the line. 

Send General Miollis to make Gier, as and when he can, all he can on the 4th Italian 
Light, so that this regiment has a strength of 2,400 men. 

There are in Illyria two companies of Italian artillery, which are only 60 men; Ask 
General Vignolle to complete them to 120 men. The two French artillery companies are 
complete with 120 men. 

I would not be far from passing Trieste the 4th Battalion of the 3rd Light, which is at 
Parma, as soon as the cohorts of National Guards of the 28th Military Division are formed. 

The 5th battalion of the 10th of the line, which is at Placentia, must receive men and be of 
real utility soon.”

I believe that General Bertrand must always hold in the Tyrol, on the side of Lienz, a

There are still in the 27th and 28th military divisions the 4th battalion of the 7th, which is

18717. - TO GENERAL CLARKE, DUKE OF FELTRE, 
MINISTER OF WAR, IN PARIS. 
Dresden, May 23, 1812. 


Duke de Feltre, write to Marshal Perignon, who commands at Naples, that it is almost 
certain that he will be attacked before the end of the summer; that it is necessary, therefore, that 
the cavalry should be actively engaged in organizing cavalry, arranging light and foot artillery 
batteries, recruiting cadres, and training new ones; that I think it is indispensable that there 
should be in the kingdom of Naples 50,000 men and 4,000 horses, and sixty to seventy: pieces of 
cannon; that General Grenier's corps is included in this strength; that to have sixty to ten or 
eighty pieces of drawn cannon, it requires more than 300 wagons, which requires 1,500 to 2,000 
horses of the train; that it is necessary that there be two spare batteries of pieces of 12 and 
howitzers; that it will be only the great activity which the queen will put in her armaments and 
the aspect of the respectable state of defense where the kingdom will be placed which will 
impose on the enemy; that I would desire that 500 Neapolitan horses and two batteries, one on 
horseback of six pieces and the other on foot of eight pieces, forming fourteen pieces of cannon, 
should be joined to the corps of General Grenier; that it is my intention that General Grenier 
should remain in his present cantonments and in healthy places, ready, according to events, to go 
to Home, to Ancona, or to Florence. Write the same thing to General Grenier. 

NAPOLEON.
