18720. - TO THE PRINCE OF NEUCHATEL AND WAGRAM, 
MAJOR GENERAL OF THE GREAT ARMY IN DRESDEN. 
Dresden, May 23, 1812. 


Cousin, write to General Rapp that you have put before me the letter of May 9th; that I 
saw there vessels of three kinds; that those of the first species only go from Konigsberg or Elbing 
to Pillau and from there to the Baltic (it seems that these vessels are numerous, but General Rapp 
does not make known what exists in Konigsberg), that those of the second kind are fifty-four; 
that these are vessels which make the navigation of Frische Haff, but which they can not reach, 
as far as Danzig; that finally the vessels of the third kind are those which can sail, from 
Konigsberg to Danzig; that their number is only forty-two, which can go without unloading from 
Danzig to Konigsberg, and that these forty-two vessels can not*”° 


425 


Page 426 


carry together only 30,000 quintals. General Rapp does not make known the tonnage of the fifty- 
four vessels of the second kind, nor how much this number of vessels could carry; but in general 
it must be a small thing, and even if these vessels bear 60,000, that would be very unsatisfactory. 
It is true that the number of vessels of the first kind is not determined; if there are many, it should 
be stopped as many as possible; and, as there must be sufficient vessels in the Vistula to go from 
Danzig to Elbing, the service thus shared could always be done. Whenever we have boats of the 
third kind that can go from Danzig to Konigsberg, we would prefer them. When we do not have 
one, we would first load on boats from the Vistula, which would transport to Elbing, and there 
the cargo would pass on boats of the second and even the first kind. Lastly, it is necessary to 
have sufficient boats to transport two or three hundred thousand Danzig to Koenigsberg, either 
by breaking the load at Elbing or without breaking the charge. It is my intention, therefore, that 
General Rapp assemble in council the two cons-admirals, engineers, and the principal boatmen 
of the country, and that he should take their advice on the following questions: 

How many vessels are there to go from Danzig to Konigsberg? how much do they wear? 
could we increase the number? are there in Danzig any vessels which, with a slight reparation, 
could be made fit for this service, so that the transport of Danzig to Koenigsberg could be 
effected without breaking the load at Elbing? How many boats are there to go from Danzig to 
Elbing? how much can they wear? how many days do they need to go back and forth? How 
many boats can go from Elbing to Konigsberg? and how many days does it take for this trip? Is it 
advisable to repair the lighters at Danzig and send them empty to Elbing to increase the transport 
from Elbing to Konigsberg? or are there enough already? 

I should also get information on this other question: What vessels could go from 
Konigsberg to the Niemen and up the river? what should their dimensions be? Do they have 
locks to cross? I guess there will be enough of these boats. 

It is of the utmost importance that the boats do not fail and that this navigation is done 
under the direction of the naval officers. Rear-Admiral Dumanoir will be responsible for all the 
details of the service from Danzig to Konigsberg. Rear Admiral Baste*”° 


426 


Page. 427 


will be placed at Konigsberg and will be in charge of the same service in Frische-Haff and in all 
the communication channels of Konigsberg at Niemen. It is necessary that these two cons- 
admirals concert the organization of their service and report it to you. They must have naval 
officers everywhere, and seamen placed on all the vessels should shelter us from the bad will of 
the boatmen of the country. You will send a copy of my letter to the Intendant General. You will 
also send him to Prince Eckmiihl, who, being on the spot, will be able to take information from 
his side. 

Three highway engineers arrive from Russia. I gave an order to detain them; they will be 
attached to this service. It is necessary that you have at the general district a naval officer to 
follow the correspondence and the details of this service.

My cousin, you will let General Heudelet know that my intention is to have his 
headquarters at Miinster and to correspond with the commander of the 32nd Military Division, 
with that of Mecklenburg, with the governor of Mecklenburg, with the general commanding the 
31st division, with the commander of the 17th division and with the minister of war of the 
kingdom of Westphalia; he will be under the orders of the Duke of Bellune, who is at Berlin, and 
commands all my troops between the Rhine and the Vistula. General Heudelet has under his 
command the 2nd division of the reserve, composed of the 6th demi-brigade, strong of 4 
battalions; of the 7th demi-brigade, strong of 4 battalions; the 8th demi-brigade, strong of 4 
battalions; the 9th demi-brigade, strong of 4 battalions; of the 17th demi-brigade, strong of 4 
battalions; total, 20 battalions. He also has under his command the brigade which meets at Erfurt 
and is composed of six battalions; which makes a total of 26 battalions. My intention is that he 
send the 7th demi-brigade without delay to garrison Hamburg; the 6th to garrison in 
Mecklenburg: the 8th to garrison Bremen; the 9th to garrison at Miinster, and the 17th at 
Osnabruck, that these troops should serve the coast only in case of extraordinary events; that they 
must be kept together in the cities, to facilitate their formation*”’

18723. - TO GENERAL CLARKE, DUKE OF FELTRE, 
MINISTER OF WAR, IN PARIS. 
Dresden, May 26, 1812. 


Duke de Feltre, I reply to your letter of the 18th, by which you account for the 
recruitment of cohorts of National Guards; but you do not make me forget to read the brigade 
generals whom you have charged with the command of each brigade, which is very important, 
since each brigade must have a chief who presides over his organization, which corresponds with 
you for the vacant places, and who takes care of his instruction. 

Take care that the brigade composed of the 55th, 56th, 57th, 58th, and the 18th and 19th 
cohorts, that; must meet in Utrecht, be divided between Utrecht, Arnheim and Nijmegen; that it 
be placed in healthy places; that it does not do any service on the coasts under any pretext 
whatsoever, unless a landing of enemies; otherwise, these six cohorts, composed of men born in 
the heart of France, will be reduced to nothing. 

Cohorts composed of Belgians, belonging to the 3rd brigade, must serve the coast and 
unhealthy places, as acclimatized. The cohort composed of old Frenchmen must not be placed in 
these parts; it must be placed in Bruges and even in Ghent. It is necessary to place in Ostende, 
which is an unhealthy country, the Belgian cohort. If the institutions can not contain the cohorts 
that will not be placed on the island of Cadzand, we can put two**” 





430 


Page 431 


in Ghent. The commander of the brigade will reside in Bruges, where he will be able to move the 
different cohorts according to the events. One could even dispense with sending cohorts to 
Cudzand before November, and leave the Scheldt cohort, which would be abolished only in 
November. 

The brigade of five cohorts which is organized at Lille, which is to keep garrison at 
Mechlin, must extend to Brussels and occupy only the healthy places. I do not like to see cohort 
in Breda, Brussels, on the contrary, is healthy. It is sufficient if the general who commands these 
five cohorts resides in Mechelen and is authorized to unite them at the slightest movement; they 
will have more latitude and will benefit from existing institutions. The surroundings of Brussels, 
Mechelen, Louvain, Antwerp, the beautiful village of Saint-Nicolas, can very well contain the 
brigade of Lille and that of Besancon. 

I wish you to give me a picture of the formation of the brigades, the generals designated 
for the brigades, and the place occupied by each. 

Attach it to the spirit of the order I dictated, and depart from the letter. One or two days 
apart are nothing when it comes to the health of the troops; healthy countries first and foremost. 
What is the use of sick men, who can not do anything when the enemy presents himself? 

I recommend especially the cohorts of J'ancienne France, which I manage on Antwerp 
and Utrecht. Go into the smallest details, and seriously take care of placing them in extremely 
healthy countries.

18725. - TO MARSHAL DAVOUT, PRINCE OF ECKMUHL, 
COMMANDING THE Ist CORPS OF THE GREAT ARMY, AT ELBING. 
Dresden, May 26, 1812. 


My Cousin, the Major General, has made known to you my intentions for the movement 
of your army corps. Everything is subordinated to the arrival of the deck crew, because all my 
campaign plan is based on the existence of this well-braced deck crew as mobile as a piece of 
cannon. I gave orders that he had arrived on the Ist at Elbing; I hope that it will be at least on the 
3rd. I suppose that the siege crew will also have arrived at Elbing and embarked on vessels 
suitable for Frische-Haff navigation. The powders and everything must be there, but it is less ina 
hurry than the deck crew; if, therefore, this crew needed a few hundred horses and could not be 
obtained from Nogat Island, I would prefer a few wagons of your second supply to remain 
unhitched. I can not recommend that you take the most effective measures to keep as little 
baggage as possible, and that all the clothes, shoes and saddles that the corps have with them 
should be sent to Marienburg and Danzig, so that all caissons can be used and loaded with flours, 
bread, rice, vegetables and spirits, except what is necessary for ambulances. The result of all my 
movements will bring together 400,000 men on one point; there will be nothing then to hope for 
the country, and it will have everything to have with you. Luggage left behind can be returned 
after the first shipment. 

The pass of Pillau is only 600 toises in width; batteries set up on both sides will cross 
their balls at 300 fathoms, and, by adding some mortars and howitzers, not one boat will pass. 
Booming ideas are ridiculous; it would be more convenient to build at Pillau three or four 
buildings forming gunboats and able to lend the flank to a frigate and go to sea. I will see that 
when I am at Danzig. I will arrive on the 29th at Posen, the 31st at Thorn, the 2nd at Marienburg, 
and the 3rd at Danzig. Do not say anything about it; it's only for you alone. As soon as I saw 
Danzig and** 





432 


Page 433 


that I will be assured of important things, I intend to enter the field, and the army will move 
everywhere. You have badly enough alarmed Prussia for Pillau. It's simple. We must first detach 
the Prussian corps. I intend to form a 10th corps of the Prussians and of the 7th Division, and to 
give the command to the Duke of Taranto. 

It will be difficult for me to see the bodies in detail, other than on the battlefield and in 
the lost moments. However, prepare the replacement statements, including the service records of 
each officer, so that I can finish the job in a moment. The way I see the corps is too tiring and 
takes too much time, I will be able to see them in the lost moments. 

I have here the Emperor of Austria, the Empress, the King of Prussia, the Prince Royal, 
many princes, and many people. 

The Ist Austrian Army Corps, commanded by the Prince of Schwarzenberg, meets at 
Lemberg and goes on the march. He is 35,000 strong. I guess all your furnace builders are at the 
forefront. Those of the Duke of Reggio have orders to establish a handling at Guttstadt; those of 
the Duke of Elchingen at Osterode; those of the viceroy at Willenberg, and those of the 5th corps 
at Pultusk and Ostrolenka. Tighten your light cavalry on your left, since that of the 2nd corps 
occupies Guttstadt. 

NAPOLEON. 

From the original comm. by the Marechal Princess Eckmiihl. 


18726. - TO EUGENE NAPOLEON, VICE-KING OF ITALY, 
COMMANDING THE 4th AND 6th CORPS OF THE BIG ARMY, PLOCK. 
Dresden, May 26, 1812, 


My Son, the Major General, will have made known to you the movement which you must 
execute to your army corps, which must be formed in three columns. You must have, on the 6th, 
your headquarters at Soldau, you will not stay there long, my intention being to open the 
campaign without delay. I'll be on the 30th at Posen. I wish to know by one of your officers that 
you will send me there the situation of your army corps. General Poniatowski will occupy 
Modlin and be on your right at Sierock and Pultusk; the Duke of Elchingen, on his left, will have 
his headquarters at Osterode, occupy Allenstein and Hohenstein, and join with your light cavalry. 
It is possible that from the 7th to the 8th I give you orders to march on Rastenburg, Loeitz, & c. 
Let the geographers know the roads*** 





433 


Page 434 


in the direction of Ortelsburg, Sensburg, L6tzen, Rhein, Arys and even Johaunisburg, Push the 
most, food you can on Willenberg. Place on your left the French, that is to say the 4th corps, the 
Bavarians on the right. Find out if you can find some resources near Rastenburg. You must have 
with you for twenty days of food, and your convoys quickly go in the direction of Plock, 
Ulyszogrod, Lipno and even Thorn. I do not speak of cavalry, it will be able to subsist. At this 
moment we find new fodder. You will keep the secret on this later movement. Make believe, on 
the contrary, that you will march on Warsaw. My headquarters will be at 1 June in Thorn and 
immediately after at Osterode. 

I suppose that you have grinded the wheat with the greatest activity, and that from 10,000 
quintals you have increased your flour supplies to 20,000 quintals. The whole army will 
eventually be reunited on the same field; every corps huddled together will soon exhaust the 
resources of the country: only the grass will remain. Have oxen, brandy, pulses, rice, etc .; do not 
wear clothing or harness; take it all to Plock and put a good officer to drive it. Decrease the load 
of your vans, it will be necessary for the transport of the biscuit; besides, we must expect to be 
harassed by the Cossacks. Send Willenberg ahead of time, have a nice seven to eight furnace 
built there. Once the movement begins, your communication route will be through Thorn, for 
both the 6th and the 4th corps. I will raise Plock's bridge as soon as it is deemed useless. Take 
effective means to gather at Willenberg all you can from flour, wheat, cattle, & c. Always have a 
company of builders of ovens, bakers, sappers, etc., to establish your handling before your 
arrival in Rastenburg and other places where you must take a stand. 

Has your oxen transport battalion arrived, as well as General Guyon's Corps? Are the 
troops incorporated? The cadres of the 5th battalions must be sent back to Italy. 

NAPOLEON.

18727. - TO JEROME NAPOLEON, KING OF WESTPHALIA, 
COMMANDING THE Sth, 7th AND 8th COPRS OF THE GREAT ARMY IN WARSAW. 
Dresden. May 26, 1812. 


My Brother, the Major General has made known to you my intentions for the movement 
to be carried out, from the 5th to the 6th of June, by the 5th, 7th and 8th Corps. The Intendant 
General has given orders for the re-establishment of the handling of Pultusk, Ostrolenka and 
Przasnycz, and to make flour on Pultusk, Makow, Przasnyez, Ostrolenka and Praga. 

The commander of the engineers will have given orders to bridge Pultusk, to raise the 
bridgehead, to arm it and restore the batteries which, from the right bank, defend the left, to 
restore the bridgeheads and the redoubts which had been established at the intersection of Narew 
and Bug. 

It is necessary that you establish on the Bug a bridge to communicate easily in the 
peninsula. This bridge should be as close as possible to Praga, at a point, however, where 
communication with Pultusk is not hampered by swamps and easy. 

It is essential that your movement be done in such a way that the advanced cavalry posts 
are not disturbed, and that what is in front of the enemy remains in its positions, because the war 
is not declared so as to prevent communication on enemy borders. The Grand Duchy must have 
customs which have orders to leave nothing of the Grand Duchy in Russia, receiving all that 
would happen. 

Hold a staff officer vis-a-vis Brzesc at the outlets. The bridges on the Narew and the Bug 
must be such that the bodies can easily communicate with each other. I recommend you the 
bridgehead of Pultusk and Sierock on the Narew and the Bug, because it would be possible that, 
in a second movement, I leave the master enemy of the country since the glacis of Praga, 
contenting myself with to preserve Praga, Modlin, the left bank of the Vistula, and the right bank 
of the Narew, from Modlin to Sierock, and thence, according to the circumstances, I would also 
abandon the peninsula and hold myself at the right bank of the Narew to Hozan and Ostrolenka; 
or I'll keep Bug from Sierock to Brok. It is, therefore, fitting that the bridge which you will 
establish on the peninsula should be as near as possible to Sierock. As for the Sierock Bridge, as 
it is supplemented by that of Modlin, one could be content with the Bug Bridge and the Pultusk 
Bridge over the Narew, and remove the Sierock Bridge.**° 





435 


Page 436 


(if it became necessary and of no value) located at Nieporent, that is, placed on both banks 
together. 

It will be fitting that after making your arrangements you go to Sierock, Pultusk, 
Ostrolenka, the banks of the Omulew, and that you come to Brok. Leaks recognize the small 
river Liwiec, which could serve as an outpost in case the outposts were too close to the Bug. 

Order Lublin 100,000 rations of biscuit bread, and spread the noise of your arrival on this 
side with 100,000 men. You must make all the demonstrations to make believe that you will 
meet with the Austrians with 100,000 men; but the truth is that your movement will be reversed, 
which I confide to you only for you alone, and what I desire you to keep very secret, without 
even communicating it to your chief of staff. 

The 4th Cavalry Corps, which is to carry its headquarters to one or two Praga marches, 
may push light cavalry to the Bug to observe the enemy's movements. It is necessary that the big 
cavalry does not exceed the Liwiec. This corps will always be able to maneuver according to my 
general projects and to approach the Bug and the Narew, if I judge it suitable. Place General 
Latour-Maubourg's headquarters near Stanislawow, where he will be able to watch the path of 
Brzesc. 

Let me know how many pontoons you have to your three corps. Have with you twenty 
days of provisions in biscuit and biscuit bread, flour, dirty touching the general stores. 

It is possible that on the 6th of June I begin warlike movements, without, however, being 
at war, since I have six or eight days' march on the territory of Prussia or the Grand Duchy. 

The bread which you will have made at Lublin, for your pretended movement on this 
point, may be of use to the Austrian corps, which I will probably have to tighten to my right. 
Maneuver and place your positions of light cavalry as if you were going to Volhynia. Send spies 
on this side, and have your accommodation prepared in Lublin, 

No one should be in your confidence, not even your Chief of Staff. 

NAPOLEON

18728. -NOTE 
FOR THE MINISTER OF EXTERNAL RELATIONS, IN DRESDEN. 
Dresden, May 27, 1812. 


The Duke of Bassano will discuss this note with the Chancellor (1). He will make him 
understand that, as a politician, I trust Prussia, and that it would be absurd not to trust it; but that, 
as a soldier, I can not leave the places of Pillau and Spandau in other hands than mine, and that I 
must be master to change the garrison every day and whenever I judge it fit; that my first feeling 
had been to ask for the surrender of these places by the treaty, but that it would have been a 
dishonorable clause for Prussia; that the two places are besides very little, and that I find that the 
bias which I took is the most suitable; that there is one simple thing to do for Pillau, is that the 
king increases his army of the 2,000 men of the garrison of that place; that then, this place being 
without garrison, when we advance forward, I will put in it the one which will suit; that these 
2,000 men will please General Grawert and the whole Prussian army, who will prefer to be a 
little stronger than a little weaker, and that this arrangement will remove all difficulty; that, as to 
Kolberg's place, it is necessary that the general who commands there, independently of the 
garrison necessary for the defense of that place which is to remain in his precincts, should have 
at his disposal mobile columns with artillery for to enlighten the country and oppose a landing, 
yielding only to major forces and withdrawing to Kolberg fort. 

NAPOLEON. 

From the original. Foreign Affairs Archives. 


18729. - TO GENERAL CLARKE, DUKE OF FELTRE, 
MINISTER OF WAR, IN PARIS. 
Dresden, May 27, 1812. 


Duke de Feltre, there are in the kingdom of Italy more than 30,000 men of infantry and 
2,000 horses. 

The first active division commanded by General Fresia, whose headquarters are at 
Treviso, is composed of two brigades, namely: General Schill's brigade, composed of four 
battalions of the 13th of the line, strong of 3,000 men, and two gun, placed at Udine; and General 
Zucchi's brigade, consisting of four 





1) M. de Hardenberg, Chancellor of Prussia.*°” 


437 


Page 438 


battalions of the 5th of the Italian line, a battalion of the 1st of the line, and a battalion of the 7th 
of the Italian line, which makes six battalions or 4,000 men, placed at Padua. This division, with 
the 3rd Italian artillery company, 160 horses of the train hitching six pieces of cannon, and the 
Ath regiment of Italian hunters, 600 horses strong, presents a force of 8,000 men. Warn of the 
existence of this division General Bertrand, so that, if Trieste was threatened, this division could 
be brought to his aid. Order at the same time that a squadron of the 4th Italian fighter be placed 
closer to Trieste. 

With these provisions, Trieste and Illyria have nothing to fear. It is important that General 
Bertrand and the generals who command this division get on well together, so as not to wait for 
orders from Milan. 

The 2nd active division commanded by General Barbou is composed of a brigade, 
consisting of a battalion of the 4th Italian regiment, a battalion of the 6th, a squadron of the Ist 
Italian fighter and a squadron of the Napoleon dragoons. The 4th battalion of the 6th Italian is at 
Sinigaglia. Let General Barbou master leave him there, or even put him in Mantua, if he deems it 
necessary. 

The 2nd Brigade of the 2nd Active Division is composed of two battalions of the 112th 
which the Grand Duchess sends to Bologna, whence they will be ready to go to Ancona or to 
such other part of Italy as might be threatened. 

This division must be able to go to Rome, Venice, Ancona or Genoa, depending on the 
circumstances. 

Independently of these forces, the places have their garrison; Palmanova has 1,500 men; 
Venice, 4,200; Legnago, 700; Mantua, 3,000 men, etc. 

Trieste seems to me much too bald, since two French battalions and the three Italian 
battalions are in Dalmatia and Ragusa. It would be good to have a French battalion in Trieste. 
Before the 23rd league has arrived, which may be long, order General Schill to send a French 
battalion of the 13th line; which, joined to the squadron of the 4th chasseurs, which will be 
placed on Isonzo, and to the Croats, will place this place safe from any insult. Also send to 
Trieste two French artillery companies of the 3rd regiment, each of 120 strong, to assure this 
important point. 

NAPOLEON.

18730. - TO GENERAL CLARKE, DUKE OF FELTRE, 
MINISTER OF WAR, IN PARIS. 
Dresden. May 27, 1812. 


Duke de Feltre, send to Bayonne, to increase the reserve of General Lhuillier, the 3rd and 
the 105th, who were ordered to go to Nantes. 

As soon as the 5th provisional demi-brigade, composed of the 6th battalions of the 26th, 
66th and 82nd, and 3rd battalion of the 121st fort of more than 200 men, will be organized, you 
will direct this demi-brigade on Bayonne, where it will increase the reserve, since there are in the 
12th division the cohorts which meet at La Rochelle, which are sufficient for the guard of the 
islands and coasts. 

Order General Dumuy as soon as the cohorts are dressed he employs them in the defense 
of the islands and the coast of Provence, so that we have nothing to fear from the attempts of the 
enemy. 

Also give orders to General Miollis that as soon as his cohort is formed he will use them 
to garnish the most important points of the coast. 

NAPOLEON.

18731. - TO THE PRINCE OF NEUCHATEL AND WAGRAM, 
MAJOR GENERAL OF THE GREAT ARMY, TO DRESDEN. 
Dresden, May 27, 1812. 


Cousin, I ordered the general of artillery to assemble in Elbing, well hitched, two deck 
crews, and to have them driven in the first days about the height of Tilsit, as well as all that is 
necessary in ropes, anchors, etc., for the construction of a third bridge with the boats and the 
woods of the country; the existence of three bridges is therefore ensured. The engineer must also 
have three bridges on stilts, ropes and irons for two, whole woods for one, with bells and other 
utensils to be able to build them quickly. My intention is that you give orders to the engineers 
that these crews be shipped without delay and go to Elbing, where they can follow the 
movements of the army. It is important that in the first days of June all this be gathered and en 
route. Write to the commander of the engineers to get along with the governor of Gdansk for 
embarkation and departure at all. By this means, I will have for the Niemen three boat bridges 
and moreover three piling bridges.”

Page 440 


Give orders to the King of Westphalia, the Viceroy, the Duke of Elchingen, the Duke of 
Reggio, and the Prince of Eckmiihl to send you without delay the stall of all the boats, boats, 
tackle, etc. who are following their army corps. It is also necessary that the Poles harness what 
they have of these crews. Ask the commander of the engineers the condition of the boats, ropes, 
bells, etc., which are with the companies of the engineer's train, so that I have all my means on 
this object.

18732.-TO PRINCE OF NEUCHATEL AND WAGRAM,

My cousin, order the governor of Danzig to assemble the vice-admirals, the best captains 
and practical pilots, in order to know exactly the draft of the pass of Pillau and Frische Haff, and 
the ordinary course of the navigation of this gulf and the canals of Danzig and Konigsberg. I 
wish to be presented with a project to build on one of the Frische Haff points war-ships capable 
of defending the Frische Haff, the Pillau pass, and even the sea at Pillau.

18734.-INSTRUCTIONS FOR THE ARCHBISHOP OF MALINES (1), 
AMBASSADOR OF THE EMPEROR TO THE DUKE OF WARSAW, 
Dresden, May 28, 1812. 


The King of Saxony, by his decree of the 26th of this month, has created a kind of special 
government of the Duchy of Warsaw, and has conferred on him extraordinary powers for all that 
concerns the administration. 

It is with the Duke of Warsaw, and especially with the government, that he has invested 
with his authority, that the Archbishop of Malines will have to exercise his functions with the 
character of ambassador of the Emperor, 

This government resides in a council of ministers. 

The Council of Ministers was created by Article 8 of the Constitution; he has a president 
appointed by the king out of the members of the ministry. Business is discussed in this council to 
be presented to the King for approval. Such is its constitutional existence, and such are its 
attributions according to the constitution. 

Its existence and powers have been extended by the decree of the King, which confers 
upon it, in cases of urgency which present circumstances may present, all the full power 
conferred on the King by the constitutional statute. 

The exercise of this authority must be determined according to the present circumstances 
and according to the circumstances to come. 

In the present circumstances, the council must rule on all matters relating to the 
administration, and refer to the requests which will be made to it for the interest of the 
maintenance or the preservation of the allied armies. 

As for the maintenance of the allied armies, the first task which it must endeavor to 
complete with activity is to form stores and use all the means of the country to make the 
resources which it presents the subsistence of troops and the good state of all services, 

As for the preservation of the armies, it must take all the measures of high police which 
would be required for this purpose. He must also 





1)These instructions, signed by the Duke of Bassano, Minister of Foreign Relations, were 
dictated by the Emperor.“ 





441 


Page 442 


pay particular attention and zeal to all matters relating to the proper organization, recruitment, 
completion, arming, equipment and maintenance of all the corps and services of the Army of the 
Duchy. 

The ambassador of the Emperor to this government has given a first duty and an 
immediate duty to fulfill is to procure the execution of all that matters to the maintenance and 
preservation of the allied armies. He must, for this purpose, enter into all the details of the 
administration of the Duchy, of which it is proper that no one should be a stranger to him. It must 
support all the requests that will be made by the French military authorities and procure the 
quickest execution. He must correspond on this subject with the major-general of the army and 
with the generals commander-in-chief of the corps which compose it. 

The circumstances to come, during which the Council of Ministers will have to exercise 
its authority, are those which will procure for Poland its re-establishment as a nation, and the 
union of the members of this body politic who have been separated by violence. 

The council of ministers will give the first impulse, in summoning the diet by a 
proclamation; he has the power, since the king has delegated to him all his. 

The Diet convened, the Confederation of Poland will leave from its bosom and according 
to the mode of execution which will be indicated hereafter. The council of ministers will not 
have a necessarily active part in the insurrection; he must favor it with all his influence, with all 
his means; he must above all devote himself particularly to the administration and fulfill the 
important and difficult task of maintaining order in the midst of the insurrection itself, of 
regulating the levies, the armaments, the perception and the use of the resources of the 
Confederate countries. The ambassador will exercise on this part of the functions of the Council 
of Ministers the same supervision and the same superior direction which the exercise is entrusted 
to him in the present situation of things. 

The developments in which we have just entered do not yet include the part of his 
functions for which the Emperor relies most on his activity, sagacity, and enlightenment. It is for 
all that is due to the recovery and confederation of Poland that he will have to make use of it, to 
respond to the views of the Emperor. 

His first care must be to consult the Poles who know Poland best, its history, its national 
character, the powerful men and the provisions of the provinces currently occupied by Russia. 
After hearing them and appreciating them, he will form a sort of committee which he will chair 
and which he will consult*” 


442 


Page 443 


on the most suitable measures and the steps to be taken to give a great impetus to the nation. He 
will form an opinion of his own, and he will be able to judge what must be preserved or modified 
in the plan to be drawn. 

The decree by which the king gave extraordinary powers to the council of ministers 
would be first published. He would already begin to fix the attention of the Poles on their future. 
The council of ministers would then convoke the diet, as has been said above, by a proclamation 
drawn up in such a manner as to excite in the highest degree public attention and curiosity. It 
would be advisable, if it were possible, that its opening should take place from the 10th to the 
15th. 

When the diet was convened, she might receive a petition of eight or ten of the most 
important personages of Poland by name and existence in the Russian provinces, such as Prince 
Adam Czartoryski, the eldest of the Radziwill, Prince Jahlonowski, etc., etc. This petition should 
be written in a style that is already making a strong impression. 

Motions would be made in the diet to demand that in the present circumstances of the 
country a committee, appointed in the heart of the diet, be charged with proposing the means by 
which they require the use. This committee should be composed of the most distinguished and 
influential men; he would make a long report on the misfortunes of Poland, on the hope of the 
revival of the country, etc.; he would propose to proclaim the existence of the kingdom of Poland 
and the body of the Polish nation, which the force alone could have destroyed. He would 
establish that wherever Poles are united they have, like their fathers, the right to confederate for 
the safety of their country. He would propose a decree to declare Poland restored and to 
constitute the diet in the confederation of Poland. 

The dieticians of the Duchy of Warsaw would at once be summoned to join the 
confederation. All mixed subjects, all subjects of the Russian provinces would be allowed to 
confederate. The dieticians of the provinces which are still occupied by the Russians, not being 
able to meet publicly, could join secretly and send their adhesion to Warsaw. 

The report of the diet committee should be European and Polish, but focusing on 
developing the low intrigues, the violence that caused the ruin of the Polish homeland; Prussia 
and Austria should be carefully guarded, who, far from being opposed, advance in advance to the 
events which are being prepared. The report would be entirely directed against Russia.“ 


443 


Page 444 


One of the first acts of confederation would be a reminder of Poles, officers or soldiers, 
who serve the Russians. 

At the moment when the diet confederates, it would appoint a marshal and a council of 
the confederation. This marshal and this council, whose choice is extremely important, would do 
a few days after their proclamation. 

The diet could also name various confederation committees in different palatinates. These 
committees would also make proclamations. 

The proclamations, the speeches of the members of the Diet, the declarations or 
manifestos of each Confederate, etc., would be printed published and profusely disseminated. 

These various measures and the other provisions which the more perfect knowledge of 
the country will put in the case of proposing must be taken in such a way as to strike the opinion 
strongly. It is not enough for a proclamation; it requires multiplied acts. Proclamations, dietary 
reports, motions of the deputies, and, if possible, as many speeches, declarations, and particulars 
as there are individual adhesions to confederation, are necessary at the same time. It is necessary, 
finally, to publish every day pieces of all characters, of all styles, tending to the same end, but 
addressing the various sentiments and spirits. Thus we will succeed in putting the whole nation 
into a sort of intoxication. 

The committees of the various Palatinates will send agents everywhere to peddle all the 
printed documents and to introduce them into all parts of Poland. The Russians can not occupy 
the immensity of the country. We must create intelligences on their rear establish foci of 
insurrection wherever they will not be in force, finally place them in a situation similar to that 
where the French army was in Spain and the Republican army in the time of the Vendée and the 
chouannerie. This movement must be easily printed, and must become general as soon as it is 
supported by a military event of some importance. It is necessary then that all Poland is stirred 
up and that it enters entirely in insurrection. The only precautions to be kept are relative to the 
provinces still Austrian. One must not be offended by an ally who goes in front of these 
operations. 

As ambassador, the archbishop of Mechelen must take no ostensible part in these 
movements; but he must see everything, know everything, direct everything, animate everything. 


When the confederation will be formed, it will send line deputation - 
Page 444 





444 


Page 445 


to the Emperor to present him confederate sword and ask him for his protection. The Emperor 
will answer the deputies by praising the feelings that animate the Poles. He will tell them that it 
is only to their zeal, to their efforts, to their patriotism, that they may owe the revival of their 
country, This measure, which the Emperor proposes to keep, indicates enough to his ambassador 
the attitude he must have and the conduct he must take. 

These developments are sufficient to make him acquainted with the three objects which 
the Emperor has in view, confiding to him the mission with which he is clothed, 

First object. To have at Warsaw a French embassy which, by its rank, existence, and 
house, dominates all the authorities, whether French or Polish, civil or military. A general 
officer, of whatever rank, would hardly have dominated the generals of his rank, the ministers 
and the great of the country. An ambassador will succeed with all the less difficulty because his 
political character, his rank in the ecclesiastical hierarchy and his personal character will impose 
more. His house must be a center where all classes, all interests will come to fruition. He will 
give to all the complaints, to all the revelations and even to all the councils a natural and suitable 
organ. 

Second object. The ambassador must exercise not only a great influence, but a real 
authority over the administration. He attends council meetings. His rank will not be disputed, 
since his character authorizes him to give way only to the crowned heads and princes of the 
blood. Thus placed, his influence will naturally be exercised with authority and without 
wounding any self-esteem. Nothing will prevent him from interfering in all the details: first, 
because he will see in all his steps the authority of the Emperor, and that all resistance would be 
useless; secondly, because he will not worry about anyone's ambition: He must take advantage of 
his position, as has already been established, so that the duchy may be as useful as it can be to 
the army, and that he may concur, by all the resources he can offer, with that war, the 
consequences of which will be so happy for Poland. The duchy had long called for a central 
authority; it exists for the country by the somewhat royal power of which the council of ministers 
is clothed; it exists especially by the presence of the ambassador, who will bring together, as it 
were, ministers, generals, commanders, authorizing officers, etc. 

The third object contains all that is due to the insurrection and confederation of Poland. 

There is another point on which it is advisable to enter some"? 


445

details. Baron Bignon, resident of the Emperor, had established a service to obtain information 
on the composition, the state of situation, the location and the movements of the troops. With the 
aid of this information and the various ministerial correspondence, the State has been formed, a 
copy of which is attached. The ambassador must continue this work and look upon it as one of 
the most important cares entrusted to him. He will especially charge his first secretary. M. 
Bignon will inform him of his methods and means. The ambassador will give an even greater 
development. The necessary funds will be made available. It must have a dozen Polish agents at 
the various points of the frontiers, on the roads, in the neighboring countries of the Russian 
provinces, and even, if possible, in the enemy country. Warsaw will be the fixed and central 
point where everything will come to fruition, and a rapid correspondence will be established 
from this point with the office which follows these operations under my direction, at 
headquarters. The inhabitants of the country, put in motion with skill, questioned with 
discernment, must furnish the ambassador with a useful and abundant harvest. 

He will also be in touch with the prefects and sub-prefects of the frontier, with the 
Austrian authorities at Lemberg, with the ambassadors of France at Vienna and at 
Constantinople, with the consuls of the Emperor at Jassy and Bucharest. He will invite them to 
correspond with him and to communicate to him all that may make known the plans and 
movements of the enemy on the various countries where his operations may be extended. 

Baron Bignon will be ordered to remain in Warsaw for as long as the ambassador needs 
to receive from him the local information of which he has perfect knowledge. The ambassador 
will have to choose a Polish interpreter and a Russian interpreter. Mr. Bignon will be able to 
direct him in this choice, which is of great importance. 

The four auditors attached to his embassy (1) are versed in several parts of the 
administration; they will be for the ambassador of the species of bureau chiefs for the various 
services. 

The ambassador, upon his arrival at Warsaw, will inform the Council of Ministers of the 
character with which he is clothed. He will proceed with his installation. He will take office 
immediately, but he will not let anything print until he receives new orders.

18735. - TO GENERAL CLARKE, DUKE OF FELTRE, 
MINISTER OF WAR, IN PARIS. 
Dresden. May 28, 1812. 


Duke de Feltre, I refer you the Spanish correspondence. 

Write to General Lhuillier to keep an eye on San Sebastian, and always have 3,000 men 
in his hand to direct them to this place, if it needs to be rescued. 

It is necessary to have a lot of people in Bayonne; activate the march of the 3rd and the

General Lhuillier can always have a great deal of strength, to be able to act according to the 
circumstances. Reunite a thousand cavalry men, drawn from the depots of the Spanish army, and

to train and harness a battery of six pieces of cannon. 

Prescribe to General Lhuillier to keep his troops in the Bastan Valley, at Bayonne, at

18740. - NOTE TO THE PRINCE MAJOR GENEHAL, IN DRESDEN.

The Major General will write to the commander of the artillery that I ordered the siege 
crew to descend on their boats to Elbing, to follow the movement of the army over the Frische 
Haff; but this crew must leave Elbing only when they receive a special order. 

There must also be, brought to Elbing and embarked, an attraction of ropes, anchors and 
all that is necessary to build a bridge with boats of the country. 

We will ship all these materials if it is not possible to hitch them. There must be, on board 
the Frische - Haff, two deck crews on stilts; it is necessary that before 6 they are in Elbing on 
boats ready to sail. 

20,000 quintals of flour, 2,000 quintals of rice and 500,000 rations of biscuit must be 
ready to be sailed from Elbing by the 6th at the latest. Finally the engineer's siege crew must also 
be ready to leave with the artillery crew. 

Write to the General Rapp that it is necessary that he ensures that all the following orders 
are punctually executed. 

Artillery. - The artillery must have put in operation two crews of deck with boats and a 
drawn crew, which must be returned to Elbing in the first days of June; ropes, anchors; 
horseshoes for a deck crew to be made with boats from the country, which must be harnessed, if 
possible, and, if it is not possible, it must be embarked at Elbing on Frische Haff.*””

18743.-TO THE COUNT COLLIN DE SUSSY,

Count de Sussy, the taxation of wheat by the prefect of Caen at 33 francs per hectolitre is

to tell me a word about the motives that decided it. approve that you have given him the 100 
francs from the sale of the flours; but I think that the best operation that the municipality of Caen 
should do would be to bring wheat from the department of Roer. Give permission, making sure 
that wheat comes from the Roer. By employing 100,000 ecus for this object, it is the best way to 
loan 100,000 ecus to the inhabitants of Caen. If you want to use Vanlerberghe for this operation, 
I do not object to it.

18752. - TO EUGENE NAPOLEON, VICE-KING OF ITALY, 
COMMANDING THE 4th AND 6th COPS OF THE BIG ARMY, PLOCK. 
Posen, June Ist, 1812. 


My Son, I receive your letter of May 31st, from your aide-de-camp who has passed 
through Thorn. Since there is no Thorn at Plock but seven hours, come and see me at Thorn on 
the 3rd or 4th. 

There is no problem in leaving a hospital of 300 patients at Plock; they will join after 
Thorn. I wrote to you in great detail today to allow you to tap into the shops in Wloclawek, grind 
flour and direct it to Willenberg. 

I ordered a horse-lift at Glogau: it will be necessary for the Italian carters you have with 
you to return to Glogau. 

At Glogau I had some oxen sent to the Italian crew battalion, which is going well; you are 
wrong to despair of it; I hope it will be before the 10th at Plock. If General Guyon passes 4 or 5, 
he can easily join you, and the marching battalions be dissolved. If the cadres belong to the five 
battalions, it will be appropriate to send them back. I authorized you to enter into markets to 
bring flour to Willenberg; when you send twenty thousand quintals, it would not be too much. I 
suppose you will not eat your oxen and keep them until you are moving. 

Make me pass the recognitions of the countries you have visited. 

The staff here has no trace of the movement of the 2nd battalion of the Mediterranean. 
Send me the itinerary of this battalion, which, being composed of refractory conscripts, does not 
belong to any army corps. As for the Ist Battalion, if it left on May 19th, it will arrive at Glogau 
around June 15th. I order him to keep a garrison at Glogau; the men will be very tired, I wish that 
they rest entirely there; shouted I will be able to remove the two battalions that are cut. 

Make convoys talk every day about Plock and Wloclawek to maintain your handling. I 
suppose that“

you have cartridges, and you will not wait at the last moment to empty the caissons of cartridges 
into the caissons, and after return the caissons when the corps goes forward, which would be too

18753.- TO EUGENE NAPOLEON, VICE-KING OF ITALY, 
COMMANDING THE 4th AND 6th CORPS OF THE BIG ARMY, PLOCK. 
Posen, June Ist, 1812, 


My son, I have named General Dessolle for your chief of staff. Brigadier General 
Plauzonne could be the Chief of Staff of the Duke of Abrantes. You will keep General 
Charpentier a few days, until you are certain of being satisfied with General Dessolle, then I will 
place General Charpentier in a government. 

As long as you have only the 4th corps and the Bavarians, you can always keep the 
command of the 4th corps at once; but, as it may happen that you sometimes have three corps 
d'armee under your command, it would be proper for the duke d'Abrantes to have a separate 
staff, but that does not bother you to give your orders immediately to the 4th corps, while you are 
there and you have only two army corps.

18755. - TO JEROME NAPOLEON, KING OF WESTPHALIA, 
COMMANDING THE Sth, 7th AND 8th CORPS OF THE GREAT ARMY IN WARSAW. 
Posen, June Ist, 1812. 


Brother, I have been in Posen since yesterday. You have received a letter from me 
containing general instructions, which must have been preceded by orders of the General Staff to 
be executed from the Ist to the 7th of June. 

The authorizing officer of the right will have informed you of the measures which I have 
prescribed to the intendant general for the supply of Pultusk, Modlin, and Warsaw. It is 
necessary that there be 10,000 quintals of flour at Pultusk and 25,000 at Modlin for the supply of 
the army which will follow the course of the Narew; it must have been in addition to 25,000 
quintals in Warsaw. I have these supplies pulled from the different shops along the Vistula River 
from Plock. The Authorizing Officer will also have made known to you my agenda for the 16th 
Battalion Crew and the measures taken to have 600 wagons in the country following your corps. 
Press the execution of these measurements. We are in a season*™ 


462 


Page 463 


where horses can not perish from hunger; the grass must already be good to eat. 

I am probably leaving this night for Thorn, where I will be tomorrow, and after, and hear 
from you. 

I want you to recognize the Omulew, Pultusk, Ostrolenka, Nowogrod, Lomza; but if you 
go so far, you have to go incognito. 

Hold an officer at Tykocin and one at Terespol vis-a-vis Brzesc to report to you on what 
is happening in Bialystok and on the Russian border. Get the line from Johannisburg to 
Nowogrod. Accredit by all means the noise of your march on Lublin. Accredit also the sound of 
my prompt arrival in Warsaw. Let General Reynier make the rumor that he saw the bridge of 
Pulawi pass to Zamosc, inform the commander of Zamosc, that arrangements be made to receive 
this body. You will order the officer you will observe at Tykocin to send reports on Osterode and 
Thorn, and by courier, whenever it matters. The department whose county seat is in Siedlce must 
provide you with resources. It is important that you have your twenty days of food independently 
from the shops of Pultusk, Ostrolenka and Modlin.

18758. - TO GENERAL CLARKE, DUKE OF FELTRE, 
MINISTER OF WAR, IN PARIS. 
Thorn. June 4, 1812. 


One can not be more dissatisfied than I am about the two sapper companies that were on 
the island of Elba. They are naked. How could the authorizing officer let them go in this state? 
You will see that by an order of the day I have ordered an inquiry on this subject. 

I am extremely unhappy that the Authorizing Officer Jacqueminot left the army when he 
began to know the service and without waiting for the arrival of the person who was to replace 
him. If I had not remembered the services of his father, senator, I would have loved him at the 
command of the army and dishonored him. We are asking to come to the army and not to fight. 
Give him the order that in a month he has joined, and make the senator understand the danger his 
son has run and the bad prejudice that it leaves in my mind. 

NAPOLEON. 

According to the copy. Deposit of the war. 


18759. - NOTE TO THE PRINCE MAJOR GENERAL AT THORN. 
Thorn, June 4th, 1812. 


There will be in Thorn hospitals for 1,200 patients, namely: the town hall for 600; three 
of the existing hospitals, 300; and convents for 300. The Intendant General will be given these 
establishments during the day. The feverish hospital will be immediately suppressed, which is 
very bad, and, as there are only 300 men, they will be placed without delay in a part of the town 
hall. The other part of this house may be evacuated only in eight or ten days. The municipality 
will move elsewhere. A hospital in Wloclawek will be established in a convent and a house that 
has already been*™ 


464 


Page 465 


assigned to this purpose. This hospital will be assigned to the 4th Corps and the Bavarians. The 
5th, 7th, and 8th corps will send their patients to Warsaw hospitals; 3rd Corps and Guard at 
Thorn; the 2nd, at Marienburg; the Ist, in Elbing. 

It was ordered to establish a hospital in Danzig in Oliva Abbey. This establishment is 
very important, because the air of Oliva is very healthy, an advantage which does not exist at 
Danzig. 

It will be convenient to establish a hospital at Osterode, one at Konigsberg, one at 
Wehlau, one at Soldau, and one at Willenberg for the 4th Corps and the Bavarians; one to 
Pultusk for the 5th Corps. The Thorn Hospital will be maintained by army funds. 

The Major-General will give all the necessary orders to the Intendant General, the 
Commanding Officer, and the Commander of the Engineers, so that Thorn's hospitals may be 
established without delay. 

NAPOLEON. 

From the original. Deposit of the war.

18764. - TO PRINCE OF NEUCHATEL AND WAGRAM, 
MAJOR GENERAL OF THE GREAT ARMY, AT THORN. 
Thorn, June 4th, 1812. 


Cousin, it seems to me that there is anarchy in the place of Thorn. I do not see the 
necessity of keeping as commanders a French general and a Polish general; the Polish general 
seems to me sufficient. It is necessary to give him as deputies the French officers who are 
necessary, so that there is to Thorn only one commander, having the proper means. See to 
organize this staff in the morning. 

I have just written to you to keep at Thorn the Wurtemberger battalion which was to 
leave it today. When the battalion of the 3rd regiment of the Vistula, which I ordered to form at 
Posen, has arrived at Thorn, it will be possible, according to the circumstances, to dispose of the 
Wurtemberger battalion and to have it rejoined. 

Charge an adjutant commander to remain at Thorn for the inspection of the depots, stores 
and cavalry depots which are at Thorn, and to correspond exactly with you on the service of the 
army, but under the military orders of the commandant of the place. As soon as the service of the 
place of Thorn is assured by the Wurtemberger battalion, you will order the depot of the 5th 
Polish regiment to leave Thorn to go on Danzig by the left bank, so that it does not interfere with 
our movements.

18768. - TO EUGENE NAPOLEON, VICE-KING OF ITALY, 
COMMANDING THE 4th AND 6th CORPS OF THE GREAT ARMY, AT THORN. 
Thorn, June 5, 1812. 


My Son, you will receive from the Major General orders for your movement on 
Rastenburg. This is only a first movement, because it has to continue on Seyny, my intention 
being to gather there, on the 17th and the 18th, all your army corps, while the Ist, the 2nd, the 
3rd, and the 4th. Guard will be gathered at Wilkowyszki, that the king of Westphalia will be at 
Pultusk with the 5th and 8th corps, the 7th corps on Praga, and the Austrians arrived at Lublin 
already on us. It is easy for you to understand that in this position, if the enemy took the 
offensive to march on Warsaw, if he debouched by Bialystok, you would find himself on his 
right flank, and that, if he debouched by Olitta, you would be on his left flank. If he debouched 
on you, you would rely on the army; hence, the need for your corps to change line of operation. 
He can still keep that of Plock for a long time. But as soon as the enemies begin their movement, 
on the 18th, your line will have to go to Thorn and even to Marienburg. So, assuming the King of 
Westphalia withdraws to Modlin, your line is not compromised and you can maneuver, on the 
contrary, quietly to place yourself on the enemy's line of operation. 

NAPOLEON. 

According to the copy comm. by S. A. I. The Duchess of Leuchtenberg. 


18769. - TO JEROME NAPOLEON, KING OF WESTPHALIA, 
COMMANDING THE 5th, 7th AND 8th CORPS OF THE GREAT ARMY IN WARSAW. 
Thorn. June 5, 1812. 


Brother, I receive your letter from your aide-de-camp. The major-general writes you to 
let you know the plan of operations you have to do. In this business, and in such a great theater, 
one succeeds only on a well-established plan and with very good agreement. It is therefore 
necessary to study your orders well and to do here neither more nor less than what one tells you, 
especially with regard to combined movement.* 





469 


Page 470 


Announce that I am going to see the deposit of Danzig, and that immediately afterwards I 
return to pass the review of the corps of the viceroy, that of the Poles at Pultusk, and at Warsaw 
that of the two other corps. Make Warsaw do anything that can give credence to this news. 
Establish a good police at the borders, and make sure nothing happens in Russia, neither couriers 
nor posts, under any pretext whatsoever. Everything that comes will have to be sent to 
headquarters. Order Prince Poniatowski to correspond with the Viceroy and General Rapp, to let 
them know what is new. 

It is also necessary that your three corps correspond with the major general. It is the 
major general who must correspond only with you; but the commanders of these corps must send 
exactly the details of their position to the major general. 

It seems that there is enough wheat in Modlin; what is missing is flour. Pultusk, 
Ostrolenka and Warsaw must have enough means of food. I gave all the necessary orders for it. 
Let me know how far, in the months of June and July, the Narew is navigable. Is it carrying boat 
right now to Nowogrod and Lomza? 

I believe I have made known to you what you have best to do naked beginning of the 
campaign: first, make believe that you will enter Volyn and keep the enemy as much as possible 
on the party, while, overflowing on his extreme right, I will have won twelve or fifteen steps in 
the direction of Petersburg, I will be on his right wing, I will pass the Niemen and remove Villa, 
which is the first object of the campaign. 

The movement of the Prince of Schwarzenberg on Lublin will not fully demonquer this 
design, since the enemy will be able to go black, which, assembled at Zamosc, we will leave 
from there to enter Volhynia. 

When this operation is unmasked, the enemy will take one of two parties: either he will 
rally in the interior of his states to find himself in force to fight, or he will take the offensive 
himself. Thus, while the extremity of the right is overflowing, it could march on Warsaw, either 
by opening on Ostrolenka and Pultusk, either by opening on Nur and Sierock, or by coming 
straight into Praga. All the depots of my army must be assembled in Modlin, but slowly and 
without precipitation. Your body is destined to defend Warsaw; and for this purpose, the 5th 
corps at Ostrolenka, the 7th corps at Sierock and Praga, your neighborhood*”° 


470 


Page 471 


General to Pultusk, this is the position you will receive order to take towards the 10th. The 7th 
corps, returning from Lublin, will put your whole corps in your hand; and then, if the enemy 
attacks by Ostrolenka or between Bug and Narew, the Viceroy's corps is on its right flank; if he 
attacks by Brzcsc and Zamosc, or if he comes straight to Praga with considerable forces, the 8th 
corps first, then the 7th, and after the 7th the Austrians, guard Praga and Warsaw. Modlin and 
Sierock will be covered with the 5th and 8th corps, and later with the 5th, 7th and 8th corps. 
While the enemy is on the ramparts of Pruga and on the banks of the Vistula, merely supporting 
Modlin, Sierock, and Pultusk, you will find yourself in the army, and by my movement to the 
right all his army would be overflowed and thrown into the Vistula. 

It is not out of place that the National Sardinian of Warsaw should be organized, at least 
several battalions; they can only be useful to the service. 

Besides, I will always find myself in a position to be able to give you greater 
explanations and to add developments to that general instruction. 

If the enemy took the offensive abruptly and General Reynier had some difficulty in 
returning to Warsaw, which is hardly probable, you would support him by the 4th corps of 
cavalry and the 8th corps. But, in general, you must calculate as probable that all your army 
corps will end up wearing Pultusk on Ostrolcnka, Nur, Bialystok or Grodno. It is necessary that 
the bridgehead of Pultusk be completed and well armed, as well as the works of Sierock. Or 
make sure that there is a bridgehead on the left bank at Sierock, it is necessary to put it in order. 

I will keep the right bank; but it is possible that I abandon the whole left bank, although I 
will leave it only to superior forces, and not to a division of. 12 to 13,000 men, not to some 
Cossack regiments. 

NAPOLEON. 

According to the copy comm. by S. A. I. Prince Jerome.

18771. - TO MARSHAL DAVOUT, PRINCE OF ECKMUHL, 
COMMANDING THE Ist CORPS OF THE GREAT ARMY, AT ELBING. 
Thorn, June 5th, 1812. 


Cousin, I receive your letters of June 4th. My intention was indeed to occupy Pillau only 
when your corps was in Konigsberg. All that has been done to make me think that I attach great 
importance to Pillau is contrary to my intentions. The artillery general ordered the deck crew to 
meet at Marienburg; the island of Nogat has appeared a more advantageous position. Since then, 
this deck crew, who is under the command of General Eble, has been ordered to go by the 
shortest way to Heilsberg, he must leave tomorrow. The Danube battalion and the crew of sailors 
leave Danzig to join him. Engineering Park also left to join him, from Thorn on the 3rd; which 
will bring together, under the command of General Eble, an important material which will 
include all that is necessary. Being informed that the siege crew did not have enough water to 
come from Danzig to Elbing, I ordered him to come to Dirschau and from there to Marienburg, 
he is there more secure. This siege crew must not arrive at Konigsberg before receiving new 
orders. I was glad to know where he is, out of all danger; my intention is that he leave it only 
when I have unmasked my movement. 

I think the guns for the Baden troops are on the way; their government sends them 
French-style rifles. The battalion you left at Dirschau can go to Danzig to garrison there, or to 
garrison Marienburg. 

I delayed my departure to see the Guard, put the affairs of the administration in order, 
give the last orders, and set everything in motion. I intend to leave this night and go through the 
left bank. I will be in Marienburg tomorrow, where I intend to see you. You have to get moving 
on the 7th; you will receive orders from the Major General to occupy the banks of the Pregel. 
Your corps will have to march in columns to occupy the points of Insterburg and Wehlau, at the 
same time as Konigsberg. The 20,000 quintals of flour that I have shipped must not be 
unloaded*”” 





472 


Page 473 


to Konigsberg, but to turn on the Pregel, when my troops have arrived there, and be disembarked 
at Insterburg, where I intend to establish a large center of provisions and handling. The boats will 
return to Konigsberg for food. 

I sent General Hogendorp to command Konigsberg. Appoint a very reliable officer to 
command Pillau under his orders. The pass being only 400 toises, there is nothing to fear, and 
the entry of enemy buildings is impossible. 

Bring me to Marienburg the state of all the flours that are available in Elbing: I would 
like to send as much as I can to the Pregel. The Duke of Taranto must have arrived at 
Konigsberg, and the Prussian corps will be on the 9th or 10th at Labiau. General Kleist's brigade 
crossed the Vistula and is on the march to join the Prussians. You will see from the attached 
letter that General Lepin was against my intentions by sending an officer to Memel. You should 
not have suffered it; it was a big mistake. 

NAPOLEON. 

From the original comm. by lime the Marechal Princess Eckmiihl.

18774. - TO MARSHAL DAVOUT, PRINCE OF ECKMUHL, 
COMMANDING THE Ist CORPS OF THE GREAT ARMY, IN ELBING, 
Danzig, June 8, 1812, 


Cousin, I chatted a moment with your officer. He told me that the Niemen was 60 toises 
wide at Tilsit; that he had not measured this river at Kovno; that, however, he had made the 
recognition of it, and had judged its breadth only by evaluation. I did not think it expedient to 
hear it more, I send it back to you. If this officer is accustomed to doing his reconnaissance and 
making a mistake of two-thirds, he will often mislead you. 

NAPOLEON. 

From the original comm. by the Marechal Princess Eckmiihl,

18781. - TO THE PRINCE OF NEUCHATEL AND WAGRAM, 
MAJOR GENERAL OF THE GREAT ARMY, IN DANZIG. 
Danzig, June 10, 1812. 


Cousin, write to the King of Westphalia that I suppose that, as I have ordered, the head of 
General Reynier's corps will have arrived at Lublin; that as soon as the heads of the Austrians 
have arrived at Zamosc, which I suppose will take place from the 15th to the 18th, it will be 
necessary for General Reynier to retrogress by forced marches on Praga; that all the 8th corps is 
on Sierock and Pultusk; that the headquarters of the King be carried to Pultusk on the 14th, and 
to Ostrolenka on the 17th, and that the headquarters of Prince Poniatowski be taken to Nowogrod 
on the 18th, occupying the line of Pisek; these movements must take place only from the 15th to 
the 18th; that General Saint-Cyr, with the 6th corps, will be the 16th at Ortelsburg, and will have 
his light cavalry at Johannisburg: the Viceroy will be at Rastenburg; the 3rd cavalry corps at 
Lotzen and Oletzko; that, at this time, the 7th Corps should as soon as possible repass the Narew 
to come and support the 5th and 8th Corps, leaving, however, strong garrisons at Praga, Modlin 
and along the Vistula, until the Austrians, having arrived at Praga, may cover Warsaw and the 
left of the Vistula. 

If the enemy took the offensive on the right of the Narew, whether the King took the line 
of the Pisek, or he backed down on that of the Omulew, the enemy would lend the flank to the 
Viceroy, who would fall to his right. If it was between the Narew and Bug that the enemy came 
to make an offensive move, the 5th and 8th corps could lead by Ostrolenka and Pultusk and fall 
to the right of the enemy. While the enemy would thus sink into operations that would lead to 
nothing, since in the final analysis he would find the Vistula, he would have lost many marches, 
and the left of our army, which would have passed the Niemen, would arrive on his side and on 
his rear before he could get up. What if, on the contrary,**° 


Page 481 


the enemy makes no movement, the King must threaten him, by movements of light troops, to go 
on Grodno and Bialystok, which he must for this purpose advance his pontoons and openly 
announce this project; but the general plan being to refuse the right and to advance the left, it 
would not really be until after the left would have passed and this movement would have had its 
effect on the enemy cantonments of Grodno and Bialystok, that the right should would pursue 
the enemy, in order to occupy him and prevent him from going all the way to the left, without 
ever compromising himself; that it is therefore indispensable to study the positions carefully, not 
to engage in a skirmish and to be well acquainted with the general plan of operations; that he 
must correspond often with the Viceroy. 

You will tell him that [am going to Konigsberg from my person; that I will probably be 
on the 15th at Insterburg; that he must address his letters by Rastenburg, from which the viceroy 
will give them a later direction; that he must always make the rumor that I arrive.

18782. - TO EUGENE NAPOLEON, VICE-KING OF ITALY, 
COMMANDING THE 4th AND 6th CORPS OF THE GREAT ARMY, AT WILLENBERG. 
Danzig, June 10, 1812. 


My son, I see from your letter that you will not have arrived until the 18th at Rastenburg. 
The Ist corps will be at Insterburgle 13; the 3rd corps will be in Gerdauen; the headquarters will 
be at Schippenbeil, the Grand Headquarters of the Cavalry (King of Naples) at Gumbinnen; 2nd 
Cavalry Corps at Goldap. 

I leave tomorrow morning to be at daybreak in Konigsberg. I will stay there on the 13th, 
the 14th, the 15th; I think I'll be on the 16th at Insterburg. You will find yourself in the position 
of Rastenburg, twenty leagues from Konigsberg, twenty-four leagues from Nowogrod, and fifty 
leagues from Warsaw. General Saint-Cyr, meeting at Ortelsburg, will be less than eighteen 
leagues from Nowogrod and fifteen leagues from Johannisburg. 

It is necessary that you know what Prince Poniatowski is doing and the news he has, in 
order to be constantly informed of what is new on the right of the army. 

After the 14th, if you had important news, you would have to“! 


481 


Page 482 


send them to me from two directions: Insterburg and Konigsberg. We are still at peace: with 
Russia; however, here we are at the last moment. If the enemy took the offensive on you, you 
would be supported by General Saint-Cyr; the 2nd Corps, the 3rd Corps, the Guard, which will 
be at Schippenbeil the 11th and even the 1st Corps, which is on the Pregel, would easily come to 
your aid. 

Change your line of operation; do not take it by Plock and Willenberg, but by Thorn and 
Osterode on Rastenburg, that should not stop you from drawing the resources you can get from 
Plock. 

If the enemy took the offensive on the Ist corps, you would receive orders on what you 
would have to do. If he took the offensive on your right, that is to say on the 5th corps, which up 
to this day is still behind the Omulew; you would fall easily on the right flank of the enemy. If it 
were necessary, the 5th Corps could make retrogressive marches to join the 7th and 8th corps 
and draw the enemy to Pultusk. You could, if necessary, be supported by some corps of the left 
and fall on the right of the enemy. Hear this with the King of Westphalia and Prince 
Poniatowski. 

The march of the army is a movement that I am doing on my left, constantly refusing my 
right, since the 7th corps, which is going partly on Lublin to make believe to the enemy that it 
will meet with the Austrians to march in Volyn, on the 12th, will quickly relocate to Warsaw, 
making available the 8th corps, which will strengthen the 5th. The 7th Corps itself will soon be 
available by the arrival of the Austrians on Praga. So that around the 20th, Ist, 2nd, and 3rd 
Corps, the Imperial Guard and two cavalry corps will maneuver to pass the Niemen, either 
between Kovno and Grodno, or between Kovno and Tilsit. The 4th and 6th corps, which are 
under your command, and a corps of cavalry, forming the center, will maneuver, having their 
lines of operation on Thorn and the lower Vistula, to be always bound with my left. Worry the 
enemy on the side of Grodno, and when the passage is made, come on forced marches to cross 
the same bridge or pass over Olitta and Meretch, if the enemy does not resist. I will give orders 
for that. Around the 18th, the 5th and the 8th corps will move to Nowogrod, a few days later, 
they will be supported by the 7th corps. This line is destined to keep Warsaw, to remain always 
supported by the Narew, always communicating with you by its left, but keeping its line of 
operation on Warsaw; and in case the enemy was so strong on Nowogrod that the King of 
Westphalia felt*®”

to retreat a few steps, he would retreat on Pultusk, and the enemy would lend his right flank to

I make known to you the various combinations of my march, so that you know well the

18784. - TO THE PRINCE OF NEUCHATEL AND WAGRAM, 
MAJOR GENERAL OF THE GREAT ARMY, IN DANZIG. 
Danzig. June 11, 1812. 


Cousin, write to the King of Westphalia that, in his letter of the 8th, he makes it known 
that the corps of Bagration returns to Brzesc and that the corps of Essen meets at Bialystok; that 
it is unfortunate that the King has not, in place of his simple analysis, cast off the original 
reports, so that we may compare them with those we have. Tell him that the letter you wrote him 
on the 10th, makes him sufficiently aware of my intentions; but we are. so remote that it is now 
up to him to maneuver, according to the circumstances, in the general spirit of his instructions; 
that the movement of General Bagration on Brzesc may have the object of regaining the marches 
which I have upon him, in order to be able to defend the passage of the Niemen, and to be able to 
cover Vilna with all the forces united to give a battle there; that, if he perceives that the 
movements of the enemy have this goal and that Bagration, of Brzesc, goes back on Grodno, he 
must himself accelerate his movements to go on Ostrolenka and Nowogrod with his army corps 
and always be able to oppose the enemy's left, that is, Bagration's army; if, on the contrary, the 
enemy, perceiving that I come to overtake him by his right, wishes to take the offensive on my 
flanks, a hypothesis which has been calculated in time, and wishes to go either from Brzesc to 
Praga, or from Bialystok on Pultusk, in this case he must also activate the passage of his forces 
on Pultusk and Ostrolenka, in order to keep always the right bank of the Narew and maintain his 
communications with the viceroy; that the viceroy has orders to always lean on my left; that his 
line of operation is on Thorn; that the King of Westphalia must always keep his line of operation 
on Modlin, keep himself always well united, correspond with the viceroy, so that he may fall on 
the right flank of the enemy; that this attacking movement of the enemy, which is natural enough 
and has been foreseen from the beginning, can in no way influence my offensive operations; that 
the important thing is that the right does not commit itself against superior forces and maneuver 
together, from position to position; that if the greater part of the Russian army were to be 
attacked by flank, it could never happen on the right, which would always have for refuge the 
entrenched camp of Modlin and the left bank of the Vistula; but as soon as such a movement on 
the part 


484 


Page 485 


Russians would be decided I would fall with all my army on their right flank and on their rear; 
that it is very difficult for the enemy to expose himself to total loss; that, if he does so, the march 
which has just been traced must make known to the King how he must act. 

Send an intelligent aide-de-camp to Prince Poniatowski; let him come back to 
Schippenbeil and bring us news from the right and what we think on this side. Tell this officer to 
make sure if the enemy wants to take the offensive, or spin to regain his right. 

NAPOLEON 

From the original, Depot of War. 


18785. - TO EUGENE NAPOLEON, VICE-KING OF ITALY, 
COMMANDING THE 4th AND 6th CORPS OF THE GREAT ARMY IN ORTELSBURG. 
Danzig, June 11, 1812, 


My son, I will be at Konigsberg tomorrow. I sent you yesterday an officer of the order; I 
still send you an officer before leaving. My little headquarters is going to Schippenbeil. I 
suppose you have news from Warsaw. I ordered you to send officers directly to Prince 
Poniatowski and to send also to the King of Westphalia, in order to hear from the right. My latest 
news from Warsaw is 8; it was then said that Bagration's army was coming up on Brzesc, from 
Lutsk where he was, and that of Essen was on Bialystok. You must have had accurate news of 
that of Essen by Prince Poniatowski and the prefect of Lomza. It seems to me that I asked you to 
have staff officers with respect to Grodno and Lomza. I suppose you are well acquainted with the 
course you must follow; instruct General Saint-Cyr. Assuming the true news that Bagration is 
going back to Brzesc, I do not think he can be reunited before the 16th. As for Essen, as he was a 
short distance from Bialystok, if he wanted to meet there, he will have been very soon. In this 
movement, the enemy can have two goals: or to run quickly north to defend the Niemen, seeing 
that I have already won many steps, and try to arrive to cover Vilna, and then your role is to be 
the same as that of the army; or else, from Bialystok and Brzesc, he will take the offensive by 
falling on my flank, and debouching from Bialystok on Ostrolenka, from Brzesc to Warsaw, and 
perhaps even from Grodno.*® 





Page 486 


I made known to you in these circumstances what you had to do, which is always to support you 
on the left, to change your line of operation and to make sure that the enemy does not begin 
anything. But nevertheless I continue in my project, and, if he embarks himself thus, I will find 
myself having passed the Niemen and be on his rear. 

Please write to Prince Poniatowski and the King of Westphalia to know if all these 
movements are well understood. The King, with his three corps on the right, having his line of 
operation on Modlin, must beat the enemy if the enemy is inferior, and dispute the ground if he 
is stronger. Assuming that the enemy with considerable forces was stubborn in his movement, I 
would not see any objection to the King withdrawing into the entrenched camp of Modlin, 
occupying Praga and the bank of the Vistula. Your operation liana lying on Thorn, you would 
have nothing to fear from this state of things. 

As soon as I know the plans of the enemy, I will get closer to my person from 
Schippenbeil, in order to be better able to give orders. 

But, I recommend it to you, arrange the pickets so as to frequently have news of Prince 
Poniatowski and of the right. Independently of the posts, which are often badly mounted, your 
officers may pick up picket horses placed every three leagues. 

NAPOLEON 

According to the copy comm. by S. A. 1. The Duchess of Leuchtenberg,

18788. - TO THE PRINCE OF NEUCHATEL AND WAGRAM, 
MAJOR GENERAL OF THE GREAT ARMY IN DANZIG, KOENIGSBERG. 
Konigsberg, June 13, 1812. 


Cousin, I am sending you a letter from the authorizing officer Deschamps, dated this day, 
which makes known the bad situation in which the second corps is in terms of subsistence. The 
fault lies entirely with the Duke of Reggio and the authorizing officer. If the duke had written to 
you every day to inform you of his situation, and if the authorizing officer had likewise written 
to the intendant general, one would have known what to expect and provided for. Write to the 
Duke of Reggio that he does not render any account. Give him the order to send his contributions 
twice a day; to write what is new and what is relative to the administration; that his corps is the 
only one we do not know**’ 





487 


Page 488 


not every day the situation. Also write to his chief of staff to express my dissatisfaction: the 
moment I knew the shortage where the 2nd corps was, I ordered that, independently of the 4,000 
quintals which were granted to him at Wehlau by My decision of this morning was to-day sent 
2,000 of Konigsberg to it, and that another 4,000 quintals were also at the disposal of the Duke 
of Reggio at Konigsberg: I still order that 200,000 rations of biscuit and 40,000 rations of biscuit 
bread be made available to him; but it is essential that he send cars. Tell this marshal that he must 
go to Wehlau, and from there follow the movement of the army; that there will only be one day 
left in Wehlau; it is therefore important that he take steps to have all these supplies, which will 
provide him twenty or twenty-five days of food. 

NAPOLEON. 

From the original. Deposit of the war.
